nodes.title: [P00] Lux Didi program tracker
nodes.body:
## What this is

The program tracker for the Lux Didi build: five implementation lanes, 13 epics and 106 work items. This repository is the planning home. No application exists yet, and every behavior is proposed until its issue records evidence.

## Lanes

- A, runtime and local execution (E01, E02) and portable service (E11): A01 to A24. Service stack, versioned contracts, local service, store, durable jobs, replaceable providers, tool turns, action receipts, harness adapters, MCP transport, diagnostics and measurement.
- B, evidence and persona (E03, E04): B01 to B18. Source identity, transcript originals and external resolution, recall, preferences, correction and suppression, consolidation, public persona specification, private customization, memory inspection and recall evaluation.
- C, accounts and trust (E05, E06), channels and authority epochs (E12): C01 to C23. Per-account identity and OAuth, Google, chat and Trello adapters, grants and the effect broker, capability registry, provider egress policy, adverse security tests, revocation and optional company integration.
- D, commitments and proactivity (E07, E08): D01 to D18. Commitment lifecycle, promise extraction with attribution, prioritization, daily planning, reminders, interruption policy, follow-through and calibration.
- E, native experience (E09, E10) and client surfaces (E13): F01 to F22. The F prefix keeps leaves from colliding with epic ids. Hotkey and menu bar, text and duplex voice, notifications, onboarding and review surfaces, computer control, lifecycle, packaging, companion and portability.

## Milestone entry points

- M0, proof and contracts: start at A01 (service stack decision record) and A02 (versioned contracts and fixtures), in parallel with A03, A04, B01, B07, B12, B17, C01, C02, C14 and D01. Exit when the service stack is recorded and implemented as the loopback service seam, the contract package is consumed by concrete storage, provider and domain contract consumers, and no task claims a figure it has not recorded. MCP transport is deferred to M3 and is not an M0 exit condition.
- M1, useful daily loop: A05 to A08 and A15 to A18; A08 (action receipts) and C12 (grant broker) are first-loop prerequisites, not late hardening. B02 to B05, B08, B09, B11, B13 and B16; C03, C04, C05, C12, C15, C16 and C17; D02 to D10 and D17; F01, F02, F09, F10, F13 and the Stage A pilot install in F15. Exit when the first-loop acceptance scenarios pass on the Stage A pilot with the real surfaces they name, including the essential injection, account-isolation, egress-denial and revocation cases.
- M2, voice and proactive beta: F03, F04 and F06 to F08; B10, B14 and B15; C07 to C10; D11 to D14 and D18; plus the extended adversarial corpus. Exit when duplex voice with barge-in and honest cancellation works, reminders follow the interruption policy, and the extended security tests pass.
- M3, controlled execution and integrations: A09 to A13 and A14 (optional transport), B06 (optional adapter), B18, C06, C11, C13, C18, D15, D16, F05, F11, F12, F16 and F17. Exit when every effect passes the broker with a receipt and unknown outcomes are reconciled, and the companion works as a controller without holding authority.
- M4, portability and polish: F14 (wake phrase, gated on a measured energy delta) and F18 (Windows seam and conformance guide). Exit when the wake decision is recorded with numbers and a non-Mac conformance guide exists.

## First-night execution plan

The root-reviewed first-night execution plan is [docs/overnight-execution.md](https://github.com/PEAT-AI/lux-didi/blob/docs/lux-didi-plan/docs/overnight-execution.md). It is proposed until a target is selected, it does not change this program's issue scope and it closes no partial product task.

## Status and expectations

No dates and no effort estimates are asserted. Dependency edges are completion order, not start order: a producer contract can be finished and tested against a consumer's fixtures, so lanes overlap deliberately. No optional integration is ever mandatory, and the product is useful with the local core alone. Open questions with their owning issues are listed in docs/decisions.md; material risks in docs/risks.md. The planning package is checked locally by scripts/backlog_validate.py; remote CI is not configured, and none is added during planning.

Evidence baseline: internal planning research is non-public and carries no link; public references are named in the text and in docs/research.md.

nodes.title: [E01] Runtime and local execution
nodes.body:
User outcome: Didi runs as a small, dependable local core that reasons, calls tools, executes bounded actions and survives crashes, with no hidden dependence on any one machine or vendor.

Boundaries: this epic owns the service stack decision, the shared versioned contracts, the local service and its lifecycle, the application store, durable task progress, model-provider abstraction, tool-turn orchestration, action receipts, and resource measurement. It does not own the Mac user interface, the memory and persona model, the account connectors, the commitment and proactive layer, or the harness control surface (those are other masters). It never reimplements scheduling owned by the existing harness; the harness remains the only coding-worker scheduler.

Children: A01 service stack, client roles and license boundary; A02 versioned cross-track contracts and fixtures; A03 local service lifecycle; A04 application storage, migrations and backup/restore; A05 durable task progress and cancellation; A06 replaceable model providers and budgets; A07 tool-turn orchestration; A08 action intents, receipts and unknown-outcome reconciliation.

Phase: M0 proof and contracts. Exit criteria: the service stack is recorded in an ADR and implemented by the loopback service seam; the cross-track contract package and fixtures exist and are consumed by concrete storage, provider and domain contract consumers; MCP transport is deferred and is not part of this exit; a spoken-answer spike and a crash-recovery walk are demonstrated; no task asserts a measured figure it has not recorded.

Parallel ownership: A01 and A02 start immediately and in parallel. A03, A04 and A06 depend only on the service stack record or the contract package and can proceed side by side. A05 follows storage. A07 follows providers. A08 follows storage and orchestration.

Evidence gaps: there is no application, so every behavior here is proposed until a spike or test exists. The service stack choice and the reuse-license boundary rest on a council decision record and two design reports, not on measured proof. There are no energy or latency baselines yet. Public delivery must carry no private prompt, no personal profile and no internal identifiers, and synthetic fixtures only.

Evidence gaps: internal planning research is non-public and carries no link; every epic outcome is design until its leaves record evidence.

nodes.title: [E02] Harness supervision and operational reliability
nodes.body:
User outcome: Didi can discover, watch and (only where explicitly authorized) steer existing harness masters and workers, and it stays truthful and recoverable when something crashes, stalls or goes offline.

Boundaries: this epic owns read-only harness discovery and identity, the harness event and session-evidence stream, the authorized steering and cancellation surface, delegated concurrency and admission discipline, scoped command and filesystem tools, the MCP transport and server lifecycle, the core event outbox and crash recovery, redacted diagnostics, a lean local quality gate, and latency and resource budgets. It does not own the harness controller itself and never writes its state or reimplements its admission, queue or wake logic. Read-only observation must work with no upstream change; mutation is gated on a harness-granted scoped identity or owning-master delegation, never on a global override.

Children: A09 discovery and identity read-only; A10 events, session evidence and replay; A11 authorized steering and cancellation; A12 delegated concurrency and admission; A13 scoped command and filesystem tools with an explicit broad mode; A14 MCP transport and server lifecycle; A15 core event outbox and crash recovery; A16 diagnostics with redacted evidence; A17 lean local quality and recovery gate; A18 latency, energy and resource measurement and budgets.

Phase: M3, when the controlled-execution tasks (A11-A13) and the live-harness observation closure exit; the reliability baseline (outbox, gate, diagnostics, measurement) lands in M1 and does not depend on MCP, which is deferred to M3 with A14. Harness observation is deliberately NOT critical to the first standalone loop, so it is M3/P1 and may run in parallel only if explicitly prioritized. Exit criteria: the reliability baseline (outbox, gate, diagnostics, measurement) runs locally; and, for the M3 observation closure, an end-to-end observation scenario runs against a live harness without any upstream change; the reconciliation walk rebuilds state after a simulated crash; the quality gate runs locally without paid CI; every measurement task records host pressure at measurement time.

Parallel ownership: A09 unblocks A10; A14 and A15 are independent of the harness work; A16 follows the outbox; A17 and A18 can start from the contract package. A11 and A12 are blocked on the upstream scoped companion-controller contract and must not be worked around.

Evidence gaps: the harness control surface is verified only by reading its source and CLI; no live supervision scenario has been executed by this lane. The upstream identity gap is confirmed at source and by a sibling review. Public delivery must carry no private path, no internal endpoint and no personal data.

Evidence gaps: internal planning research is non-public and carries no link; every epic outcome is design until its leaves record evidence.

nodes.title: [E03] Evidence and durable recall
nodes.body:
## User outcome
A person installs Didi on a clean machine and, after using it for a while, can ask what happened in earlier sessions and get accurate answers whose every assertion points at a source. Memory survives restarts, app updates and conversation end. The person can correct a wrong memory, forget one, and export their data, and none of these operations silently loses or invents information. This epic makes memory trustworthy before it makes it clever.

## Boundaries
This epic covers evidence, local transcript originals, retrieval, the optional private-knowledge adapter, explicit preferences, correction/suppression and export/forget. It does not cover commitments, planning or proactivity (that is E07 and E08), and it does not cover fetching external accounts (that is E05). Persona expression is E04. Memory stores only private local data; company knowledge is a separate optional adapter owned elsewhere.

## Child tasks
B01 evidence and source identity model; B02 local voice/session transcript originals; B03 external transcript resolution and coverage; B04 session gists with evidence links; B05 exact and semantic session recall; B06 optional private knowledge adapter; B07 authoritative explicit preferences; B08 correction, conflict and suppression semantics; B09 export, forget and cache propagation.

## Phase and exit criteria
Exit milestone: M1, when the first real-user slice has recall the user can trust; the identity model and preferences land earlier in M0. Exit criteria: a clean install with no optional adapters recalls a prior session and an explicit preference after restart; every recalled assertion carries an evidence class and a source reference; a forgotten item never reappears; export round-trips; a result with missing coverage says so instead of implying completeness.

## Parallel ownership
B01 and B12 can start immediately. After B01, the remaining leaves split into two largely independent groups (evidence/recall: B02-B06; preferences and trust: B07-B09) that different implementers can hold. Shared contract conventions are requested from A02; source adapters that B03 consumes come from the connectors track; the suppression gate in B08 is exposed for the commitments track to reuse rather than duplicate.

## Evidence gaps
The cost of a local single-user store versus the existing multi-service memory persistence is read from schema only and not benchmarked. Portable cache and reindex behavior is unproven. The recall evaluation corpus is proposed, not built. All interface names in this epic are proposed, not existing APIs.

Evidence gaps: internal planning research is non-public and carries no link; every epic outcome is design until its leaves record evidence.

nodes.title: [E04] Evolving personality and memory quality
nodes.body:
## User outcome
Didi feels like a consistent, warm, direct and witty character that gradually learns how its user likes to work, while never shipping a profile of a real person and never letting an inferred trait override a stated fact. The character is authored once as a public specification, then personalized only through each user's private local configuration. Over time Didi consolidates memory, keeps it lean, compiles a bounded context for each turn, and lets the user inspect and revert anything it inferred.

## Boundaries
This epic covers consolidation and retention, bounded context compilation, the public persona specification, private customization, gradual persona learning, memory inspector services, a recall evaluation corpus, trust separation in retrieved context, and optional embeddings portability. It does not author prompt text for the runtime orchestration layer, does not own the user interface, and does not introduce a shipped profile of any real individual. All learned personalization is derived inference and must be labelled and reversible.

## Child tasks
B10 consolidation and retention; B11 bounded context compilation; B12 public Naya-inspired persona specification; B13 private customization and onboarding; B14 gradual persona learning with inspectable provenance; B15 memory inspector services; B16 recall evaluation corpus; B17 trust and epistemic separation in retrieved context; B18 optional embeddings, index portability and reindexing.

## Phase and exit criteria
Exit milestone: M2, when the persona-quality work lands; the first daily loop already has a consistent character and bounded context from M1, and optional portability work extends later. Exit criteria: the persona specification is public and contains no personal data; a compile for one user never contains another user's private strings; a bounded context stays within its budget and reports what it omitted; every inferred adaptation is labelled and can be reverted; the evaluation corpus is synthetic and reproducible.

## Parallel ownership
B12 stands alone and gates the style used by B13 and B14. B11 depends on B05 and B17 and can proceed once context selection and trust tagging exist. B15 is a services layer for a future inspector UI owned by the native-experience track. B16 pairs with B05 and B17 so recall quality is measured, not assumed.

## Evidence gaps
Persona-learning thresholds and retention windows are unmeasured. Transplant cost of existing memory persistence is read from schema only. Whether an embedding index is needed at all is deferred until a concrete recall requirement proves it. The persona specification is a new authored artifact; no existing public prompt is reused.

Evidence gaps: internal planning research is non-public and carries no link; persona quality is evaluated by the B16 corpus once it exists.

nodes.title: [E05] Accounts and work sources: connect a user's own accounts and read their sources safely
nodes.body:
**User outcome.** A person who installs the product can connect their own Google account, read their own calendar and mail, see what is waiting on them, and prepare an unsent reply, without the product shipping any profile, token or sample data of anyone else. After this epic, one account on one machine is a normal, auditable, revocable state rather than a special case.

**Why it is an epic.** Every claim the assistant makes about the user's work life comes from a source it does not own. Account identity, credentials, per-source ingestion, per-source freshness and per-source write authority are separate concerns that must agree on one keying scheme, or the product mixes one person's data into another account's answer. The sibling identity and security research lane in this planning set reached the same conclusion independently: multi-account Google is greenfield, not configuration, because the existing local tooling resolves a single token root at import time and offers no account selector.

**Children.** C01 identity map and account binding; C02 per-account credential records and Google installed-app OAuth; C03 Gmail incremental ingestion; C04 Gmail reply drafting with receipts; C05 Calendar incremental sync; C06 authorized Calendar actions; C07 document original resolver; C08 Mattermost archive coverage and live repair; C09 Mattermost draft and action adapter; C10 Trello board read and mapping; C11 Trello actions with idempotent reconciliation.

**Boundaries.** This epic owns how a source is identified, authenticated, read, labelled with freshness, and prepared into a proposal. Consequential external effects belong to their own leaves under E06 authority rules. Commitment extraction, planning and nudging belong to the commitments master. Voice and UI surfaces belong to the native experience master; this epic supplies view models and never renders. Storage layout and migrations belong to the runtime master, and each leaf here proposes its schema change instead of racing shared migrations.

**Phase and exit criteria.** M1, because the first real-user slice is exactly "one account, read the calendar, prepare an unsent reply". The epic exits when a fresh install can add one account, read upcoming events with a stated freshness, list unanswered mail, prepare one unsent reply, and report a revoked or missing credential as an explicit failure rather than an empty success, with no code path that reaches a send or an attendee-visible action.

**Parallel ownership.** C01, C02 and C14 are the contracts and should be authored first; C03, C04 and C05 follow the Google authorization leaf, while C07 to C11 depend only on the identity contract and on their own provider credentials, so a chat or board source installs without Google; all of them can proceed in parallel behind their own fixtures. C13 and C18 are intentionally outside this epic's critical path.

**Evidence gaps.** Which distribution path a self-installed user will take (per-user test client, published but unverified, or verified) is an assessment task in C02, not a settled fact. Whether the hosted inference route changes a restricted-scope obligation is assessed in C15. Mattermost history freshness depends on a local archive whose sync state is owned by another component, so the freshness contract is consumed, not owned, here.

Evidence gaps: internal planning research is non-public and carries no link; every epic outcome is design until its leaves record evidence.

nodes.title: [E06] Authority and optional company integrations: deterministic grants, egress policy and adverse isolation
nodes.body:
**User outcome.** The assistant can read, prepare and remind under standing permission, and cannot send, delete, pay or act on the user's behalf because a model suggested it. Every external effect has a named grant, a durable intent, a receipt, and a visible way to revoke it. Optional company integrations work under the company's own permissions rather than by copying company data into the product.

**Why it is an epic.** Authority is the product's trust boundary. It cannot be a per-adapter afterthought, because a decision made inside a connector (for example "this reply is safe to send") is exactly the kind of inference that must not create authority. The design direction recorded for this program is a deterministic, host-owned broker with per user, account, tool, action and resource grants, durable intents and receipts, credential references rather than credential values, and a destination and data-class egress policy. Reasoning text and untrusted tool output never create authority.

**Children.** C12 grants, allowlists and the effect broker; C13 Mongoose per-user permission adapter; C14 tool capability registry and adapter manifests; C15 provider egress and credential policy; C16 injection and account isolation adverse suite; C17 disconnect, revoke and cache propagation; C18 optional Coworker consultation adapter.

**Boundaries.** This epic owns policy enforcement, not runtime mechanics. The job queue, process lifecycle, storage engine and transport are the runtime master's. Persona and memory quality are the memory master's. What this epic decides is whether a given call is permitted, under which grant, with what effect class and destination, and what durable evidence results. Consequential local execution is a separate explicit mode with its own honest risk statement.

**Phase and exit criteria.** M1 for the authority core (C12, C14, C15), because the first slice already needs standing read permission and an egress decision before any content reaches a hosted model. C13 and C18 land in M3 with the optional integrations. The epic exits when a read is allowed under a standing grant without any confirmation, a send or delete is refused without an explicit grant and performs zero network calls on refusal, every attempt is recorded, and the adverse suite proves that an injected instruction inside tool output or a second account's data cannot widen authority or leak across accounts.

**Parallel ownership.** C14 and C12 are the contracts; C15 can proceed beside them. C16 depends on a real tool-result path, so it starts once C03 exists and can then run independently. C13 and C18 are optional and must not block the slice.

**Evidence gaps.** Company permission semantics are a peer lane's source claim and were not re-read against the company service source in this lane, so C13 stays deliberately generic and validates against the upstream permission model at implementation time. The exact current service terms and data-handling position for the preferred hosted model provider are not verified here; C15 carries them as an assessment with a decision record rather than assuming an exemption.

Evidence gaps: internal planning research is non-public and carries no link; every epic outcome is design until its leaves record evidence.

nodes.title: [E07] Commitments and daily planning
nodes.body:
User outcome: after an ordinary day of mail, chat, calendar and calls, the user asks what they owe and gets one trustworthy answer, where every item shows the sentence that created it, when it is due, and whether it is waiting on them or on someone else. Nothing in the plan is a summary the model wrote about the user; each line is a record the user can inspect, correct or close.

Boundaries: this epic owns the commitment record and its lifecycle, extraction into that record with attribution and evidence, dedup and closed-state suppression, unanswered mail and chat prioritization, meeting preparation, the realistic daily plan, the incremental trigger and due loop, reminder intents, and the snooze, dismiss and defer conversation. It does not own source transport or accounts (master C), retrieval, transcript resolution and correction semantics (master B), job durability, storage and provider seams (master A), or any native or voice surface (master E, leaves F01-F18). It does not own authority: what may be read, drafted or acted on comes from the grant broker and allowlist owned by the trust master, and model output never creates permission.

Child IDs: D01 through D09.

Phase: M1. The useful daily loop is the first artefact a colleague can actually live with, and everything in this epic is reachable against fixtures before any account is connected. The record contract belongs to the M0 proof phase through its own leaf D01, which is the only part of this epic that must precede implementation of the loop.

Exit criteria: one, a synthetic corpus produces commitment rows with relocatable evidence anchors, owner attribution and no invented attribute. Two, re-running extraction, re-harvesting a source and restarting the process leave terminal states and user corrections untouched. Three, the daily plan renders a coverage line per configured source and refuses to claim that nothing is outstanding when a source is degraded or disconnected. Four, a reminder fires once, survives a process restart, and can be snoozed or dismissed with the reason recorded and inspectable. Five, a commitment that the user resolves is never raised again by a later ingest of the same source. Six, the first-slice proofs hold end to end: one reminder is suppressed by the default night window with its reason logged and stays visible on request, a resume after a short sleep produces at most one reminder and never a burst, and a restart leaves the resumed conversation with the same outstanding items and no duplicate reminder. The fuller urgency policy and the multi-day catch-up arrive later and may extend these guarantees but never weaken them.

Parallel ownership: D01 gates the rest. After D01, D02 and D03 are the critical path because every surface depends on the quality and stability of the record. D04, D05 and D06 can run in parallel against the same schema, as can D07, D08 and D09 against the job and outbox contracts of master A. Master C cursor work (C03, C05, C08) is an external gate for D04 and D07 but not for D01 to D03, which must develop and test against fixtures so the loop is never blocked on account authorization.

Evidence gaps: no measured extraction quality exists at authoring time and none is claimed here; a labelled synthetic corpus is required before any quality statement. The storage engine, the reminder delivery mechanism and the app surface are decided by other masters (A04 and the native leaves), so this epic is authored against a stated contract rather than a chosen implementation. Private baseline material is non-public and carries no links.

nodes.title: [E08] Proactive follow-through
nodes.body:
User outcome: Didi raises the right thing at the right moment without becoming noise. It notices that a promise is nearly due, that a meeting moved and its preparation moved with it, that a project has gone quiet, that a conversation with a colleague needs continuity, and that a long investigation is still running; each of those arrives with a reason, respects quiet hours and focus time, and can be deferred with one action.

Boundaries: this epic owns interruption policy, asynchronous investigation with conversational progress, calendar change and replanning, dormant project and open-loop follow-up, one-on-one preparation and recurring follow-through, optional external task reconciliation, outcome learning and nudge calibration, the proactivity and false-promise evaluation gate, and sleep or offline catch-up without notification bursts. It does not own notification transport or the notification-to-conversation surface (native leaves F09 and F02), calendar sync itself (C05), Trello transport (C10, C11), durable job progress and cancellation mechanics (A05), or the policy that decides which effects are permitted (C12).

Child IDs: D10 through D18.

Phase: M2. Proactive behaviour is only credible after the daily loop is trustworthy, and the first proactive release is deliberately narrower than the loop: reminders, replanning, progress and catch-up. Learning from outcomes and external task reconciliation land in M3 because both need history that does not exist in M2, and they are the two leaves most likely to be re-scoped once real usage data exists.

Exit criteria: one, every interruption carries the evidence quote, the due state and the rule that fired, and the interruption budget is respected with refusals logged rather than silent. Two, a calendar change of time, place or cancellation moves the affected preparation and reminders instead of duplicating them. Three, a catch-up after a sleep or offline period produces at most one consolidated message and never a burst per item. Four, a delegated investigation reports that it is working, returns a result, and reports an honest failure or partial result with the coverage gap named. Five, the false-promise gate over the frozen corpus blocks a release when a decoy class starts producing auto-accepted commitments; and the first-slice guarantees stay in force, because the leaves here may extend the night-window hold, the opt-out, the suppression log and the no-burst rule and may never weaken them.

Parallel ownership: D10 and D07 are the shared prerequisites for the rest; D11 and D12 can proceed in parallel once D10 exists, and D13, D14 and D15 are independent of each other on the same policy. D17 must be authored alongside D02 and D03 rather than after them, because it owns the labelled corpus that those leaves use for their own fixtures. D16 depends on accumulated outcome records and therefore follows the beta window rather than gating it.

Evidence gaps: no long-run nudge outcome data exists; the calibration leaf is specified as a mechanism with a fixed starting policy, not as a tuned result. Mobile and voice delivery semantics are owned by other masters, so this epic defines the logical notification identity and the acknowledgement contract it requires from them. Private baseline material is non-public and carries no links.

nodes.title: [E09] Mac conversation surface: hotkey, duplex voice and native notifications
nodes.body:
**User outcome.** On a Mac, a colleague presses one global hotkey, speaks or types to Didi, hears a warm, direct, witty companion answer, can interrupt it, and can be pulled back into the conversation by a native notification. The surface is the product's face: it must feel immediate, never fight the frontmost application, and recover cleanly from sleep, device changes and dropped sessions.

**Boundaries.** This epic owns the native experience only: the menu bar and hotkey shell, the conversation window, audio device handling, the duplex voice adapter, the fallback speech and text provider path, barge-in and cancellation, session reconnect, voice personality and accessibility, and notification-to-conversation entry. It does not own memory, persona content, accounts, connectors, commitments, storage or the local core runtime. It consumes versioned local contracts and provides presentation only.

**Child IDs.** F01 native hotkey and menu bar shell; F02 text conversation and async job cards; F03 microphone, audio devices and permissions; F04 Gemini Live duplex adapter; F05 alternate speech and text fallback provider capabilities; F06 barge-in, echo and cancel; F07 session reconnect, expiry and recovery; F08 voice, personality, localization and accessibility; F09 native notification-to-conversation.

**Phase and exit criteria.** Phase M2 (voice and proactive beta), with the MINIMAL notification and deep-link baseline pulled into M1 alongside the text conversation and the minimum sleep/offline honesty, because the first real-user slice must schedule a reminder and open the conversation from it. Exit when a clean install reaches the first real-user slice with text, then with voice as soon as the duplex stream works: hotkey opens the surface, a voice turn completes, an interruption cancels the answer, the session survives a provider drop, and a notification opens the conversation at the right context. Proactive content itself is owned by the follow-through track; this epic only renders and routes it.

**Parallel ownership.** F01, F02, F03 and F09 can proceed in parallel with F04 to F08 once the shell exists. The E10 review surface shows what this surface produces. Fixtures for the local contracts are shared with the contracts leaf and the B, C and D tracks, but this track races no shared migrations.

**Evidence gaps.** The client host choice is settled by the service stack decision (A01): the Swift app is the Mac companion and the browser is the portable client, so nothing here reopens it. Real latency and energy numbers are unmeasured and must not be asserted. Gemini endpoints and account coverage are unverified; the provider is replaceable and this epic must not hardcode a model. No private prompt text or personal details are used to specify any child.

Evidence gaps: internal planning research is non-public and carries no link; every epic outcome is design until its leaves record evidence.

nodes.title: [E10] Installability, computer control and companion portability
nodes.body:
**User outcome.** A colleague installs Didi from a clean Mac account, connects their own accounts and grants, sees exactly what it remembers and what it is allowed to do, can hand it bounded computer control when they choose, and can extend or move the assistant to a paired companion device, a phone, or later Windows without losing the Mac as the authority.

**Boundaries.** This epic owns installation, onboarding, review surfaces, native computer-use controls and their operating-system permission prompts, background and power behavior, an optional wake phrase, packaging and distribution, companion device pairing, mobile control of one Mac authority, and the Windows seam. It does not own the account and connector internals or the grant broker logic (those live in the accounts and trust track), memory storage, commitments or the runtime. This epic presents and enforces the local platform constraints around them.

**Child IDs.** F10 clean-user onboarding, accounts and grants; F11 memory, authority and action review surfaces; F12 native computer-use controls, TCC and screen capture; F13 login, background, sleep and power; F14 opt-in wake phrase feasibility; F15 packaging, with Stage A and Stage B; F16 companion device pairing, revocation and transport; F17 mobile notifications and control with one Mac authority; F18 Windows port seam and conformance guide.

**Phase and exit criteria.** Phase M3 (controlled execution and integration), with F15 Stage A pulled earlier because the first real-user slice begins from a clean account on a locally built or ad-hoc pilot install. F15 Stage B, signed and notarized shareable distribution, stays later and is gated on the owner's developer-identity and spending decision, so no paid enrollment is required to reach the first slice. Exit when a clean account can install a pilot build, sign in through the local identity, connect one account, grant a bounded capability, review and revoke it, exercise one supervised computer action under an explicit mode, and pair a second device that can notify and issue queued commands while the Mac stays the single writer of record.

**Parallel ownership.** F10 and F15 Stage A gate the rest. F11, F12, F13, F16 and F17 can proceed in parallel after F10. F14 and F18 are later and may land after the core beta. F15 Stage B needs a real Apple developer account decision from the owner, so it states a staged plan and a fallback rather than a final distribution choice.

**Evidence gaps.** The ownership story for a bundled helper or subprocess, and the honest limits of same-user isolation, are policy questions carried from the trust track. Wake phrase feasibility depends on platform entitlement and is explicitly opt-in. Mobile is secondary and the Windows seam is a port guide, not a shipping target. No private paths, prompts or personal data appear in any child.

Evidence gaps: internal planning research is non-public and carries no link; every epic outcome is design until its leaves record evidence.

nodes.title: [E11] Portable assistant service and cloud deployment
nodes.body:
Outcome: the assistant service that already runs on the user's laptop runs unchanged on a
Linux virtual machine. The deployment path is designed and rehearsed, not assumed, and there is
never a second authority: the same Node service process is the only writer whether it is bound to
the loopback interface on the laptop or listening on a virtual machine.

Scope: the service boundary, the deployment artifacts and the operational runbook. Delivery covers
a container image built from the same entry point the laptop runs, a systemd unit with restart and
resource bounds, a provider-neutral deployment runbook with interchangeable notes for two major
providers, a secret reference scheme in which the image and the repository hold names and never
values, backup and restore plus a migration rehearsal performed on synthetic data, suite endpoint
configuration so sibling tools address the service through one declared base URL, and an explicit
hosting boundary statement that separates hosting this assistant from any later, separate
migration of other Lux services.

Out of scope: provisioning any cloud account or virtual machine, any paid run, any
provider-specific managed database as a first requirement, and any change to another repository.

Interfaces and ownership and reuse: this epic owns the service deployment boundary, the runbook
and the hosting boundary statement. A03 owns the loopback control surface, A04 owns storage,
backup and restore primitives, C15 owns the model-provider route table, C02 owns credential
records, and A02 owns the versioned envelopes. The deployment reuses those contracts rather than
restating them.

Dependencies: A19 for the service seam, A20 for the image and runbook, A21 for secret
references, A22 for backup, restore and rehearsal, A23 for suite endpoint configuration and A24
for the cloud egress and hosting boundary. Evidence lives in this epic's leaves.

Exit at M4, Portability and polish, is a clean host deployed, backed up, restored and rehearsed
from the runbook alone, with the loopback laptop mode still the default.

Public references: https://systemd.io/ and https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/.
Privacy baseline: the deployment runbook names no real provider project, account or host.

nodes.title: [E12] Channels, authority epochs and device grants
nodes.body:
Outcome: the assistant is reachable through several communication channels while one
authority remains active, and a device or channel can never become a second writer by asking.

Scope: a channel-neutral inbox and outbox, channel identity separated from source-account
identity, one active authority epoch with a defined host transfer, device-specific grants
expressed as scoped expiring intents that the device pulls outbound, revocation epochs and an
offline delivery queue. Signal, email and Mattermost are channels and transports; none of them is
identity proof and none is an administrative bypass.

Out of scope: cloud and laptop writing the same store at once, any multiwriter synchronisation or
last-writer-wins merge, any implicit grant created by a channel message, and any assumption that
a verified sender address proves who is speaking.

Interfaces and ownership and reuse: this epic owns the authority epoch record and the channel
envelope. C01 owns the account identity map, C12 owns the grant lifecycle and the effect broker,
C17 owns disconnect and revocation propagation, F16 owns companion pairing and transport, and A15
owns the durable outbox. Channel adapters reuse the A02 envelopes and never write domain state
directly.

Dependencies: C19 and C20 for the channel model, C21 for the authority epoch and host transfer,
C22 for device grants and pulled intents and C23 for revocation and offline delivery. Evidence
lives in this epic's leaves.

Exit at M3, Controlled execution and integrations, is one declared authority epoch with a tested
transfer, a revoked device that cannot act on a stale intent, and a queued delivery that replays
once after connectivity returns without duplicating the effect.

Public references: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749 for the authorization framing reused
here. Privacy baseline: the channel model names no real workspace, address, handle or account.

nodes.title: [E13] Responsive and mobile client surfaces
nodes.body:
Outcome: a person can use the assistant from a phone or a tablet browser through a
responsive client that renders the same service contract as the Mac companion, without a second
backend and without leaking private data into a shared cache.

Scope: a responsive progressive web application shell, a shell-only serviceworker cache policy
with an explicit private-data offline rule, an installable Android access path on the same
contract, and conformance across laptop, tablet and phone breakpoints. The browser client is a
client, never an authority.

Out of scope: a second service, a native mobile rewrite, offline writing of private records,
push beyond what the platform grants, and any cache of session content, commitments or
credentials in browser storage.

Interfaces and ownership and reuse: this epic owns the browser client surface and the responsive
breakpoint contract. F02 owns the conversation surface, F16 and F17 own pairing and notification
transport, F19 owns the shell, A19 owns the command, query and progress contract, and C15 owns
what may leave the process. The client reuses the A02 envelopes.

Dependencies: F19 for the shell, F20 for the cache and offline policy, F21 for the Android access
path, F22 for cross-breakpoint conformance and F23 for the shared web UI host inside the Mac
companion. Evidence lives in this epic's leaves.

Exit at M2, Voice and proactive beta, is the first daily loop working in a phone browser against
the loopback service with a shell-only cache and no private record in browser storage.

Public references: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Progressive_web_apps and
https://web.dev/responsive-web-design-basics/. Privacy baseline: the client surfaces hold no
private record outside the service.

nodes.title: [A01] Service stack, client roles and license boundary decision
nodes.body:
User outcome: a fixed runtime and deployment stack that later tasks can build against, with the reuse-license boundary recorded and no later task betting on an unvalidated shell.

Decision (PLAN-R1, council b9bdda79, architect ruling): one authoritative single-user service written in TypeScript on Node with SQLite storage; the mac app is a Swift companion that owns native operating-system surfaces; a responsive progressive web application is the portable client. The same service process runs against the loopback interface on the laptop and on a linux virtual machine later, with no contract change and never two authoritative writers. Commands and queries are REST JSON and progress is a server-sent event stream; a WebSocket framework is not required. Devices pull scoped expiring intents outbound and enforce their own local grants. Native operating-system adapters and language-neutral domain invariants are preserved, and one database per assistant is the initial shape with instance isolation as a later question.

Superseded: the earlier Swift runtime and domain prototype, which was a feasibility spike for the host shell. Its findings are retained as evidence for the companion's audio, permission and wake behaviour, and it is not landed as the product core. The comparison and the alternatives considered are recorded in the research document and in D-13.

Scope: the stack decision, the client role split, the loopback to virtual-machine path, the reuse and licence boundary, and the record of what is superseded. Out of scope: provisioning any host, any paid run, and any change to another repository.

Interfaces and ownership and reuse: this task owns the decision record and the licence and notice basis for any retained third-party component. A19 owns the service seam that implements the decision, C21 owns the single active authority epoch, F19 owns the browser client and F01 owns the companion shell. No third-party host code is reused without a recorded permissive licence and notice review pinned to the release used.

Dependencies: none. Later tasks depend on this decision record rather than reopening it.

Acceptance and adverse: the decision record names the stack, the client roles and the loopback to virtual-machine path; a later task that assumes an unresolved host choice is a defect in that task. Adverse scenarios: a retained component appears without a licence and notice entry and the reuse is refused; a client embeds domain logic and the boundary review rejects it.

Validation and evidence: the decision record is reviewed against the research document's primary sources, and the validation is that no published document still describes the host as unchosen. Public references: https://nodejs.org/api/ and https://www.sqlite.org/. Privacy baseline: the record names no private repository, host or credential, and the internal licence review is non-public and is not linked here.

PLAN-R3 adds the reuse authorization: first-party components may be cloned from the Naya codebase, and the orb and interaction surface, the generic personality and system-prompt structure and the verified memory patterns are the intended source. Asset and dependency rights are verified before any public source reuse, third-party attribution and licence notices are preserved, and private persona payloads, family details and real transcripts are never published.

nodes.title: [A02] Versioned cross-track contracts and shared fixtures
nodes.body:
User outcome: every track speaks one versioned contract, so the host, core, storage, connectors and user interface can be built in parallel without racing shared files.

Problem: five tracks will write code simultaneously. The roadmap contract fixes directory ownership but the interfaces between them do not exist. Uncontrolled interface drift is the most likely way a parallel effort stalls.

Proposed work: define a small set of local, versioned interface contracts shared by host, core and adapters, and a fixtures package that lets a track test against a neighbor without that neighbor being present or finished. Candidate contracts: the job and task envelope (id, kind, phase, cancellation level, receipt), the model request and response envelope (provider, model, effort, budget, evidence), the memory query and result envelope (query, claims, provenance, coverage), the connector result envelope (source, cursor, item, capability, error class), the action intent and receipt envelope, and the event outbox record. Each carries an explicit version and a compatibility note. Provide synthetic fixtures for each contract so tests never depend on a live account, a private store or a real transcript. State clearly that a shared-contract change is proposed to this track and sequenced here, while each owning track proposes its own schema change and does not race migrations.

Acceptance criteria: a checked-in contract package with a version per interface; a fixtures module covering every contract with synthetic data; at least the storage, provider and MCP tasks consuming the package; a documented rule for proposing and sequencing a contract change; no contract containing a personal profile, a private path or an internal identifier.

Dependencies: none, to keep contract work unblocked. Evidence: the roadmap contract's ownership map and the sibling lane reports for the shapes each track needs. Gaps: contract shapes may need revision once the host and connectors start; versioning is the mitigation. Phase M0.

Minimal scope note: the contract package is versioned envelopes and domain ports proven by concrete first-loop fixtures, not a universal schema frozen forever. Updates are deliberate and coordinated, and no speculative universal engine is built here.

Out of scope: product features, per-track tables, and any universal schema or speculative engine beyond the first-loop fixtures. Interfaces and ownership: the single versioned contract package consumed by storage, providers, MCP, connectors and commitments; changes are coordinated through the runtime lane. Validation: a fixture-based conformance test showing the storage, provider and MCP consumers build from the same envelopes; no command exists yet. Evidence: internal planning research on cross-track shapes (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [A03] Local service lifecycle and control surface
nodes.body:
User outcome: a single local core process that starts, stops and reports health predictably, reachable through one stable local surface that is authenticated.

Problem: the client shells and the core must be separable and independently testable. Without a defined lifecycle, a shell crash takes the core with it, and no client can reason about readiness. A local control surface on a port is not private just because it binds loopback: any process running as the same user can call it, and a web page can attempt a request against it unless the origin is validated.

Proposed work: implement the local core as a background service with explicit states (stopped, starting, ready, degraded, stopping, failed), a readiness probe, a graceful shutdown with a bounded drain, and a restart policy. Expose one stable control surface over the decided transport: the Node service listens on loopback and speaks the REST JSON command and query contract with a server-sent progress stream (A19). If the surface is loopback HTTP: mint a per-session bearer token at startup, require it on every request, and reject any request whose Origin header is present and not the core's own, because a browser can reach a loopback port. Provide adverse tests: an unauthenticated same-user request is refused; a request carrying a browser origin is refused; and the test documents that a same-user process holding the token can still call the surface, so this is authentication plus origin validation and NOT a same-user isolation claim. A local socket surface follows the same authentication rule. Degraded mode must name its cause (a missing credential or an unreadable store) rather than failing silently. Log lifecycle transitions with timestamps and a redacted summary. Document state locations from the owning packages' configuration, never a hardcoded private path.

Acceptance criteria: start, readiness, graceful stop and crash-restart are each observable; a killed core is detected and restarted or reported within a bounded time; a missing credential yields a named degraded state; any loopback HTTP surface refuses an unauthenticated call and a browser-origin call, and the same-user limitation is documented rather than claimed away; a lifecycle plus authentication test asserts each case.

Dependencies: A19 for the command, query and progress transport; A01 for the service stack record. Evidence: platform lane host stack; the model context protocol local-server security guidance on loopback authentication and origin validation; the contract's statement that same-UID is not an isolation guarantee. Gaps: the transport is not yet chosen. Phase M0.

Out of scope: user interface, provider session ownership, scheduling and harness supervision. Interfaces and ownership: the host owns microphone and playback, the core exposes one authenticated local surface to host and adapters, and both consume the A02 contracts. Validation: a future lifecycle test for start, readiness, graceful stop and crash restart, with a killed core detected and either restarted or reported. Evidence: public model context protocol guidance on loopback authentication and origin validation (https://modelcontextprotocol.io) and internal planning research (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [A04] Application storage, migrations and backup/restore
nodes.body:
User outcome: one local transactional store for Didi's own product state that survives upgrades and can be backed up and restored without losing the user's history.

Problem: the contract requires one writer per entity and explicitly forbids collapsing the whole suite into one database. Didi owns operational sessions, jobs, voice originals, commitment lifecycle, action receipts, notifications and explicit preferences. Those need a durable, migration-safe local store, and the sibling memory and company stores keep their own ownership.

Proposed work: select a local transactional store (a single embedded database is the default candidate) and define the Didi-owned schema for sessions, jobs, commitments, action receipts, notifications and preferences. Define a migration mechanism with ordered, idempotent migration files, a schema version marker, and a rule that this track sequences migration files while each owning track proposes its own change. Implement backup and restore using the store's own safe backup mechanism, never a copy of a live file, and a bounded retention policy for high-volume tables such as voice originals. Document the ownership statement: this store is Didi's product state; general private retrieval stays with the memory service; external authorized source caches are versioned caches, not new mutable source truth.

Acceptance criteria: create, migrate forward and read back across two schema versions; a backup taken while the service runs restores to a consistent state; a corrupted store fails into a named recovery state rather than a crash; a retention job bounds voice-original growth; a test proves the store is separate from the memory store and the session store.

Dependencies: A02 for the contract envelope. Evidence: the roadmap contract's storage ownership statement. Gaps: the exact store engine is a candidate, not a measured choice. Phase M0.

Access boundaries: the store is opened by one writer process with a bounded reader surface for the user interface, and all writes take a short transaction so no write lock is held across a model call or a network call. Backup uses the engine's own online backup path so a snapshot is consistent while the service runs. Restore refuses a snapshot from a newer schema version and reports the version gap. Column-level and row-level details stay internal; the contracts in A02 are the only cross-track shape. State explicitly that this store does not absorb the memory store, the coding-session store or any company store.

Out of scope: memory tables and connector caches, whose schema changes are proposed by their owning lanes; no second store. Interfaces and ownership: the single transactional application store consumed by jobs, receipts and commitments; this leaf sequences migration files for proposals from other lanes. Validation: a future migration forward-and-back test on a scratch store plus a backup and restore walk; no command is claimed. Evidence: internal planning decisions on storage ownership (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [A05] Durable task progress and cancellation semantics
nodes.body:
User outcome: work the user asked for keeps running or stays recoverable when the conversation ends, and cancellation is honest about what actually stopped.

Problem: Didi owns simple durable product work queues and due timers, not a universal workflow engine. Jobs may outlive the conversation. Cancellation must distinguish several different situations, and the platform lane already distinguishes a voice stop, queued work, dispatched effects, unknown outcomes and completed work.

Proposed work: implement a job model with states (queued, running, waiting on a due time, blocked on input, done, failed, cancelled) persisted in the application store, plus progress reporting and bounded retries for retryable failures. Implement cancellation as a set of explicit levels that match the platform lane's contract: stop the current utterance, remove a queued job, abort a dispatched effect when it is safe, mark an outcome unknown when a side effect may already have occurred, and never report a cancelled job as completed. Cancellation must be idempotent and must record which level was applied and what was blocked from stopping. Due timers must survive a restart and must not require a model call to fire.

Acceptance criteria: a job survives a core restart and resumes or reports; each cancellation level is observable and recorded; a job whose effect may already have landed is marked unknown, not cancelled-as-if-nothing-happened; a due timer fires after a restart without a model call; tests cover queue, due, retry, each cancel level and restart.

Dependencies: A04 for durable storage. Evidence: the roadmap contract cancellation clause and the platform lane's cancellation levels. Gaps: retry budgets are proposed, not measured. Phase M1.

Why not a workflow engine: the harness already owns coding-worker scheduling and admission, and the product needs only simple durable product work queues and due timers. A job is a unit of user-visible work with a small state machine, not a graph, and it must not be able to schedule a second orchestrator. Coexistence rule: a job that delegates coding work hands off to the harness admission path in A12 and then watches that delegated run; it never synthesizes its own worker lifecycle. Progress must be readable without a model call so a status view is cheap.

Ownership note: this leaf owns the durable task lifecycle. Action intents, receipts and reconciliation semantics belong to A08, and the one generic transactional event and delivery outbox belongs to A15, which consumes these task primitives. No leaf creates a second outbox or retry queue.

Out of scope: the event outbox (A15), action receipts (A08) and any universal workflow engine. Interfaces and ownership: defines task lifecycle and cancellation levels consumed by A08 and A15, and respects harness admission for delegated work. Validation: a future kill and restart test across task states showing no lost or duplicated work and honest cancellation classification. Evidence: internal planning decisions on cancellation semantics (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [A06] Replaceable model providers and configured budgets
nodes.body:
User outcome: Didi answers through a preferred provider but is not trapped by one, and every call has a visible, configurable budget.

Problem: the product prefers one provider but must be replaceable, must not hardcode a forever-model identifier, and must not send sensitive content to a non-approved provider. Budgets must be enforced, not merely displayed.

Proposed work: implement a provider abstraction that resolves a request to a provider, model and effort through configuration, with no model string hardcoded in call sites. Integrate at least the preferred cloud provider and one alternate, and route by the harness data-class policy so that sensitive content fails closed unless an approved provider, endpoint and credential binding exist. Enforce per-call and rolling budgets with a configurable action (warn, pause, refuse), and record usage locally. Support a direct real-time transport beside the generic request path for voice, but keep the generic path usable for text and tool turns. Provider errors must be classified (missing credential, rate limit, timeout, policy refusal) and surfaced as user-visible actions.

Acceptance criteria: swapping the preferred provider is a configuration change with no code edit; a request with an unknown or disabled provider is refused with a clear reason; a sensitive request with no approved binding fails closed; a budget breach triggers the configured action and is recorded; error classes are distinguished in tests.

Dependencies: A02 for the request envelope. Evidence: baseline findings on the existing model registry and routing records are a naming reference only; the sibling lanes' provider notes. Gaps: no measured latency or cost figures yet. Phase M1.

Boundary between the generic and live paths: the generic request path serves text and tool turns and is the default; a direct real-time transport may sit beside it for low-latency voice, but the product must not assume the live path speaks for tool turns or that the generic path handles duplex audio. Credentials are never placed in a request body or a call site; they resolve through the keychain broker described in the policy track. A provider that is configured but unapproved for a data class is treated as absent for that class, not silently used.

Safe model-call entry: this is the single entry for model calls. A call refuses content when its route policy is unresolved, and the initial posture is default-deny until C15 supplies policy. Model availability is never treated as approved data handling.

Out of scope: route policy (C15), tool turns (A07) and any hardcoded model identifier. Interfaces and ownership: the single safe model-call entry for A07, D02, B04, B11, D04 and D05; consumes C15 route decisions and exposes configured budgets. Validation: a future test that no content leaves before a route decision exists, plus a provider swap without code changes. Evidence: internal provider-abstraction research (non-public, no link); provider behaviour is design intent until an adapter is exercised.

nodes.title: [A07] Tool-turn orchestration and bounded agent loop
nodes.body:
User outcome: Didi can answer a request that needs tools, calling them in a bounded loop and stopping safely.

Problem: the core must orchestrate model turns and tool calls without becoming an unbounded agent and without reimplementing the harness. An ordinary read must not be routed through a coding master, and scheduling stays with the existing harness.

Proposed work: implement a bounded tool-turn loop: assemble context, call the provider (A06), execute at most a configured number of tool turns, fold tool results back, and stop on a completion condition or the turn bound. Tool calls resolve through the capability registry and deterministic grant broker owned by C12, so a tool with no grant is not callable, and every side-effecting call records an intent and a receipt through A08. The loop records every turn and tool result for replay, is cancellable at each boundary using the A05 levels, and never calls a tool outside the user's or the organization's grants. Reasoning text and untrusted tool results never create authority. A text-only request skips the tool loop entirely.

Parallel work via stubs: because the A06 provider, the A08 receipts and the C12 grant broker may not exist yet, this task defines their interfaces first and ships a stub for each, so the orchestration loop can be built and tested independently while those tracks proceed. The stubs are replaced as the real dependencies land, and the loop must never bypass a real grant check once C12 exists. Stub use is temporary and must be visible in the tests so a green result is not mistaken for integration.

Boundaries: no harness scheduling, no second orchestrator, no direct writes to a sibling store. The loop stays usable for text-only requests with zero tool turns.

Acceptance criteria: a request needing two tools completes within the turn bound and returns a grounded answer; exceeding the bound stops with a clear message, not a hang; a tool with no grant is refused; every turn and tool result is replayable from the local log; cancellation at a turn boundary is honoured; the loop runs against the stubs before its dependencies land.

Dependencies: A06 providers, A08 receipts, and C12 grants (a cross-track leaf). Evidence: baseline controller and council tool-turn surfaces and the A02 contracts package. Gaps: the turn bound and the context budget are proposed, not measured. Phase M1.

Completion note: source-content cloud paths cannot complete before the C15 route policy lands; authoring and fixture-based testing may proceed in parallel.

Out of scope: coding-worker scheduling, harness admission, and any unbounded agent behaviour or second tool registry. Interfaces and ownership: consumes the A06 model entry, A08 receipts, C12 grants and C15 route policy; tool definitions come from the C14 registry and the MCP transport. Validation: a bounded-loop test with an injected tool failure, an iteration cap and a receipt per call; no command exists yet. Evidence: internal planning research on turn orchestration (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [A08] Action intents, receipts and unknown-outcome reconciliation
nodes.body:
User outcome: when Didi takes an action with a side effect, the user can see exactly what was intended, what happened, and what is genuinely unknown, from the first useful daily loop onward.

Problem: sending mail, changing a calendar, moving a card or running a local action can partially succeed or become unknown after a crash or timeout. Reporting an unknown outcome as success, or as failure, breaks trust. This baseline must exist early because the first daily loop already prepares drafts and durable tool jobs whose outcome has to be recorded honestly.

Proposed work (minimal baseline at M1): represent every side-effecting action as an intent recorded before dispatch and a receipt recorded after, with states proposed, dispatched, confirmed, failed and unknown, persisted in the application store. Record the target, the parameters and the grant used, and the owning source's own identifier on the receipt when it is available. Support idempotency keys so a retried action is safe where the source supports it. Expose a small local journal so a review surface can show intent, receipt and unknown states honestly. The contracts come from A02 and the durable storage from A04, so this baseline does not depend on the tool-turn loop and can be built in parallel with it.

Hardening, later phase: on restart or timeout, reconcile any intent left in the dispatched state by querying the owning source where that source supports it, and otherwise mark the outcome unknown rather than guessing. Bound retention and archive resolved intents, and extend coverage to every connector and local action class.

Boundaries: a receipt is never synthesized from a log line; it comes from the owning source or an explicit local confirmation. Reconciliation limits are stated honestly per source. Reasoning text and untrusted results never create authority.

Acceptance criteria: an action records an intent before dispatch and a receipt after; once hardening lands, a crash between the two reconciles to confirmed, failed or unknown, never a silent success; a retried idempotent action does not double-apply; the baseline journal lists intent, receipt and unknown states; tests cover each transition including the unknown path.

Dependencies: A02 contracts and A04 storage. Evidence: the roadmap contract's action-receipt ownership and the baseline controller's receipt vocabulary. Gaps: source-side reconciliation support varies by connector, so the M1 baseline records states and defers cross-source reconciliation to hardening. Phase M1.

Ownership note: this leaf owns action intent, receipt and reconciliation semantics and consumes the task and outbox primitives of A05 and A15. It never creates a second outbox or retry queue.

Out of scope: the outbox itself (A15), the grant broker (C12) and any blind retry of dispatched effects. Interfaces and ownership: consumes A05 task primitives and the A15 outbox; every effect leaf records intents and receipts here, and unknown outcomes stay unknown until reconciled. Validation: a future unknown-outcome reconciliation test with a process killed between dispatch and response. Evidence: internal planning decisions on receipts and reconciliation (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [A09] Harness discovery and identity, read-only
nodes.body:
User outcome: Didi can show the user which harness masters and workers exist, what they are doing and whether a reported identity is really that run, without changing anything.

Problem: supervision must begin read-only and must work with no upstream change. The control surface is a command-line controller, not a network API; the transports are a machine-local server socket, a command-line subprocess and read-only files. Identity must be proven, and a title is never identity.

Proposed work: implement read-only discovery through the controller's documented observation verbs and its read-only state and event files. List masters and their runs with the master identifier, run status, the bound pane identity (pane id, process id and start time), the report reference and the check state. Provide a run-detail view and an identity check that compares the stored binding to live evidence and reports a mismatch or an absence as not-the-run. Never infer identity from a window title. Keep every call read-only and prove it: a before-and-after diff of the controller state directory must be empty. Treat missing or unsupported evidence as an explicit unknown, never as an empty success.

Acceptance criteria: a live inventory matches the controller's own list output; a run whose pane process has died is reported not-live; the read-only invariant is tested by a state-directory diff; the adapter works with no upstream change; identity fields are documented for reuse by A10 and A11.

Dependencies: none, so observation is unblocked. Evidence: the installed controller revision and its source, plus the baseline and verification reports confirming the guard fails closed. Gaps: no live scenario has been executed by this lane yet. Phase M1.

Why read-only is unblocked: observation needs no caller identity and no upstream change, because the guard protects mutation only and read-only verbs are explicitly safe. This task therefore delivers user value before the mutation contract in A11 exists. The identity fields discovered here become the shared vocabulary for A10 and A11, so they are documented as a small struct rather than ad hoc. A missing run record, an unreadable state directory or an unknown field each become an explicit unknown, and the adapter never presents an empty result as a healthy empty fleet.

Out of scope: steering, cancellation, scheduling and any mutation of harness state or records. Interfaces and ownership: consumes the harness public discovery surfaces and feeds A10, A11 and A12; it never writes run records. Validation: a future discovery test against a running harness with a missing run record and an unknown field handled explicitly. Evidence: internal harness research (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [A10] Harness events, session evidence and replay
nodes.body:
User outcome: Didi can follow what a supervised run is doing and reconstruct what it did, even after a restart, without reading anything it should not.

Problem: the run's own event journal is an append-only record with a monotonic sequence, and the full conversation lives in a separate session log that is canonical. A client that reads the journal must detect gaps and must not pretend a summary is a transcript.

Proposed work: consume the append-only event journal by sequence, normalize its event types into a stable internal model, and persist a consumer cursor so a restart resumes without loss or duplication. Detect a sequence gap and report it explicitly. Provide bounded session-evidence and transcript retrieval that never loads an entire transcript into memory and never follows a report path. Keep declared state, observed activity, process liveness and independently verified artifacts separate in the model. Where a transcript is not exposed by a source, report the coverage limit rather than assuming completeness, and retrieve originals only through supported references when authorized.

Acceptance criteria: replay from a stored cursor yields every event once; an injected sequence gap is reported; memory stays bounded on a large transcript; a missing transcript is reported as a coverage limit; the four evidence kinds are not conflated.

Dependencies: A09 for discovery and identity. Evidence: baseline findings on the event journal and canonical session log; the verification report's note that full transcripts are not exposed by the memory service. Gaps: event-type coverage may grow; the normalizer must be forward compatible. Phase M1.

Cursor and retention: the consumer cursor is stored in the application store so it survives a restart, and it is advanced only after an event is durably processed, so at-least-once with de-duplication is the contract. Journal rotation into compressed segments must be read transparently, and the reader must be able to tell whether a writer is alive rather than assuming the stream ended. Retention on cached events is bounded and separate from the canonical session log, which is never copied wholesale. When the canonical transcript is unavailable, the coverage limit is surfaced, never filled with a summary.

Out of scope: mutation, full state copying and any event normalization that drops unknown types. Interfaces and ownership: consumes the harness event journal and feeds A11 evidence and A16 diagnostics. Validation: a future replay test reconstructing a recorded session after restart, including an unknown event type that is preserved rather than discarded. Evidence: internal harness research (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [A11] Authorized harness steering and cancellation
nodes.body:
User outcome: Didi can steer or cancel a supervised run only when explicitly authorized, and it never bypasses the harness's ownership rules.

Problem, confirmed at source and by an independent review: the harness mutation verbs refuse another master's run, and a caller with no resolvable identity is refused outright. The single override is bound by policy to a proven dead owner of the caller's own socket, that is recovery, not general control. A Didi process launched outside a run manifest therefore has no caller identity and no legitimate steady-state way to steer several masters. The correct fixes are an owning-layer one, a scoped companion-controller identity granted by the harness with an explicit verb allowlist, an audit trail in each target run's history and dry-run/apply discipline, or owning-master delegation where the owning master performs the action under its own identity.

Proposed work: implement steering and cancellation ONLY behind the authority granted by that scoped contract, never behind a global override, an environment spoof, or a direct write. Until the contract exists upstream, this task is observation-only and mutation is blocked and reported as blocked, not worked around. When authority is granted, every mutation must require an explicit apply step after a dry run, verify the target's identity, stay inside the allowlist, and never touch a run outside the designated master set. Record the acting identity, target, verb and reason in the target run's own history.

Acceptance criteria: with no granted identity, every mutation attempt is refused and reported blocked; with the scoped contract present, steering, interrupt and idle-confirmed stop succeed, are audited in the target history, and respect dry-run then apply; a target outside the designated set is refused; no code sets another master's identity or uses the recovery override as a general path.

Dependencies: A10 for events and identity. Upstream dependency: a scoped companion-controller contract in the harness (named here, not filed elsewhere). Evidence: the custody guard source, the operator policy, and the independent review. Gaps: the contract does not exist yet, so this task cannot complete until it does. Phase M3.

Out of scope: any global override, environment spoof or direct state write; observation-only until a scoped contract exists. Interfaces and ownership: requires the harness-granted scoped controller contract or an owning-master delegation, and consumes A10 evidence. Validation: a future authorization test where a blanket override is refused and a scoped delegation works. Evidence: internal harness research and the independent cross-lane verification finding (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [A12] Delegated concurrency and admission discipline
nodes.body:
User outcome: when Didi asks the harness to run work, it never overloads the machine and never opens a second scheduler.

Problem: the harness already owns admission, the host worker cap, the disk floor, the processor budget and the per-lane test-job cap. Didi must be a client of that admission path, not a parallel scheduler, and it must not send ordinary product reads through a coding master.

Proposed work: implement delegated launches only through the controller's documented launch path, respecting its admission outcome and its admission-wait behavior. Enforce a user-configurable ceiling on the number of concurrently delegated runs that is at or below the harness cap, and never use the harness override flags automatically. Provide a queue for delegated work that respects the harness admission result, surfaces a launch that has not yet produced a ready receipt as starting rather than running, and reports an overload as a wait, not a failure. Record the delegated run identifiers and their owning master so later steering is scoped. Nothing here reimplements admission; it only respects and displays it.

Acceptance criteria: a delegated launch past the user ceiling is queued, not forced; an admission refusal is surfaced and waited on, not overridden; a run without a ready receipt is shown as starting; the user ceiling never exceeds the harness cap by default; a test proves no override flag is used automatically.

Dependencies: A11 for the authorized control path. Evidence: the operator card's admission and cap section and the baseline admission findings. Gaps: the user ceiling default is proposed. Phase M3.

Reporting rule: a queued or waiting delegated launch is shown as waiting with the harness's own reason, a launch without a ready receipt is shown as starting, and only a confirmed ready run becomes running. The user ceiling is a local product cap layered under the harness cap, and lowering it must never cancel work already admitted. The delegated run's owning master and identifier are recorded so later steering stays inside the designated set. Any launch refusal, disk-floor hold or processor hold is surfaced verbatim as a wait or a refusal, and the override flags are never used automatically.

Out of scope: a second scheduler, fan-out beyond harness admission, and any local admission policy that bypasses the harness. Interfaces and ownership: delegates to the harness admission path and consumes host caps and budgets. Validation: a future concurrency test showing queued work respects admission and a saturated host refuses rather than overcommits. Evidence: internal harness research (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [A13] Scoped command and filesystem tools with explicit broad mode
nodes.body:
User outcome: Didi can perform local actions the user authorized, and broad shell or computer access is an explicit, honest mode rather than a silent default.

Problem: broad local access carries real residual risk, same-user processes are not an isolation boundary, and the product must not quietly authorize sends or deletions. Scoped tools are the default; broad access is opt-in.

Proposed work: implement a small set of scoped local tools (read a file in an authorized root, list a directory, run an allowlisted command with an allowlisted environment, write within an authorized root) whose grants are per user, per tool, per effect and per resource, with standing grants that the user can review and revoke. Provide a separate explicit broad mode with a clear warning and honest residual-risk statement, off by default. Never grant authority from reasoning text or an untrusted tool result. Secrets are supplied as broker handles resolved from the system keychain into an allowlisted subprocess environment, never pasted into a command line or a log. A granted action is not re-confirmed on every call, but a not-yet-granted send or delete is never auto-authorized.
