Acceptance criteria: a scoped tool refuses a path outside its authorized roots; broad mode is off until explicitly enabled and states its risk; a secret is passed as a keychain handle and never appears in a log or command line; grants can be listed and revoked; an untrusted result cannot create a grant.

Dependencies: A07 for the tool-turn loop. Evidence: the roadmap contract permission model and the existing policy lessons on same-user processes. Gaps: the initial allowlist contents are a design decision. Phase M3.

The effect broker returns a handle for a secret, and the handle is resolved only inside the allowlisted subprocess environment, so a secret never enters an argument list, a file or a log. Revocation must propagate to subsequent calls and to any standing grant. Computer control and shell access share the same grant model: a broad mode is one grant the user can see, not an implicit widening of every scoped tool. The residual-risk statement must say plainly that same-user processes are not an isolation guarantee and that a granted broad mode can act on the user's files and accounts.

Out of scope: default broad access, operating system permission bypass and any same-user isolation claim. Interfaces and ownership: exposes scoped command and filesystem tools to the core under C12 grants and consumes A16 redaction; broad mode is an explicit capability. Validation: a future scoped-tool test with path traversal and an explicit broad-mode grant showing the gate and the audit trail. Evidence: internal planning decisions on residual risk (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [A14] MCP transport and server lifecycle
nodes.body:
User outcome: Didi can use external tool servers through a standard protocol, with correct token audience handling and without inventing a central broker or a second approval engine.

Problem: the model context protocol is an interoperability adapter, not the only internal interface and not inherently a permission system. A loopback HTTP transport needs real authentication and origin validation, and the HTTP transport has a token-audience rule: a server must validate that a bearer token was issued for it as the audience, and a client must not send a token issued by, or intended for, another server. Tool descriptions can also change after approval, which is a supply-chain risk.

Proposed work: implement a transport layer that starts, connects to, health-checks, restarts and stops registered tool servers over at least one standard transport. For any HTTP transport, enforce the token-audience rule (validate the token was issued for this server) and apply the same per-session authentication and origin rejection as the local control surface. Expose only the tools a server actually registers, and treat a server as an external tool provider whose results are untrusted and carry no authority. Record each server's tool definitions (name, description, schema) at first approval; a changed name, description or schema must re-prompt. That re-approval is OWNED by the capability registry and grant broker (C14 for the tool capability registry and manifests, C12 for grants), so this task surfaces the current definitions and delegates the approval decision to them; it must not build a second approval engine. Nothing is auto-updated, and an inspector view lets a person read every server's tool descriptions without a model in the loop. A server that needs no network runs with egress disabled. Provide a health canary that reports ok, degraded or failed with the mode and the cause, and never paper over a missing server.

Acceptance criteria: a server starts and its tools are listed; a stopped or unreachable server is reported failed or absent; a degraded server is named with its cause; a changed tool definition routes to C14/C12 for re-approval rather than being auto-accepted; an HTTP transport rejects a token not issued for that server and a browser-origin request; a tool result cannot grant authority.

Dependencies: A02 contracts. Evidence: baseline server registry and health canary; the identity lane's MCP token-audience and tool-definition findings. Gaps: the transport is the service process boundary decided in A01, with the MCP server owned by the service rather than by a shell. Phase M1.

Optional by design: this transport is deferred to M3 unless a real first-slice dependency proves otherwise.

Out of scope: permission decisions, the internal API, a central broker and any home-grown approval engine; optional transport deferred to M3. Interfaces and ownership: consumes A02 contracts and the C14 registry, and validates token audience for remote servers. Validation: a future lifecycle test for server start and stop, plus a token issued for a different audience being rejected. Evidence: public model context protocol specification (https://modelcontextprotocol.io) and internal planning research (non-public, no link).

The MCP transport stays an adapter seam owned by the service. It is not a native bridge into the companion and it carries no operating-system authority.

nodes.title: [A15] Core event outbox and crash recovery
nodes.body:
User outcome: nothing important is lost when the core or the machine stops mid-operation, and a restart can tell exactly what happened.

Problem: the core will dispatch actions, emit notifications and advance jobs. If it writes an effect and then crashes before recording it, the user sees a lie. An outbox pattern makes the record and the effect recoverable.

Proposed work: implement an append-only core event outbox in the application store. Every state transition and every intent to act is written to the outbox before the effect and marked delivered after, with an idempotent delivery marker. On startup, scan the outbox for undelivered records and reconcile them, distinguishing an effect that certainly did not start from one that may have landed (unknown). Provide a bounded retention and compaction policy so the outbox does not grow without limit, and a replay tool for support that reads only redacted records. The outbox must survive a hard kill, and a restart must not double-apply an effect whose delivery marker is present.

Acceptance criteria: a hard kill between write and effect recovers to the correct state on restart; an undelivered record is reconciled and marked unknown when appropriate; a delivered record is never re-applied; retention bounds the outbox size; a support replay shows redacted records only.

Dependencies: A04 for storage. Evidence: the roadmap contract crash-recovery requirement. Gaps: the exact compaction policy is proposed. Phase M1.

Writer and reader guarantee: a single writer appends to the outbox inside the same short transaction as the state change it describes, so the record and the change are atomic and a reader never sees one without the other. Startup reconciliation is bounded and idempotent, and it must be safe to run twice. The outbox lives in the Didi application store from A04, not in any sibling store. A support replay is read-only and redacted, and it must never re-dispatch an effect; replay reconstructs history for a human, it does not retry work.

Ownership note: this is the one generic transactional event and delivery outbox for the product. Other leaves consume it rather than building their own retry queues.

Out of scope: a second retry queue, a workflow engine and the task lifecycle itself, which belongs to A05. Interfaces and ownership: the one generic transactional outbox consumed by A08, D08 and notifications. Validation: a future crash-recovery walk that kills the core between outbox write and effect and asserts reconciliation rather than duplication. Evidence: internal planning decisions on outbox semantics (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [A16] Diagnostics with redacted evidence
nodes.body:
User outcome: when something goes wrong, the user or a maintainer can get a useful diagnostic packet built from a typed allowlist of fields that carries no secret or raw body, and that does not claim more than it can prove.

Problem: diagnostics are the usual way private data leaks, and an absolute claim that a packet never contains secrets is unprovable. The packet must be structurally incapable of carrying a credential or a raw payload, and the claim must be bounded to what the design guarantees.

Proposed work: implement a diagnostics collector that assembles a support packet from the core event outbox and health state using a TYPED ALLOWLIST: every field is a typed, enumerated value (timestamps, states, error classes, versions, counts, redacted summaries), and there is no free-text field a caller can fill with a raw body or a credential. Assert structurally that no code path can pass a credential value or a raw body to the writer, by type and interface, and add a leak test that injects a secret-shaped value into every free-text field and confirms it is refused or redacted. Add a redaction pass as a second, empirical line, and note that user-visible exports share this same writer, so the guarantee is one writer rather than one call site. Bound the corpus: assemble the packet from a bounded, declared set of sources, only the local outbox and health state, never by following a report path or reading a session transcript. Default to local-only: the packet is written to a local file, previewed to the user with every section shown, and uploaded only on explicit user action. State the limitation honestly: a typed allowlist plus redaction is not a proof that no secret can ever appear; the structural criterion is the primary defence and the redaction test is the empirical backstop.

Acceptance criteria: the writer's interface admits only typed allowlist fields, proven by a structural test; a secret-shaped value injected into any free-text field is refused or redacted; the packet is assembled from a bounded declared corpus and never reads a transcript or follows a report path; a user preview precedes any share; no absolute leakproof claim is made.

Dependencies: A15 for the outbox. Evidence: the contract's public-safety rules and the identity lane's diagnostics and log finding (structural criterion first, redaction test second, exports share the writer). Gaps: the allowlist must be extended as new sources appear. Phase M1.

Out of scope: raw request or response bodies, secrets, and any completeness claim beyond the typed allowlist. Interfaces and ownership: consumes audit events from A05, A08 and A15, redacts them, and feeds support plus the A17 gate. Validation: a future redaction check that feeds representative secrets and private paths and fails on any leak. Evidence: internal planning decisions on diagnostics (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [A17] First daily-loop integration and lean validation gate
nodes.body:
User outcome: the first daily loop works end to end from one account, and a contributor can prove a change is safe locally with no paid continuous integration and no dependence on a shared runner.

Problem: the product must be buildable and testable by a colleague on their own machine, and the roadmap forbids paid continuous integration. Integration of the first slice spans several producers, so without one owner the seams between them are tested only by hand or not at all. A heavy gate would be skipped; a nonexistent one lets regressions through.

Proposed work: own the first daily-loop integration scenario and the lean local validation gate. The runnable scenario walks one account to an evidence-linked promise, a local plan, a reminder, a conversation, an unsent draft, next-session recall, correction or closure, and no resurrection after closure. It also exercises core restart, sleep and wake, expired or revoked token, egress refusal and an unknown effect outcome. The lean gate stays local: contract conformance against the A02 fixtures, a schema migration forward and back on a scratch store, a redaction check over diagnostics, a crash-recovery walk over the A15 outbox, and a small set of synthetic end-to-end scenarios. It runs offline, without a real account, and reports a machine-readable result. There is no second test platform and no daily full-suite schedule, and this task implements no application code.

Acceptance criteria: the scenario runs offline on a clean machine with synthetic fixtures; each gate part runs alone; a deliberately broken migration or a leaked secret fails the gate; the result is machine-readable; the scenario records its evidence against the actual slice producers rather than mocks.

Dependencies: the producers of the scenario it integrates, listed in depends_on, and the A02 fixtures. Evidence: internal planning decisions on the first slice, the no-paid-CI rule and baseline local-quality conventions (non-public, no link). Gaps: the scenario set grows with the product; nothing here is claimed to pass yet.

Determinism and isolation: fixtures are synthetic and frozen so a result does not depend on a live account, a private store or a real transcript, and each part runs in a scratch store that is discarded. The crash-recovery walk kills and restarts the core between the outbox write and the effect and asserts the reconciled state, exercising the A15 guarantee rather than a mock. Out of scope: no application code, no second test platform and no daily full-suite schedule. Interfaces and ownership: the scenario integrates the other producers through the A02 contracts and the A15 outbox. Validation: the runnable scenario is the validation, recorded with its machine-readable result at implementation time; nothing is claimed to pass now.

nodes.title: [A18] Latency, energy and resource measurement and budgets
nodes.body:
User outcome: Didi feels responsive and does not drain the battery, and the project can prove it with numbers rather than adjectives.

Problem: the platform lane's latency and energy figures are design targets, not measured facts, and it explicitly requires a measured energy delta before shipping an always-listening component. The product must not assert performance it has not recorded.

Proposed work: implement a measurement harness that records latency for the observable stages (capture to first token, first token to first audio, full turn), resource use per turn, and the always-listening energy delta where that feature is enabled, together with the host pressure at measurement time and the pinned versions. Define proposed budgets (a latency target per stage and an energy ceiling for any background listening) and make a budget breach visible, not silently swallowed. Measure the idle and background path as well as the active turn. Keep measurement local and lightweight, and never generate artificial host load.

Acceptance criteria: a measurement run records per-stage latency, resource use and host pressure with versions; a budget breach is reported; the background listening path is measured separately from the active turn; results are reproducible on the target host; no synthetic load is used.

Dependencies: A03 for lifecycle and A07 for orchestration. Evidence: the platform lane's latency targets and its energy gate. Gaps: no baseline numbers exist yet; the targets are proposed until measured. Phase M2.

Separation of measurement from optimization: this task records numbers and surfaces a breach; it does not tune the product or promise a figure. The background listening path is measured separately because an always-on microphone has a different energy profile from an active turn, and the platform lane gates that feature on a measured delta. Host pressure is recorded with each run so a result taken under contention is labelled rather than reported as a baseline. No artificial load is generated on a shared machine, and the harness stays the only scheduler for coding work.

Out of scope: product tuning, claims of measured results, and the always-listening feature itself; every target stays proposed. Interfaces and ownership: the measurement harness consumed by the voice targets of F04 and F06, the F14 wake gate and the A17 validation gate. Validation: a future measurement run recording latency stages, resource use and the always-listening energy delta together with host pressure, with a breach made visible. Evidence: platform research targets (non-public, no link), which are proposals to falsify, not measurements.

nodes.title: [A19] Portable command and query service seam
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** The Mac companion and a browser client must reach the
same assistant behaviour without embedding domain logic in either client. Outcome: one service
process exposing REST JSON commands and queries plus a server-sent progress stream, running on
the loopback interface today and on a virtual machine later with no contract change.

**Scope and deliverables.** A versioned request and response envelope reused from A02, one
command endpoint that returns an accepted job identifier, one query endpoint, a progress stream
that emits state transitions for a job, a single-writer handle on the SQLite store owned by A04,
health and readiness endpoints, and a conformance fixture set that any client can replay.

**Out of scope.** A mandatory WebSocket framework, multi-user authentication, cloud hosting,
multi-writer synchronisation, and any endpoint that mutates domain state without an intent
record.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the wire contract and the process
boundary. A02 owns envelope versioning, A03 owns process lifecycle, A04 owns persistence, C15
owns what may leave the process, and F19 consumes the contract. The service exposes A03's
control surface rather than inventing a parallel one.

**Dependencies.** A02 for the envelopes, A03 for lifecycle and A04 for storage.

**Acceptance and adverse.** A job accepted, progressed and completed is observable from a second
process. Adverse scenarios: the service is killed between acceptance and completion and the job
resumes; a client replays a duplicate command and the effect is not doubled; the progress stream
drops and a reconnect resumes from the last observed sequence number without replaying
completed steps.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario drives the real process over the loopback
interface and measures round-trip latency and reconnect behaviour, reported as measured numbers
rather than as a claim. Public reference: https://nodejs.org/api/http.html for the transport and
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events for the stream. Privacy
baseline: no field in the fixture set carries private content, and the internal fixture corpus is
non-public and is not linked here.

The listen address is configuration rather than a constant: the loopback interface for the laptop alone, or a named local network interface when a paired device on the same network must reach the same process. A request from an unpaired client on a bound interface is refused before any command is dispatched.

nodes.title: [A20] Container image, VM runbook and Linux service host
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** The service must be deployable on a Linux virtual
machine from a written runbook by someone who did not build it. Outcome: one container image
built from the same entry point the laptop runs, one systemd unit, and a runbook that takes a
clean host to a healthy service.

**Scope and deliverables.** A container image with a pinned runtime version and a non-root user,
a systemd unit with restart policy, memory and file-descriptor bounds and log routing, a runbook
covering host preparation, first start, upgrade, rollback and teardown, provider-interchangeable
notes for two major providers, and a documented single-writer rule stating that the virtual
machine and the laptop must never both hold the authority epoch.

**Out of scope.** Buying or provisioning any virtual machine, managed database services, a
Kubernetes control plane, autoscaling, and any provider lock-in that the runbook cannot express
as a note.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the image, the unit file and the runbook.
A19 owns the wire contract, A15 owns the durable outbox and crash recovery, A21 owns secret
references, C21 owns the authority epoch. The unit file starts the same binary the loopback mode
starts, so no second deployment path exists.

**Dependencies.** A19 for the service seam and A15 for crash recovery and outbox durability.

**Acceptance and adverse.** A person following only the runbook reaches a healthy service, a
restart preserves state, and a rollback to the previous image succeeds. Adverse scenarios: the
machine reboots mid-job and the job resumes; the store directory is read-only and startup fails
loudly instead of degrading; a second instance is started against the same store and refuses to
take the writer lock.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario performs the runbook against a disposable
Linux host and records the measured start time, restart behaviour and refusal of a second
writer. Public references: https://systemd.io/ and https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/.
Privacy baseline: the runbook contains synthetic host names and example.invalid values only.

An unreachable previous holder is not a reason to promote a new holder automatically. The runbook requires the fence to be demonstrated first: the new holder shows that the old holder cannot write, and only then is it promoted. An old holder that returns with its own restored store is refused the writer lock and the epoch rather than merged, and the acceptance case for this is run against a separate restored store, not only against two processes sharing one store.

nodes.title: [A21] Secret reference broker and VM credential provisioning
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** A deployed service needs model and provider
credentials, and the image and repository must never contain a value. Outcome: a broker that
resolves named secret references at call time, with a documented provisioning path for a
virtual machine.

**Scope and deliverables.** A secret reference vocabulary (provider, account, purpose), a
resolver that reads from the host's protected store or the provider's secret service and caches
only in memory, a rule that references but never values may appear in configuration files,
logs or error text, a rotation procedure, and a provisioning note covering file permissions on
the host.

**Out of scope.** Storing credential values in the repository, in the image, in a build
artifact or in model context, and any shared long-lived credential across two users.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the resolver and the reference format.
C02 owns the credential records and the account binding, C15 owns the route table that decides
whether egress is permitted, A20 owns the host, and A16 owns redacted diagnostics. The resolver
is the only place that turns a reference into a value.

**Dependencies.** C02 for credential records and C15 for the egress route table.

**Acceptance and adverse.** A call that needs a credential resolves it, and a call whose route
is not permitted never resolves it at all. Adverse scenarios: a missing reference fails closed
with a message that names the reference and not a value; a log line and an error payload are
scanned and contain no secret shape; rotation replaces a value without a restart.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario scans the built image, the repository and a
captured log for secret shapes and asserts zero matches, and records the measured scan scope.
Public references: https://cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs and
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/intro.html. Privacy baseline: no
account identifier, project identifier or host name from a real provider appears in this
repository.

nodes.title: [A22] Backup, restore and migration rehearsal on synthetic data
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Once the store can live on a virtual machine, a
corrupted or lost host must not lose the assistant. Outcome: a backup schedule, a restore
procedure and a rehearsal that is performed on synthetic data before any real deployment.

**Scope and deliverables.** A consistent snapshot method for the SQLite store, an encrypted
backup artifact with a retention rule, a restore procedure that verifies integrity before the
service starts, a documented recovery time and recovery point, and a rehearsal script that
generates a synthetic corpus, loads it, backs it up, restores it into a clean host and compares
row counts and content digests.

**Out of scope.** Real personal data in any rehearsal, replication or a hot standby, any
multi-writer failover, and any claim that a rehearsal proves production readiness.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the backup and restore procedure and the
rehearsal. A04 owns the storage schema and migration primitives, A20 owns the host, and C15
governs where a backup artifact may be written. The rehearsal reuses A04 migrations rather than
a parallel loader.

**Dependencies.** A04 for storage and migrations and A19 for the running service contract.

**Acceptance and adverse.** A backup taken from a running service restores into a clean host and
the service answers a query against the restored store. Adverse scenarios: a truncated backup
artifact is rejected before startup rather than half-loaded; a restore onto a store with a newer
schema stops; a rehearsal that drops a table is detected by the integrity comparison.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario runs the rehearsal on synthetic data and
records measured artifact size, restore duration and the row-count and digest comparison.
Public reference: https://www.sqlite.org/backup.html. Privacy baseline: the synthetic corpus
contains generated names and example.invalid addresses, and the rehearsal fixture is non-public
and is not linked here.

nodes.title: [A23] Suite endpoint configuration and independent installation
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Sibling tools and sibling Lux packages must be able
to address this assistant without depending on its internals or on a shared install location.
Outcome: one declared base URL and capability document, and a packaging rule that keeps every
package independently installable.

**Scope and deliverables.** A discovery document served by the service that names the contract
version, the available endpoints and the required scopes, an endpoint configuration file or
environment variable that clients read, a rule that the assistant shares no runtime directory
with another package, and a note recording that migrating another repository or service is a
separate decision owned elsewhere.

**Out of scope.** Changing another repository, service or package, assuming a shared database,
and any coupling that makes installing one package require installing another.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the discovery document and the endpoint
configuration format. A19 owns the contract, A21 owns secret references, C14 owns the capability
registry and adapter manifests, and A02 owns envelopes. The discovery document is generated from
C14's registry rather than hand-maintained.

**Dependencies.** A19 for the service contract and A21 for credential references.

**Acceptance and adverse.** A fresh client configures one base URL and completes a query. Adverse
scenarios: the service is unreachable and the client reports the configured endpoint rather than
a hard-coded default; a client requests a contract version the service does not serve and is
refused with the supported range; installing the client package touches no path owned by the
service.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario installs the client package into an isolated
environment and verifies it completes a query against a loopback service with only the base URL
configured, recording the measured step count. Public reference:
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110 for the HTTP semantics reused here. Privacy baseline: the
discovery document carries no personal data and no host identifier.

nodes.title: [A24] Hosting boundary and cloud egress data classes
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Moving the assistant to a virtual machine changes what
leaves the laptop, and the user asked for that boundary to be explicit rather than incidental.
Outcome: a written hosting boundary and an egress rule evaluated at the process boundary of the
deployed service.

**Scope and deliverables.** A host boundary statement naming what the deployed service owns
(its own store, its own authority epoch, its own credentials) and what it does not (the local
operating system, another repository, another assistant instance), a data-class vocabulary reused
from C15, an egress decision evaluated before any outbound request leaves the service, and a
recorded distinction between hosting this assistant and separately migrating other services.

**Out of scope.** Any grant of local operating-system authority to a cloud process, any change to
another repository, any implicit approval to deploy, and any egress of credential values.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the hosting boundary statement and the
service-side egress hook. C15 owns the route table and the data classes, C12 owns grants and the
effect broker, A20 owns the host, A21 owns credentials. The service calls C15's decision point
instead of restating the policy.

**Dependencies.** C15 for the route table and A20 for the deployed host.

**Acceptance and adverse.** A request whose destination and purpose are not in the route table
is refused before it leaves the process. Adverse scenarios: a cloud process attempts a
device-level effect and is refused because it holds no device grant; a classified payload is
attempted to an unlisted destination and is blocked; a denied route degrades to a local summary
rather than sending.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario drives classified payloads at the deployed
service and records the measured block and degradation counts. Public reference:
https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/security for the shared-responsibility framing.
Privacy baseline: the boundary statement names no real project, account or host.

nodes.title: [B01] Evidence and source identity model
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
Every memory or knowledge item Didi holds must be traceable to a source. Without a shared identity model, recall cannot be trusted, corrections cannot propagate, and caches cannot be invalidated correctly. Outcome: a single, versioned source-reference shape that every other memory feature uses, so a recalled assertion can always answer where it came from and how current it is.

## Scope and deliverables
Define a versioned source-reference record with fields for provider, account, source identifier, revision or content hash, span (offset range or verbatim quote interval), coverage level, freshness, and availability. Define a local record shape for the application store owned by this track, plus a validation helper that rejects a reference missing its identity fields and marks an unavailable source explicitly rather than dropping it. Provide synthetic fixtures covering a present source, a stale source, and a missing source. Expose a small read API that other memory features call.

## Out of scope
Fetching or authenticating sources (connectors track), commitment records (commitments track), any shared database migration (sequenced by runtime track), and any user interface.

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/memory. Cross-track fixture conventions are requested from A02 so the shape is shared without racing migrations. The model is informed by the verified behavior of the existing private knowledge service, whose retrieval exposes source metadata and per-claim spans but not full text. Reuse that proven separation of pointed-to source versus extracted claim; do not copy code or prompts.

## Dependencies
None. This is the foundational leaf for the whole epic, so independent product contracts can proceed without waiting on a host spike.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given a reference with all fields, when stored and read back, then it is unchanged. Given a reference missing a provider or source id, when validated, then it is rejected with the missing field named. Given an unavailable source, when read, then availability reports unavailable and the claim plus span is still returned, labelled a paraphrase. Given an app restart, then references persist. Given an unknown provider string, then validation fails closed.

## Validation
A future contract test over the fixtures above: round-trip, missing-field rejection, unavailable-source reporting, restart persistence, and the bounded diagnostic corpus test that asserts no source or account identifiers appear in generated diagnostics. No existing test command is claimed.

## Privacy and performance
Source identifiers and account identifiers are personal data. The typed source record is excluded from the diagnostic writer by construction, and a bounded corpus test asserts that generated diagnostics contain no source or account identifiers. The record shape stays small so lookup is cheap; validation makes no network call.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on the existing private knowledge service source-metadata behavior: non-public, no public links. The separation of source pointer, extracted claim, and verbatim span is verified there and is the model this leaf standardizes.

nodes.title: [B02] Local voice and session transcript originals
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
Didi must own its own conversation originals so recall does not depend on any external service and so a session can be re-read after restart. Outcome: an append-only local store of Didi's own voice and text session transcripts, authoritative for Didi, that survives crashes and conversation end. This leaf is deliberately limited to Didi's OWN originals. External provider transcripts are resolved in B03, and recall over these originals is B05; the three concerns are kept separate.

## Scope and deliverables
Define a session-transcript record (session id, channel, start and end, ordered turns with speaker, revision counter, a committed watermark) in the application store. Implement an append protocol that commits turns incrementally so a crash loses at most the uncommitted tail, and a recovery routine that repairs a partial trailing record on startup. Add a retention hook so policy can later age or forget whole sessions. Provide synthetic fixtures for a normal session, an interrupted session, and a resumed session.

## Out of scope
Microphone capture, audio devices and live streaming (native-experience and voice tracks), external provider transcripts (B03), and speech cleanup quality beyond making the stored text faithful to what was captured.

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/memory. Consumes the B01 reference model for the session's own identity. Cleans display scaffolding from model-generated transcript text using a deterministic text-cleanup step rather than storing raw serialized tool syntax; this pattern is reused conceptually from the existing voice stack but no code or prompt is copied.

## Dependencies
B01, because every transcript is a source with an identity and a revision that other features reference.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given a session, when it ends, then all committed turns are readable after restart. Given a crash mid-write, when the app restarts, then the last committed turn is intact and the partial tail is discarded and reported. Given speech cancellation, when the user stops, then turns committed before the cancel remain. Given a corrupt tail, then repair succeeds without losing committed data. Given a session with no speech yet, then an empty transcript is valid.

## Validation
A future integration scenario that appends turns, simulates a crash, restarts, and asserts committed turns survive and the tail is reported as discarded. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and authority
Session originals are among the most sensitive local data. They are local only, never routed to a cache or service by default, and the retention hook is the only path that may age them. No model call is made to store a turn.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on an existing voice stack's session persistence and deterministic transcript cleanup: non-public, no public links. The append-and-watermark and scaffolding-cleanup patterns are observed there; this leaf reimplements them for a single-user local store.

nodes.title: [B03] External transcript resolution and coverage
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
An important memory often refers to an external meeting or document. Didi must resolve the original through a supported provider when it is authorized and available, and must never imply full coverage from a summary. Outcome: a resolver that fetches, reports coverage honestly, and falls back to a labelled paraphrase when it cannot. The verified absence of full transcript text in the existing private knowledge service applies to that service's retrieval surface and to the optional adapter that consumes it (B06), NOT to the ecosystem as a whole: Didi's own originals (B02) and external providers may hold full text, which this leaf resolves.

## Scope and deliverables
Define a coverage report with values such as full-text, claims-only, metadata-only, and unavailable. Implement per-provider resolution that consumes the connectors track's adapters rather than talking to providers directly. When an original is resolved, store it only as an optional versioned cache (provider, account, source id, revision, fetched-at), never as new source truth. When it cannot be resolved, return the retained claim plus span labelled a paraphrase. Provide synthetic fixtures for a resolvable document, a metadata-only reference, and an unavailable one.

## Out of scope
Building a new harvester, storing full copies of every transcript by default, and OAuth or account setup (connectors track).

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/memory. Depends on the shared source reference (B01) and on connector adapters for providers. Reuses the verified behavior of the existing private knowledge service, which exposes claims, spans and source metadata but not full text; that service is consumed through its adapter (B06), not re-harvested.

## Dependencies
B01 for the reference shape; B02 because external references are often attached to a local session original.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given a reference to an available original with permission, when resolved, then coverage reports full-text and the cache records the source revision. Given only claims are available, then coverage reports claims-only and does not claim a transcript. Given an unavailable source, then coverage reports unavailable and a paraphrase fallback is returned and labelled. Given a revoked grant, then resolution fails closed and no cached copy is served as current. Given a provider whose content changed, then the cached revision is marked stale.

## Validation
A future scenario per provider stub that asserts the coverage value and the fallback label for each case. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and performance
Resolution requires explicit authorization and must respect provider egress policy. A miss is not evidence that a fact is false. Cache size and fetch latency are bounded and measured later, not assumed.

## Evidence
Private baseline research: the existing private knowledge service stores source metadata and spans but not full text, which is scoped to that service and its adapter, not to the whole ecosystem. A resolver is therefore required for verbatim use of external documents. Non-public, no public links.

nodes.title: [B04] Session gists with evidence links
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
Raw transcripts are too large to recall or to place in context. Didi needs a short, faithful gist of each session whose assertions are linked to evidence, so recall can be both fast and checkable. Outcome: a gist record per session where no unsupported claim is allowed.

## Scope and deliverables
Define a gist record (session id, headline, short summary, list of evidence links to source spans, created revision, provenance class). Implement a rule that every assertion in the gist must resolve to at least one evidence link or be marked as an inference. Compute gists from the local original (B02) and, where available, from resolved external text (B03). Store gists locally with revision history so an edit is a new revision, not an overwrite. Provide fixtures for a well-supported gist, a gist with an unlinked assertion, and an edited gist.

## Out of scope
Persona learning from gists (E04), commitment extraction (E07), and any company knowledge export.

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/memory. Uses B01 references for evidence links and B02 originals as the primary input. The evidence-linked-assertion pattern is reused conceptually from the existing extraction discipline that requires each claim to cite a verbatim span; no prompt or code is copied.

## Dependencies
B01 for evidence identity; B02 because a gist is derived from a local original.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given a session with support, when a gist is produced, then every non-inference assertion has at least one evidence link. Given an assertion with no support, then it is dropped or marked an inference, never presented as fact. Given a user edit, then a new revision is created and the prior one remains recoverable. Given a restart, then gists persist. Given a session with almost no content, then the gist is short rather than padded.

## Validation
A future unit and integration scenario that asserts the evidence-link rule, revision behavior, and restart persistence. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and performance
Gists are private and derived; they must not be shared to any company surface without the curation path. Gisting is bounded work and must not run a model call on a blind timer.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on the existing extraction discipline that requires a verbatim evidence span per claim: non-public, no public links.

The gist is the retrieval unit for the context economy: the prompt receives the bounded digest, and originals are expanded only when a turn asks for them.

nodes.title: [B05] Exact and semantic session recall
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
A person expects to ask about something that happened earlier, sometimes with the exact words and sometimes only by meaning, and to get the right session back even with typos. Outcome: a local recall capability over Didi's own gists and originals (B04, B02), and over externally resolved text where available (B03), that answers by exact term and by meaning, and always returns the evidence and source behind a result. Recall is distinct from external resolution (B03) and from the optional knowledge adapter (B06): recall reads Didi's own store first.

## Scope and deliverables
Implement a local index with at least a full-text arm, an optional semantic arm, and a merge that returns gist plus evidence plus source reference. Rank by relevance, recency, and provenance class. Support typo and spacing tolerance. Define behavior for an empty result that is explicit rather than a weak guess. Provide a rebuild path when the index is stale or the embedding model changes (detailed in B18). Provide fixtures with known expected results.

## Out of scope
Company knowledge search (optional adapter, connectors track), cross-user search, and any ranking that hides provenance.

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/memory. Depends on B01 references and B04 gists. The hybrid full-text plus optional-semantic shape is reused conceptually from the existing private knowledge service's documented two-layer retrieval; no code is copied.

## Dependencies
B01 for source identity; B04 because recall returns gists, not raw transcripts.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given a query with an exact term, when recalled, then the matching session is first. Given a misspelled query, then fuzzy matching still finds the intended session. Given a query with no match, then the result is explicitly empty and is not presented as a confident answer. Given a stale index, then a rebuild is triggered and the answer is marked provisional until complete. Given two users, then each only sees their own sessions. Given a restart, then recall works from the persisted index.

## Validation
A future scenario that seeds synthetic sessions and asserts top results, fuzzy matching, empty-result behavior, and per-user isolation. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and performance
Recall must be per-user isolated. Latency and index size are proposed targets to validate, not measured facts. A recall miss is no evidence a fact is false.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on the existing private knowledge service's two-layer retrieval and its honest empty-result behavior: non-public, no public links.

nodes.title: [B06] Optional private knowledge adapter
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
Some users already run a private knowledge service holding general knowledge and retrieval. Didi should be able to use it when present without depending on it, and without creating a second authoritative copy. Outcome: an optional adapter that maps the service's results into Didi's source-reference model and degrades cleanly when the service is absent.

## Scope and deliverables
Implement an adapter client over the service's supported protocol. Map returned concepts and claims into Didi's local source-reference and evidence-class model. Define dormant behavior when the service is not installed or not running, so core Didi works normally. Define behavior when the service is present but a call fails: return an explicit error, never a fake empty success. Provide fixtures for present, absent, and failing service states. Document that the service's retrieval exposes claims, spans and source metadata, and does not expose full transcript text for that service (B03 handles original resolution; this absence is scoped to this adapter, not the ecosystem).

## Out of scope
Reading or writing the service's database directly, making the service mandatory, and copying its full contents into Didi.

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/memory. Consumes the shared contract conventions from A02 and the B01 reference model. The adapter treats the service as an authoritative owner for general private knowledge and itself as a projection; it must never become a second writer for that knowledge.

## Dependencies
B01 for reference mapping; A02 so the adapter uses the shared cross-track contract and fixtures rather than inventing its own.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given the service is absent, when Didi starts and runs the core loop, then everything works and the adapter is dormant. Given a successful call, then results carry provenance and an evidence class. Given a call failure, then the error is explicit. Given the service returns only summaries, then Didi does not treat them as full coverage. Given a revoke or disconnect, then cached results are marked unavailable. Given direct table access is attempted by mistake, then it is rejected by design.

## Validation
A future contract test with present, absent and failing stubs asserting dormancy, explicit failure, and provenance mapping. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and performance
Do not export private knowledge to any company surface. The adapter must not write to the service's tables. Cache freshness follows B03.

## Evidence
Private baseline research confirming the service exposes claims, spans and metadata but not full text, and that it is optional. Non-public, no public links.

Optional by design: this adapter is deferred to M3 unless a real first-slice dependency proves otherwise.

nodes.title: [B07] Authoritative explicit preferences
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
A user tells Didi how they want things done, and that statement must win over anything inferred or retrieved elsewhere. Without an authoritative preference store, a retrieved insight can silently override user intent. Outcome: typed explicit preferences owned by Didi that take precedence in behavior, with inspectable provenance.

## Scope and deliverables
Define a preference record (key, value type, value, evidence class user_stated, revision, timestamps, scope). Implement read and write APIs and a conflict rule stating that an explicit preference beats an external insight, which is treated as evidence or history rather than a second mutable preference. Define a clear/remove operation that removes a preference rather than setting a falsy value. Provide fixtures for a scalar preference, a list preference, a corrected preference, and a removed preference.

## Out of scope
Implicit persona adaptation (B14), company-level policy overlays (authority track), and preferences stored by any external service.

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/memory. Uses B01 references for provenance. Exposed to the context compiler (B11) and the onboarding flow (B13). The separation of explicit user statements from model-derived facts is reused conceptually from the accepted evidence-class decision; no private prompt is copied.

## Dependencies
B01 for provenance identity. Independent of the host spike so preference work is not needlessly serialized.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given a stated preference and a conflicting retrieved insight, when a decision is made, then the preference wins and the insight is shown as history. Given a correction, then a new revision exists and the old value is recoverable. Given removal, then the preference is gone and not defaulted to a falsy value. Given a restart, then preferences persist. Given an unknown key, then write is rejected. Given two users, then preferences are isolated.

## Validation
A future contract test that asserts precedence, revisioning, removal, restart persistence and per-user isolation. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and authority
Preferences are personal and local. They must never be exported to a company surface. Authority for changing them is the user only.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on the accepted rule that explicit user statements and derived inferences have separate evidence classes: non-public, no public links.

nodes.title: [B08] Correction, conflict and suppression semantics
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
Corrected or forgotten information must not creep back from a stale index, a cache, or a background extraction. Topical contradictions and cancellations must resolve deterministically. Outcome: a lifecycle and suppression layer that is consulted before planning and before recall surfaces an item, so suppressed things stay suppressed.

## Scope and deliverables
Define an overlay record with operations assert, forbid and keep-unresolved, a revision, an active or retired state, and a provenance field. Define a read-before-plan gate that any recall step must consult. Define the rule that background extraction cannot silently reopen a suppressed or forgotten item. Define conflict handling for two sources that disagree: both are retained, an unresolved marker is set, and no silent winner is chosen. Expose the gate as a shared interface so the commitments track reuses it instead of duplicating. Provide fixtures for a correction, a cancellation, a conflict, and a stale-index resurrection attempt.

## Out of scope
Commitment lifecycle ownership (commitments track owns the states; this leaf owns the mechanism), and any automatic merge of disagreeing facts.

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/memory. Uses B01 references and B04 gists. The overlay concept (assert, forbid, keep-unresolved with revision and state) is reused conceptually from an existing correction-overlay design in the baseline; no code is copied.

## Dependencies
B01 for identity; B04 because corrections most often target gist-level assertions.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given a forgotten item, when recall runs, then it never reappears even if the index still holds it. Given a forbidden value, when extraction re-proposes it, then it is blocked and not re-guessed. Given two disagreeing sources, then both are retained with an unresolved marker. Given a just-issued correction, then a pending-propagation state is reported honestly until projections refresh. Given a stale index, when it rebuilds, then suppressed items are excluded. Given a restart, then overlays persist.

## Validation
A future adverse scenario that attempts stale resurrection of a forgotten item and asserts suppression, plus conflict and pending-propagation cases. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and authority
Suppression is a user authority. A background process may not clear a suppression. Reporting pending propagation honestly is required so the user is not misled about deletion.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on an existing correction-overlay design with bind/forbid/keep-unresolved operations: non-public, no public links.

nodes.title: [B09] Export, forget and cache propagation
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
A user must be able to take their data out and to remove it, and removal must be honest about what is and is not deleted. Outcome: export, forget and cache-propagation operations with clear, truthful outcomes.

## Scope and deliverables
Define a portable export format covering preferences, gists, transcript originals, source references and overlays, with a documented, stable envelope. Define a forget operation that removes owned rows, writes a tombstone, invalidates derived caches and projections, and reports a propagation status per derived artifact, including a pending state. Define the rule that deleting a Didi memory does not claim deletion of an external source Didi does not own. Define a reingestion guard so a forgotten item cannot be re-added by a later extraction. Provide fixtures for full export, partial forget and a reingestion attempt.

## Out of scope
Deleting external provider data, deleting company knowledge, and any cryptographic erasure guarantee.

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/memory. Depends on B01 references, B07 preferences and B08 suppression. The tombstone and pending-propagation ideas are reused conceptually from the existing private knowledge service's delete, restore and tombstone behavior; no code is copied.

## Dependencies
B01 for references; B07 because preferences must be exportable and forgettable; B08 because forgetting must integrate with suppression.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given an export request, when run, then the output re-imports to an equivalent state. Given a forget request, when run, then owned rows are gone, a tombstone exists, and each derived artifact reports refreshed or pending. Given a later extraction re-proposes a forgotten item, then it is blocked. Given an external source Didi referenced, then the forget report says the external source was not deleted. Given a restart, then tombstones and pending states persist. Given a partially failed forget, then it reports the failure honestly rather than claiming success.

## Validation
A future scenario asserting export round-trip, forget completeness, reingestion blocking, and honest propagation reporting. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and authority
Forget is a user authority and must be honest. No zero-leak guarantee is promised; a derivative may lag until it refreshes, and that lag is reported.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on the existing private knowledge service's delete, restore and tombstone semantics: non-public, no public links.

nodes.title: [B10] Consolidation and retention
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
Unchecked, episodic session memory grows without limit and degrades recall. Outcome: episodic sessions consolidate into durable, source-linked facts under a retention policy, so memory stays lean and never silently loses something the user cared about.

## Scope and deliverables
Define consolidation rules that lift durable facts out of gists with a link back to the source gists. Define retention windows distinguishing durable knowledge, which is kept, from ephemeral notes, which may expire. Define the rule that retention expiry never deletes an explicit preference or a labelled commitment. Record a summary-provenance marker so a consolidated fact can name the sessions it came from. Provide fixtures for a consolidatable cluster, a durable preference that must survive, and an ephemeral note that expires.

## Out of scope
Persona adaptation (B14), commitment retention (commitments track), and any deletion of external sources.

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/memory. Depends on B04 gists and B05 recall. Retention and tombstone behavior reuse the concepts from B09 so there is one deletion path, not two.

## Dependencies
B04 for gists as the consolidation input; B05 because consolidation quality is judged through recall.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given several related gists, when consolidation runs, then a durable fact is produced and it links to its source gists. Given a durable preference, when retention runs, then it is never expired. Given an ephemeral note past its window, then it expires and is reported, not silently dropped. Given a restart, then consolidation state persists. Given a consolidation with no clear support, then no fact is created rather than a weak one.

## Validation
A future scenario that seeds related and unrelated gists and asserts consolidation, retention survival of preferences, and expiry reporting. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and performance
Consolidation is a coalesced background task, not a per-heartbeat model call. Expiry must never remove a user authority record.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on distinguishing durable versus ephemeral memory and on honest expired-versus-deleted reporting: non-public, no public links.

nodes.title: [B11] Bounded context compilation
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
A turn must receive the right memory without dumping everything, and the model must be able to tell a stated fact from an inference. Outcome: a deterministic context compiler that selects memory under a token budget and labels the evidence class of everything it includes.

## Scope and deliverables
Implement a compiler that takes a query or turn intent and returns a bounded context block assembled from preferences (B07), recall results (B05) and evidence-class tags (B17). Selection ranks by relevance, recency, evidence class and verification horizon. Ordering is deterministic for the same inputs. Produce an omission report listing what was left out and why. Provide fixtures at small, medium and over-budget sizes.

## Out of scope
Authoring the runtime prompt text, provider selection and streaming (runtime and voice tracks), and any model call inside the compiler.

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/memory; consumed by the runtime tool-turn layer. Depends on B05, B07 and B17. The compiler is a pure function so it is cheap to test. Reuse the concept of a bounded memory bundle appended to a base prompt; no private prompt text is copied.

## Dependencies
B05 for recall results; B07 so explicit preferences are always eligible; B17 so included items carry their evidence class.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given a small budget, when compiling, then the block fits and the most user-authoritative items are kept. Given an over-budget input, then the compiler trims and reports omissions. Given identical inputs, then output order is identical. Given one user's memory, then no string from another user appears. Given an inference, then it is labelled as such. Given a restart, then compilation is deterministic.

## Validation
A future unit scenario asserting budget compliance, deterministic ordering, evidence-class labelling, omission reporting and per-user isolation. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and performance
The compiler must not include private strings from other users and must not call a model. Compilation cost is bounded and measurable independently of network latency.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on bounded memory bundles and on evidence-class separation in retrieved context: non-public, no public links.

PLAN-R3 fixes the context economy: compile a concise source-linked digest and retrieve originals on demand. Full logs, mail archives and long transcripts are never placed in a model prompt wholesale.

nodes.title: [B12] Public Naya-inspired persona specification
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
The product needs one consistent character definition that is public, generic and carries no private prompt and no profile of a real person. Outcome: a public persona specification (tone, warmth, directness, wit, challenge, safety precedence, prohibitions) that every user shares, while personal facts stay private.

## Scope and deliverables
Author a specification document with sections for voice and register, humour boundaries, when to challenge versus comply, honesty and uncertainty, safety precedence, and explicit prohibitions such as no invented facts and no humour that overrides work. Provide synthetic behavioral examples, each labelled, and a boundary list that maps a request to the correct response class. Include a rule that the specification is style only and never contains personal data. Provide a fixture that compiles the style with placeholder facts to prove it carries no personal strings.

## Out of scope
Copying any existing private system prompt, authoring runtime prompt text, and any per-user personalization (B13).

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/persona. Consumed by onboarding (B13), gradual learning (B14) and the runtime. The idea of a shared style spine plus a separate per-person bundle is reused conceptually from the existing voice stack; the text is authored fresh and public.

## Dependencies
None. This can and should start immediately so it does not block independent work.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given the specification, when reviewed, then it contains no personal data and no private prompt text. Given a compile using the style plus placeholder facts, then no real person's strings appear. Given a humour request during a safety-critical task, then the safety precedence rule wins. Given a request for an invented fact, then the specification requires an explicit unknown answer. Given two users, then the style is identical and only their facts differ.

## Validation
A future documentation and fixture check asserting that the specification compiles with placeholders and leaks no personal data. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and authority
This artifact is published, so it must be public-safe by construction. It grants no authority and describes no credential handling.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on the separation of a shared style spine from a per-person memory bundle: non-public, no public links. No private prompt is reproduced.

PLAN-R3 maps the persona requirement to the authorized first-party Naya personality and system-prompt structure. That structure is generic and reusable; the private persona payload, family details and real transcripts remain private and are never published.

nodes.title: [B13] Private customization and onboarding
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
A new user needs to make Didi theirs without Didi shipping anyone else's profile. Outcome: a private onboarding flow that collects the minimum personal configuration, stores it locally, and is resettable.

## Scope and deliverables
Define the onboarding needs (display name, preferred tone knobs within the public spec, working hours or quiet defaults, allowed and forbidden topics, and a first preference set) as contracts and view models, with the UI owned by the native-experience track. Store all of it in local application state keyed to the user, using B07 for preference records. Provide a reset that returns to defaults without leaving residue. Require no network for onboarding. Provide fixtures for a fresh user, a user who resets, and two users on one machine.

## Out of scope
Account connection and OAuth (connectors track), persona adaptation (B14), and the visual design (native-experience track).

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/persona and core/memory. Depends on B07 for preferences and B12 for the allowed style range. Exposes view models other tracks render.

## Dependencies
B07 so preferences are stored authoritatively; B12 so tone choices stay within a public, safe range.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given a fresh install and no network, when onboarding completes, then Didi uses the collected configuration. Given two users on one machine, then each sees only their own configuration and preferences. Given a reset, then defaults return and no personal residue remains in active state. Given a tone choice outside the specification, then it is clamped to the allowed range. Given a restart, then onboarding results persist.

## Validation
A future scenario asserting local-only onboarding, per-user isolation, reset cleanliness and restart persistence. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and authority
Onboarding data is personal and local. No account is required and no personal data leaves the machine during onboarding. Forbidden topics are a user authority.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on the separation of generic style from per-person facts and on local per-user configuration: non-public, no public links.

Ownership note: this leaf owns private persona and preference content; onboarding mechanics belong to F10.

nodes.title: [B14] Gradual persona learning with inspectable provenance
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
The character should grow with the user, but growth must never silently rewrite facts or hide what was inferred. Outcome: gradual adaptation recorded as labelled derived inferences with an inspectable and revertible trail.

## Scope and deliverables
Define an adaptation record (trait or style note, derived_inference class, confidence, supporting evidence links, created revision, active or retired state). Implement a learning step that proposes adaptations from interactions without applying them as facts, a review path where the user can accept or reject, and a rollback that retires an adaptation and suppresses it from re-emerging (via B08). Provide fixtures for a proposed adaptation, an accepted one, a rejected one, and a rejected one that reappears and must stay suppressed.

## Out of scope
Rewriting the public persona specification, changing explicit preferences (B07 owns those), and any automatic application of an inference as a stated fact.

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/persona. Depends on B08 for suppression, B12 for the style frame and B17 for evidence-class tagging. The rule that an inference is never auto-bound is reused conceptually from the accepted evidence-class decision.

## Dependencies
B08 so rejected adaptations stay suppressed; B12 so proposals stay within the public style; B17 so adaptations carry a correct evidence class.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given an interaction pattern, when learning runs, then an adaptation is proposed with a derived_inference label and supporting evidence, not applied as fact. Given acceptance, then it is active and inspectable. Given rejection, then it is retired and a later proposal of the same kind is suppressed. Given a restart, then adaptation state persists. Given a pattern with weak support, then no adaptation is created. Given a user asks why Didi speaks a certain way, then the supporting evidence is shown.

## Validation
A future scenario asserting proposal-only behavior, accept, reject, suppression of recurrence, and inspectability. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and authority
Learning is derived and local. It never overrides explicit preferences and never becomes a stated fact. Rejection is a durable user authority.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on provenance-classed adaptation and on the rule that a model-inferred item stays proposed until confirmed: non-public, no public links.

nodes.title: [B15] Memory inspector services
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
A user cannot trust memory they cannot see. Outcome: services behind a memory inspector that list what Didi holds, explain where it came from, allow edits and forgetting, and show what is suppressed.

## Scope and deliverables
Define read services for preferences, gists, consolidated facts, adaptations and suppressed items, each item showing its evidence class and source reference. Define edit and forget actions that route through B07, B08 and B09 rather than writing rows directly. Define view models for a future inspector UI owned by the native-experience track. Provide fixtures for a mixed list, an item with a pending promotion, and a suppressed item.

## Out of scope
Building the UI (native-experience track), and any direct database write from the UI layer.

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/memory. Depends on B07, B08 and B10. Exposes services and view models only; it is a projection and navigation surface over the authoritative stores.

## Dependencies
B07 for preference items; B08 for suppression state; B10 so consolidated facts appear with their provenance.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given a list request, when served, then every item shows an evidence class and a source reference. Given an edit, when applied, then it creates a revision through the owning path, not a direct write. Given a forget from the inspector, then it propagates as in B09 and reports pending state honestly. Given a suppressed item, when viewed, then it appears under suppression with its reason. Given a restart, then the inspector reflects the same state. Given a large history, then listing is paginated.

## Validation
A future service scenario asserting provenance on every item, revisioned edits, honest forget propagation, and suppression visibility. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and performance
The inspector shows personal data to the user only. It must never expose another user's items and must not perform model calls.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on provenance-classed memory and suppression overlays: non-public, no public links.

nodes.title: [B16] Recall evaluation corpus
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
Recall and persona quality must be measured against something reproducible, not asserted. Outcome: a synthetic evaluation corpus and harness that scores recall, provenance correctness and false-memory behavior without any private data.

## Scope and deliverables
Build a synthetic corpus of sessions, gists, preferences and queries with known expected results, using invented placeholder content only. Define metrics: recall at k, provenance correctness (does the returned item cite the right source and class), and false-memory rate (does the system assert a fact it was not given). Implement a runner scenario that produces a report. Include adversarial cases such as a misspelled query, an ambiguous query, a query whose answer is suppressed, and a query designed to tempt a fabricated personal memory.

## Out of scope
Real user data, any paid or scheduled pipeline, and changing product behavior based on results without review.

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by evals/memory. Depends on B05 for recall and B17 for class tagging. Produces fixtures other tracks can reuse for context and persona tests.

## Dependencies
B05 because the metrics test recall; B17 because provenance correctness depends on evidence-class tagging.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given the corpus, when the runner executes, then it prints reproducible metrics. Given a fabricated-memory case, then the expected result is an explicit unknown and the metric records a failure if Didi asserts otherwise. Given a suppressed-answer case, then the expected result is no answer. Given a misspelled query, then the corpus records the intended match. Given two runs, then results are identical. Given an empty corpus, then the runner refuses rather than reporting a misleading pass.

## Validation
A future local evaluation scenario that runs the corpus and prints metrics, wired into one inexpensive consolidated gate only when implementation starts. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and performance
The corpus is fully synthetic and carries no personal data. It runs locally and must not trigger network model calls in the default scenario.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on recall evaluation needs and on false-memory risk: non-public, no public links. Corpus content is invented for this task.

nodes.title: [B17] Trust and epistemic separation in retrieved context
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
Retrieved text can mix a user's statement, an observation, a model inference and an untrusted tool result. If these are not separated, an inference can be read as fact and injected instructions can appear authoritative. Outcome: a tagging and authority layer so every retrieved item carries its evidence class and untrusted text creates no authority.

## Scope and deliverables
Define the evidence classes user_stated, observed_fact and derived_inference, and an untrusted marker for content that came from a tool result or model text. Define the rule that reasoning text and tool results never create authority or trigger an action by themselves. Implement tagging on retrieved items and a defensive treatment of instruction-like content in tool results, which is surfaced as data, not followed. Provide fixtures for each class and for an injection attempt inside a tool result.

## Out of scope
The action broker and grants (authority track), and the runtime execution of tools (runtime track).

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/memory, with rules consumed by the runtime and the commitments track. Uses B01 references for identity. The separation of evidence classes from storage origin is reused conceptually from the accepted decision; no code is copied.

## Dependencies
B01 for reference identity. Independent of the host spike, so trust tagging can proceed early.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given a user statement, when tagged, then it is user_stated. Given a model inference, then it is derived_inference and not shown as fact. Given a tool result containing an instruction, when consumed, then it is treated as data and produces no action and no authority. Given an observed value, then it is observed_fact. Given a mixed context, then each item keeps its own class. Given a restart, then classes persist with the items. Given a caller tries to treat reasoning text as permission, then it is rejected.

## Validation
A future adverse scenario asserting correct class tagging and that an injection inside a tool result creates no action. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and authority
This leaf is the boundary that keeps inferred or untrusted text from becoming authority. It grants no capability and stores no credential.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on keeping evidence class separate from storage origin and on untrusted tool text creating no authority: non-public, no public links.

nodes.title: [B18] Optional embeddings, index portability and reindexing
nodes.body:
## Trigger and outcome
Semantic recall is valuable but optional, and a change of embedding provider or model must not silently break results. Outcome: an index abstraction with a no-embeddings fallback and a reindex path when the model changes.

## Scope and deliverables
Define an index abstraction with a required full-text arm and an optional vector arm. Define a provider and model stamp stored with the index, and a reindex operation that rebuilds when the stamp changes. Define that the no-embeddings mode still answers from full text and marks semantic results unavailable rather than returning noise. Provide fixtures for an index with embeddings, an index without, and an index whose stamp is stale after a provider change.

## Out of scope
Choosing or paying for a specific embedding service, and any forced dependency on an external model.

## Interfaces, ownership, reuse
Owned by core/memory. Depends on B04 gists and B05 recall. The idea of a two-layer index with a configurable backend is reused conceptually from the existing private knowledge service; no code is copied.

## Dependencies
B04 for the indexed content; B05 because recall is the consumer of the index.

## Acceptance scenarios
Given no embeddings configured, when recalling, then full-text results work and semantic results are marked unavailable. Given a provider change, when the app next indexes, then a reindex is triggered and results are marked provisional until it completes. Given a stale stamp, then the index is rebuilt, not silently used. Given a restart, then the index and its stamp persist. Given a reindex failure, then the prior index is retained and the failure is reported. Given a huge corpus, then reindexing is resumable.

## Validation
A future scenario asserting the no-embeddings fallback, reindex on provider change, resumability and failure retention. No existing command is claimed.

## Privacy and performance
Embedding calls, if any, follow the model egress policy and never send more than authorized. Reindexing is a coalesced background task, not a per-heartbeat job, and its cost is measured before it is scheduled.

## Evidence
Private baseline research on optional two-layer indexing and provider-change handling: non-public, no public links.

nodes.title: [C01] Multi-account identity map and account binding contract
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** The existing local adapter tooling identifies an account only by "me". Token files are named by tool, not by account, and the credential paths are resolved once when a module is imported, so a second Google account cannot be added without an edit. Any component that later binds a mobile device, a notification or an action receipt to an account has nothing stable to bind to.

**Outcome.** One local identity map: accounts have stable internal ids, provider subjects where the provider exposes one, a human label, an optional default, and a state (active, needs reauthorization, revoked). Every action record, cache entry, cursor and receipt names the account it belongs to. A caller that does not name an account gets an explicit "account not selected" error, never a silent default, except in the single-user convenience case where exactly one account exists for that provider.

**Scope and deliverables.** The account record schema and its migration proposal (proposed to the runtime master, not applied here). The resolver API: resolve by explicit id, by label, or by "the only account for this provider". A binding rule stating that a model-inferred account is never acceptable at execution time. A per-account keying convention for caches and cursors. The provider-agnostic credential reference record belongs here as well: provider, account subject and toolset, with rotation and revocation metadata and a backend order (OS keychain first, owner-readable file fallback), and no API returning a credential value except the resolver used at call time, so a non-Google source can hold its own credential without any Google authorization. An account list and status command surface returning machine-readable output.

**Out of scope.** Secret storage and OAuth (C02). Migration of existing single-account installs, which is a bounded follow-up once the resolver exists. UI for account management, which is the native experience master's.
