**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** This is a shared contract; changes are proposed to the runtime master, which sequences migrations. Adapters consume the resolver and never read token paths themselves. Reuse the existing pattern of a per-package contract module with fixtures so other masters can test against fakes, and keep the account id in the action receipt shape already used by the adapter CLI family.

**Dependencies and why.** None. It is the base contract for C02 and for every per-account adapter, and it is the binding that makes a later device registry meaningful. A04 owns the application store and sequences migration files, and this record is its first schema proposal.

**Acceptance scenarios.** Two Google accounts with the same human label in different domains resolve to different ids and different credentials. A read with no account named fails with an actionable error when two accounts exist and succeeds when exactly one exists. The account subject appears in the grant and in the receipt, never only inside a token file location. Restart preserves ids and states. Revoking one account marks only that account. An action record under account A never appears in a query scoped to account B.

**Validation.** Future unit tests over a fake credential and account store: id stability across restart, default resolution rules, refusal when two accounts exist and none is named, and a cross-account isolation assertion on the action record query. The scenario is the test; no existing command is claimed.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** No credential value is stored or returned here. The account label is user-visible metadata and must not be sent to a model unless the user's request needs it. Resolution is local and cheap; it must not perform a network call.

**Evidence.** Verified by reading the existing local adapter source at a pinned revision (private baseline, not public, no link): token paths are per-tool module constants and clients call with the provider's "me" identifier. Corroborated by the sibling identity and security research lane in this planning set, which classified multi-account as greenfield and named it the top cross-account leak risk.

nodes.title: [C02] Per-account credential records and Google installed-app OAuth
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** Today the only credential model is one token file per toolset, and authorization needs an interactive terminal. A product for several people, each with a personal and a work account, cannot be built on that: two consumers already need different scopes from one file, and a re-consent replaces the granted set instead of extending it.

**Outcome.** Credentials become per-account records addressed by reference, and Google authorization becomes a per-account operation: a browser loopback flow on an ephemeral port with PKCE and offline access, a refresh token per account, and a non-interactive fail-fast path for background work. The rollout assessment decides which distribution path the product targets, because the answer changes user-visible behaviour.

**Scope and deliverables.** The Google records inside the credential store C01 defines: one per account and toolset, written at authorization time and rotated on refresh, never copied into model context or an evidence export. The installed-app OAuth adapter: loopback listener, PKCE S256, offline access, per-account token records, a serialized refresh path (one refresh at a time per account, others reuse the result), and an actionable error for revoked or scope-drifted tokens. A written distribution and scope assessment as an evidence task: which scopes each capability needs, which publishing status the product targets, what each status costs the user (expiry windows, user caps, verification requirements), which option is selected, and the consequence of a published but unverified client: the unverified-app screen and the lifetime new-user cap, which trades a weekly expiry for a one-time user budget.

**Out of scope.** Distribution mechanics (no store or verification submission in this planning program). Non-Google providers use the same store in their own leaves.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Consumes C01 for the account id. Every other adapter must treat a credential as opaque. Reuse the existing shared auth helper's good behaviours: strict superset validation, atomic owner-only file write, refresh-error translation, and a retrying API client. Where existing single-token consumers must keep working, provide the union-consent path and document the recovery step for a drifted token.

**Dependencies and why.** C01 supplies the account key. Nothing else blocks: C03 to C11 all authenticate through this record, which is why this lands in the contract phase. The onboarding leaf that presents the publishing status is in the native experience track and consumes the status this record exposes.

**Acceptance scenarios.** Authorizing a second account never overwrites the first. A background refresh after days without interaction either succeeds or reports a reauthorization-needed state; it never hangs waiting for a browser. Onboarding records the configured client's observed publishing status and, when the client is in the testing audience, names the seven-day authorization and refresh-token limit and offers the publish step; a scheduled job that consumes a token older than the consent window reports reauthorization-needed with the account named. A read-only credential cannot send: the scope split is asserted, so holding a read grant alone leaves the outbound path unavailable. A revoked credential produces an actionable message naming the account. Revoking one account does not disturb another, and no credential value appears in logs, action records, error envelopes or model context. A scope-drifted token is detected before the first API call.

**Validation.** Future unit tests over a fake keychain and token files: create, rotate, revoke, per-account isolation, refusal to hand out a value, and the union-scope path; plus an adverse test simulating a revoked refresh token that asserts one actionable failure and no retry storm. 

**Privacy, authority and performance.** Credential values stay out of model context and out of evidence exports. Authorization is user-initiated; a background process may refresh but never initiate consent. Refresh is serialized per account so concurrent calls cannot race.

**Evidence.** Read from the existing private adapter source at a pinned revision (private baseline, no link): per-toolset scope sets over one token file, strict granted-superset validation, non-interactive fail-fast, owner-only writes. Verified from a public library source: the installed-app flow requests exactly the given scopes and sends no incremental-grant parameter, so a new consent replaces the previous scope set. Public references fetched 2026-10-09: Google's app audience page (support.google.com/cloud/answer/15549945), which states that a test user's authorization and refresh token expire seven days after consent and that publishing status is a separate control from verification; and the OAuth 2.0 overview (developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2).

Grant lifecycle note: expired or revoked grants are a first-class state. Stop ingestion for that account, show the account-specific coverage gap and the reauthorization path. Testing, publishing status and verification are separate concerns.

nodes.title: [C03] Gmail incremental ingestion with history cursor and full resync
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** The existing mail path recomputes a lookback window on every run and de-duplicates by message id and body hash. That finds new mail but cannot tell the assistant what changed: a label change, an archive, a deletion or an edit is invisible, and a busy mailbox re-reads the same window repeatedly. A proactive assistant needs changes, not a repeated list.

**Outcome.** Per-account mail ingestion that stores a provider history cursor, fetches changes since it, classifies them (added, deleted, label added, label removed) and keeps a local projection sufficient to answer "what is new, what was answered, what changed since last time" without re-reading a window. When the cursor is no longer usable the ingestion performs exactly one full resync, records the new cursor and reports that a full resync happened.

**Scope and deliverables.** Cursor storage keyed by account (issued through the runtime master's migration sequencing). The change-fetch path with paging and a bounded page budget. A classifier over change kinds, with a stable internal event shape so downstream consumers never parse raw provider payloads. A full-resync path with a progress record and an explicit partial-coverage flag when the budget is exhausted. A de-duplication and idempotency rule so replaying a change batch cannot duplicate a local row or resurrect a deleted message. A per-run outcome record for freshness reporting. An attachment-aware read may be split into a follow-up if body extraction alone is large.

**Out of scope.** Push notifications and provider watch renewal, which need a cloud project per user and are a separate opt-in leaf. Sending, archiving and deleting mail, which belong to C04 or to a later effect leaf. Promise extraction from mail, which is the commitments master's.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** The knowledge-retrieval master consumes events through this interface and must not query the provider. Keep the existing adapter's good shape: a client protocol with an injectable fake, an explicit error type so a source failure is never rendered as an empty inbox, and a local store that already de-duplicates by message identity. Our own evidence report records what is absent today: no history cursor, no paging on the list verb, no attachment fetch, and only shallow body extraction.

**Dependencies and why.** C02 supplies the per-account credential. Without it this task cannot authenticate a second account, and without a cursor there is nothing to store. A04 sequences the cursor and projection tables this leaf proposes, so the storage contract is a genuine blocker.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A first run establishes a cursor and a second run returns only changes. A cursor the provider has discarded triggers exactly one full resync with a recorded reason, and the run after that is incremental again. An interrupted run resumes without duplicating rows. A provider 429 or a transient 500 produces bounded retries and then an honest failure with a partial-coverage flag, never a silent empty result. Deleting a message upstream removes or tombstones it locally rather than leaving a ghost the assistant can quote.

**Validation.** Future tests over a fake provider that serves recorded change batches, including the discarded-cursor branch, an interrupted-run resume, a saturation case that forces paging, and a rate-limit case. Assertions target the classified event stream and the coverage flags, not provider payloads.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** Reading mail needs a standing read grant per account. Cache is a versioned projection of an external source, never a new authority, and it must be purgeable per account (C17). Polling must be paced by the provider's own quota signals and must not run per blind heartbeat; change windows are coalesced.

**Evidence.** Public references: the provider sync guide (developers.google.com/workspace/gmail/api/guides/sync, fetched 2026-10-09) states that history records are typically available for at least one week and that an exhausted history range returns an HTTP 404 that requires a full synchronization; the push guide states the watch renewal window. Verified by reading the existing private adapter source at a pinned revision (no link): relative-window listing, no cursor, no attachment path.

Ingestion keeps originals in the store and exposes them to a turn only through the bounded digest (B11) or an explicit retrieval (B05). The prompt does not receive a mail archive.

nodes.title: [C04] Gmail reply drafting with write receipts and duplicate-send guards
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** The first real-user slice ends with an unsent reply prepared from a real thread. The existing adapter can create a provider draft, but there is no record of what was prepared for which account and thread, no protection against preparing the same reply twice, and no boundary that keeps a draft from becoming a send.

**Outcome.** The assistant can prepare a reply draft in the user's own mailbox for a named account and thread, idempotently, with a local receipt that says what was prepared, when, and from which evidence, and with no code path in the product that sends it.

**Scope and deliverables.** A draft preparation service that takes an account, a thread reference and a body, resolves the thread to the right account, creates the provider draft with correct threading headers so it appears in the conversation, and writes a local receipt with a content hash and an idempotency key. A re-run with the same idempotency key returns the existing receipt instead of creating a second draft. An explicit capability boundary: the send operation is unavailable at the product's tool surface even though the underlying provider client supports it, and an attempt to reach it fails before any network call. A discard path for a prepared draft the user rejects.

**Out of scope.** Sending, scheduling, follow-up nudging and template management. Recipient policy (who may be addressed) beyond a resource scope check belongs to the authority leaves.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** The commitments master consumes the receipt to link a promise to an artifact. Reuse the existing protocol-based mail client with a fake implementation in tests, and the existing local triage store's audit-and-undo shape for receipts rather than inventing a second audit format. The union-scope problem must be resolved first so that a read-capable token and a draft-capable token are the same authorized account (C02).

**Dependencies and why.** C02 for the account credential and scope coverage; C03 to resolve the thread and its context. A draft without thread identity would create a new conversation, which is a visible user-facing defect. C12 supplies the grant broker, and this leaf depends on it directly rather than inheriting the authorization check from whichever caller invoked it, because preparing an external draft is an effect that has to be authorized where it happens. A08 owns the intent and receipt shape this leaf produces, so the receipt is written against that contract rather than a local invention.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A draft is created in the correct thread and visible in the provider's drafts. Re-running with the same idempotency key creates nothing new. A refused permission (a token lacking the draft scope) yields an actionable error and no partial draft. A restart between preparation and receipt write leaves either no draft or a receipt, and the reconciler reports which, never both. An attempt to invoke a send path from the product surface is refused with zero network calls. A draft is discarded on request and disappears from the provider.

**Validation.** Future tests over a fake provider client: thread resolution, receipt round trip, idempotent re-run, permission refusal, restart-in-the-middle reconciliation, and a surface assertion that no send symbol is reachable from the product's tool manifest. Manual live verification of the draft appearance in a real mailbox is documented but excluded from the default check.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** Preparing a draft is a write to the user's own mailbox and needs a prepare grant, not a send grant. Draft bodies are user content and must not be logged in full or exported as evidence. Receipts store a hash and metadata, not a second copy of the body.

**Evidence.** Verified by reading the existing private adapter source at a pinned revision (no link): provider draft creation exists with a single token file, the scope set for writes differs from reads, and no idempotency or receipt layer exists. Public reference: the same sync and push guides used in C03 for the account-level constraints. Public reference for scope semantics: developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/scopes (fetched 2026-10-09).

nodes.title: [C05] Calendar incremental sync with recurrence, timezones and stable event identity
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** The existing calendar path only looks forward from now, always expands instances, and has no delta mechanism. A user cannot ask what happened in last week's one-on-one, the assistant cannot notice that a meeting moved, and a repeated poll re-fetches the same window. Timezone handling is also implicit: the creator writes timestamps with a local offset and no explicit zone field.

**Outcome.** A per-account calendar model that can answer three questions reliably: what is coming, what changed since the last look, and what a given instance is. Event identity survives a move of an instance, recurrence is represented rather than flattened, and every timestamp is stored with its zone so a display in another zone is correct.

**Scope and deliverables.** A normalized event record: calendar id, event id, series id for instances, original start for an instance, start and end with offsets and a zone, title, attendees with response status, and a link. A bounded listing API with explicit lower and upper bounds, so both a past window and an upcoming window are expressible. A delta path that persists a sync token per account and calendar, applies changes including deletions, and on an invalidated token clears its state and performs exactly one full resync with a recorded reason. A recurring-series rule: instances are keyed by series identity plus original start, so a user-visible "this meeting moved" is a change to the series, not a lost instance. An explicit decision recorded in code about which calendars the user has enabled, never "all reachable calendars" by default.

**Out of scope.** Creating, updating, cancelling or answering invitations, which is C06. Notification channels and webhooks, which require a publicly reachable endpoint and are a separate opt-in leaf.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** The planning master consumes a stable event view. Reuse the existing adapter's API client behaviours (timeout, retry, pagination helper) and its warm service construction, but replace the forward-only listing. Keep one normalization layer so that no other component sees provider payloads.

**Dependencies and why.** C02 supplies the account credential. Nothing else blocks: this is the read half of the calendar capability and the first slice needs it.

**Acceptance scenarios.** Upcoming events list correctly across a daylight-saving boundary. A past window lists a completed meeting with an attendees and response view. Moving a recurring instance upstream shows as a change, not as delete-plus-create with a new identity. An invalidated sync token triggers exactly one full resync and the next run is incremental. Deleting an event upstream removes it locally. A calendar the user has not enabled never appears. An expired credential yields an actionable account-scoped error, not an empty calendar.

**Validation.** Future tests over a fake calendar service: normalization of a timed event, an all-day event, an instance with an original start, a delta batch containing a deletion, and an invalidated-token branch. A request-shape assertion guards the documented parameter restrictions on delta requests, because violating them fails in a way response tests would miss.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** Calendar reads need a standing read grant per account. Attendee names and emails are personal data and must not be included in evidence exports or sent to a model that does not need them. Delta polling must be paced and coalesced, and a full resync must be bounded so it cannot run unbounded in the background.

**Evidence.** Public references fetched 2026-10-09: the calendar sync guide (developers.google.com/workspace/calendar/api/guides/sync) for the sync-token model and the 410 invalid-token response; the events.list reference (developers.google.com/workspace/calendar/api/v3/reference/events/list) which names exactly which parameters cannot be combined with a sync token (iCalUID, orderBy, privateExtendedProperty, q, sharedExtendedProperty, timeMin, timeMax, updatedMin) and that deleted events are always returned; the events resource reference for series id and original-start semantics of an instance. Verified by reading the existing private adapter source at a pinned revision (no link): forward-only listing with expansion, no time upper bound, no paging, no sync token, no explicit zone field. A04 sequences the calendar cache and sync-token tables this leaf proposes.

nodes.title: [C06] Authorized Calendar actions and conflict handling
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** Creating a meeting is an outward-facing act: it can email every attendee, move other people's calendars and create a conference room that others now depend on. The existing adapter inserts with attendee notifications enabled and no authority check, no conflict view and no undo. An assistant that creates meetings from a spoken sentence therefore needs more than an API call.

**Outcome.** A calendar write path where every consequential action is derived from an explicit user request, checked against a grant that names the effect, previewed when a conflict or ambiguity exists, executed once, and recorded with a receipt that can be compensated. Ambiguous input results in a question or a proposal, never a best-guess invitation to real people.

**Scope and deliverables.** Effect classes for calendar writes (create a private block, create a meeting with attendees, change an existing event, cancel, answer an invitation) with the grant required for each. A preview object the user sees before any attendee is contacted: title, start and end with zone, duration, attendees, and the consequences (notifications sent, existing events that overlap). Conflict detection against the user's own calendar for the proposed window, and a rule for what happens when a conflict is found. Idempotency: a retried execution with the same intent reference does not create a second event. Compensation: cancelling a just-created event is a separate compensating action recorded as such. An explicit unsupported list rather than silent defaults: no unspecified zone, no guessed duration from a vague phrase, no attendee address invented from a name alone.

**Out of scope.** Creating or managing the conference link provider. Room and resource booking systems. Recurring-series editing beyond what C05 models.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Consumes C05's event model and C12's broker. Reuse the same receipt and audit shape as C04 so the product has one receipt vocabulary. The native experience master renders the preview; this task produces the preview object and the decision rules.

**Dependencies and why.** C05 for event identity (without it an update cannot target the right instance). C12 for grants: without an explicit grant this path must not exist, because a model statement must not create authority to email third parties.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A request to create a meeting with attendees without the corresponding grant is refused with zero network calls and one audit line. A request naming a person but not an address asks for confirmation instead of guessing. A proposed time that overlaps an existing event is presented as a conflict before creation. An execution that times out after dispatch reports an unknown outcome and offers reconciliation rather than retrying blindly. Repeating the same intent reference does not create a duplicate. Cancelling a created event is recorded as a compensating action.

**Validation.** Future tests over a fake calendar service: preview content, grant refusal with no network call, conflict detection, idempotent re-execution, untrusted tool output containing an instruction to create an event (which must not create authority), and a duplicate-intent case. Manual verification of one real creation and one cancellation is documented and excluded from the default check.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** This is the highest-consequence surface in the epic: creating a meeting contacts third parties. It requires explicit capability, produces durable receipts, and must never be triggered by text arriving from a document, mail or chat tool result. Attendee addresses are personal data kept out of evidence exports.

**Evidence.** Verified by reading the existing private adapter source at a pinned revision (no link): insert with attendee notifications, no authority check, no conflict look, no update path, no receipt. Public references fetched 2026-10-09: the calendar events resource reference for attendee response and notification fields, and the events.insert reference for the send-updates option. A08 owns the receipt and unknown-outcome reconciliation shape this leaf uses for a dispatched creation.

nodes.title: [C07] Document and Drive original resolver for meeting preparation
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** Meeting preparation needs the documents and notes around a meeting, and the assistant must be able to say where a fact came from. The existing document tooling assumes a scope that covers only files the application itself created or opened, so a broad search over a user's existing documents is not covered by that grant, and the retrieval path already used elsewhere asks for a different, wider read grant on the same credential file. Two consumers of one token therefore want different worlds.

**Outcome.** A resolver that, given an account and a reference (a document link from a meeting invitation, a note id, or a search phrase), returns the original's identity, revision marker, a text extraction, and an explicit coverage statement. When the reference cannot be resolved under the granted scopes, the answer says so instead of returning an empty result.

**Scope and deliverables.** A scope decision recorded in code and configuration: which capability needs which grant, and how one account satisfies several consumers without a scope war (depends on C02's union path). A resolver API returning identity (account, file id, revision or content hash, modification time), a text projection with a byte budget, and a coverage field (full, truncated, unavailable). A bounded export or text-extraction path with an explicit size limit and a clear refusal beyond it. A per-run outcome record so freshness and coverage can be reported. A deduplication rule so one original referenced twice resolves to one record, with a projection plus a pointer stored rather than a second copy.

**Out of scope.** Editing documents, comments, sheets or slide content. Building a second general document index; if a general retrieval system already owns extraction, resolve the original and defer to it. Drive change-log delta is out of scope until its retention behaviour is documented. 

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** The knowledge-retrieval master owns general retrieval and already has a per-document ledger with a content hash and a terminal-state rule; this task must feed it rather than duplicate it. Reuse the existing adapter's export and download capability, which is sound, and add the parts that are missing today: paging, coverage reporting and the scope decision.

**Dependencies and why.** C02 supplies the credential and the scope union. Without the union, a resolver call can invalidate the credential that another consumer needs, which is an observed failure mode rather than a hypothetical one.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A document linked from a meeting invitation resolves to its text with a revision marker. A reference outside the granted scope returns an explicit unavailable-coverage answer, not an empty document. A very large document returns a truncated projection. A document deleted upstream reports unavailable rather than stale content. Two meetings referencing one document produce one record. An expired credential reports an account-scoped error.

**Validation.** Future tests over a fake document and drive service: resolution by link, resolution by search, an out-of-scope refusal, an oversized document, a deleted original, and a per-account isolation assertion. A coverage-flag test asserts that a truncated extraction can never be reported as complete.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** Document text is user content: a read grant per account, no full-text logging, and no export into evidence. Extraction must be size-bounded so a single large document cannot stall the background loop. The product stores a pointer plus projection, never a second authoritative copy of the original.

**Evidence.** Public references fetched 2026-10-09: the OAuth scopes reference (developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/scopes) describes the per-file drive scope as access only to the specific files used with the application; the changes guide and the changes.list reference (developers.google.com/workspace/drive/api/guides/manage-changes) document start-page-token delta, and I could not find a documented retention window for the change log, so delta remains best-effort. Verified by reading the existing private adapter source at a pinned revision (no link): a single shared token file with a per-file drive scope, single-page listing, and a second consumer on the same file with a wider read scope.

nodes.title: [C08] Mattermost archive coverage and live repair
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** Unanswered chat is a core follow-through signal, but history lives behind a server that returns a bounded window per call, orders by creation time with no consecutiveness guarantee, and refuses some channels. A local archive already exists as a separate component with its own sync worker, and a second copy would double server load and disk use.

**Outcome.** The product reads chat history from the existing archive through its published interface, labels answers with the archive's freshness, and keeps a bounded live-repair path for what a stale archive cannot answer (very recent arrivals, and whether a recent post changed).

**Scope and deliverables.** An adapter over the archive interface: channel and direct-message search, thread retrieval, per-channel post counts, sync status with a per-channel last-sync time, and refused channels. The community credential is this adapter's own: a personal access token or session credential held as a credential reference from C01, with no Google authorization involved, so a chat-only install is usable without any Google client. A freshness rule: an answer carries the last sync time, and an archived source is labelled as archived. A live-repair path with a per-channel cursor, a hard cap on posts per call, and a documented hole-filling rule, because the provider does not guarantee consecutive results. A rule preventing a redundant third archive, with a test asserting the product stores no post body. A refusal is reported as a coverage gap, not as an empty channel.

**Out of scope.** Posting, replying, reacting or editing chat content, which is C09. Building a new archive, a new embedding index or a second full-text index. Any change to the archive component's own schema or sync policy, which its owners govern.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** The archive component owns history storage and sync; the live client owns real-time reads. This task is the seam between them plus the freshness contract. Reuse the community client's `since` usage, truncation flag, backoff and caches, and the archive's status shape (per-channel last sync, archived flag, refused-channel list) instead of inventing a second vocabulary.

**Dependencies and why.** C01 supplies the account and the credential reference that this adapter's own community token or session credential is stored against, and the live repair needs no Google authorization, so a chat-only install is complete without a Google client. A04 sequences the per-channel cursor and coverage tables this leaf proposes.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A request for history after a long offline period returns the archive answer with its sync time rather than blocking on a live scan. A live repair hitting the per-call cap reports a truncated result without pretending completeness. A channel the server refuses is reported as unreadable, once, and is not retried on every run. An archived channel is searchable and labelled read-only. An edit to an old post is caught by the live repair or reported as possibly stale, never served silently as current. A restart mid-repair resumes from the stored cursor.

**Validation.** Future tests against a fake community server (the archive component already tests against an in-memory server of its own, the pattern to copy): cursor advance, cap-truncation, refused channel, archived channel, restart resume, and a storage assertion that no post body is written locally. An edit-detection test documents whether edits are visible through the change query, and the answer feeds the freshness rule.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** Chat content is other people's data too: a read grant per account, no full-body logging, no export, and no model context beyond what the request needs. Polling must be paced and must never scan every channel on a blind heartbeat.

**Evidence.** Public references fetched 2026-10-09: the provider's API source for the channel posts endpoint (github.com/mattermost/mattermost, api/v4/source/posts.yaml) documents that `since` selects posts modified after a time, must not be combined with before, after, page or per_page, returns at most 1000 posts ordered by creation time, and that clients must fill holes themselves; the API reference introduction documents the rate-limit headers and the websocket endpoint. Verified from the local archive component source at its pinned revision: per-channel cursor with a backfilled flag, resumable backfill cursor, archived-channel handling and a refused-channel list. This planning set's connector evidence records the same absence in the existing private client: no events subscription, no thread endpoints, no search. A04 sequences the per-channel cursor and coverage tables this leaf proposes.

Evidence: internal planning baseline (non-public, no link); live chat coverage is unverified and must be confirmed against real interfaces at implementation time.

nodes.title: [C09] Mattermost draft and action adapter
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** Preparing a reply in a chat is the product's other half of "help me follow through", and the existing client can already save a server-side draft, including a threaded reply. What is missing is authority and evidence: nothing distinguishes a prepared draft from a posted message, nothing records which conversation a draft belongs to, and a retry can leave two drafts.

**Outcome.** The assistant can prepare a chat reply into the user's own draft store, in the right conversation and thread, once, with a local receipt linking it to the message it answers, and cannot post it.

**Scope and deliverables.** A draft preparation service taking an account, a channel or direct-message reference, an optional thread root, and a body, which resolves the target conversation and writes a provider draft plus a local receipt keyed by an idempotency key and a body hash. A target-resolution rule that refuses to guess a conversation when the user's phrase matches more than one. An explicit capability boundary so the product surface exposes prepare-and-discard only, and any attempt to reach a posting path fails before a network call. A channel-type rule: a draft is never prepared into a read-only or archived conversation without stating that it cannot be sent there. A discard path.

**Out of scope.** Posting, editing another person's message, reactions, file uploads and notification settings. Chat search belongs to C08.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Consumes C08 for conversation identity and C12 for the grant. Reuse the existing client's draft support and its verified rate-limit and caching behaviour. Use the same receipt and audit vocabulary as the mail draft leaf so the user sees one consistent concept of "prepared, not sent".

**Dependencies and why.** C08 supplies conversation and thread resolution, without which a draft lands in the wrong place. C12 supplies the effect class for writing into the user's own draft store, which is a write and must not be silent even though it is not yet a message.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A draft appears in the correct direct message or channel thread. Re-running with the same idempotency key creates nothing new. An ambiguous target asks for a choice. A draft into an archived channel is refused with a clear reason. Posting is unreachable from the product surface. A restart between provider write and receipt write is reconciled and reported as either prepared or unknown, never both. A permission failure yields an actionable account-scoped error with no partial write.

**Validation.** Future tests against a fake community server: target resolution with an ambiguous match, draft creation, idempotent re-run, archived-channel refusal, restart reconciliation, and a surface assertion that no posting symbol is reachable. A grant test asserts zero network calls on refusal.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** Draft bodies are user content and also describe other people: not logged in full, not exported. Writing into the user's own draft store is a low-consequence effect but still recorded. Draft creation must respect the provider's rate limits.

**Evidence.** Verified by reading the existing private client and CLI at a pinned revision (no link): the client exposes draft retrieval and saving with an optional thread root, and the command surface exposes no posting command. Public references fetched 2026-10-09: the provider API source for the draft endpoints and the channel posts endpoint, which document permissions and rate-limit headers.

nodes.title: [C10] Trello board read and per-user board mapping
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** A board is a natural place for the assistant to see work that is due and drifting, and the existing card tool already speaks it. What it does not have is a per-user mapping: board and list identifiers live in one person's configuration, and a shipped default board is exactly the kind of private detail that must never enter a public repository or another user's install.

**Outcome.** Each user configures their own board and their own list mapping, the assistant reads cards and lists through that mapping, and an unconfigured install reports the source as unconfigured rather than failing, guessing or shipping someone else's identifiers.

**Scope and deliverables.** A board mapping configuration: an account or credential reference, a board identifier, an optional label or list name mapping, and a cache policy. The board credential is this adapter's own key and token pair held as a credential reference from C01, so the board source installs without any Google authorization, all supplied by the user and validated strictly (unknown keys and missing fields fail loudly, never silently defaulted). A read surface: lists, cards, a single card, cards due in a window, stale cards by last activity, and board activity. A resolution layer mapping human list names to identifiers with an explicit ambiguity error. A machine-readable output contract so downstream consumers do not parse human text. A configuration-state report so the assistant can say "the board source is not configured" instead of returning nothing.

**Out of scope.** Creating, moving, archiving or commenting on cards, which is C11. Building a second board client. Assuming a particular board schema, workflow or vendor convention; the mapping is whatever the user states.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** The planning master consumes the card view for daily plans; this task owns the mapping and the read projection. Reuse the existing card client's credential loading order and its JSON envelope with metadata, which are already suitable, and its name-resolution helpers, extended with strict validation and an unconfigured state.

**Dependencies and why.** C01 supplies the identity and the credential reference that this adapter's own board service key and token are stored against, so the board source installs without a Google client and can proceed in parallel with the Google leaves.

**Acceptance scenarios.** With a configured board, due cards and stale cards are returned with a machine-readable envelope. With no configuration, the source reports unconfigured and no network call is made. A credential missing or revoked yields an actionable error. A mistyped list name produces an ambiguity or not-found error, never a silent fallback to the first list. A cache entry survives a restart and is invalidated by the configured policy. A card whose board the user can no longer see is reported as out of coverage rather than as deleted.

**Validation.** Future tests over recorded response fixtures plus a fake card service: mapping validation failures, unconfigured state with a no-network assertion, due and stale queries, envelope shape, and a per-account isolation assertion so two users' mappings cannot mix. No live service call is part of the default check.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** Board content can include other people's work: read grant per account, no export of card bodies into evidence, and a cache with an explicit policy rather than unbounded retention. Reads must be paced and cached so a board poll cannot become a hot loop.

**Evidence.** Verified by reading the existing private card tool source and documentation at a pinned revision (no link): credentials loaded from a secrets file with environment fallback, board and list identifiers supplied by configuration including a real board identifier and list map in the tool's own example, a JSON envelope with metadata, and write verbs. Public reference: the card service's REST API documentation for the endpoints used, to be cited at implementation time rather than assumed here.

nodes.title: [C11] Trello actions with idempotent reconciliation
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** Moving a card, commenting on it or marking it due are external effects visible to other people on a shared board. The existing tool exposes all of them with no authority layer, no idempotency and no reconciliation, so a timeout or a retry can move a card twice or leave the assistant's belief and the board disagreeing.

**Outcome.** A user-granted, effect-classed path for board changes where each action is executed once, recorded, and reconciled against the board when the outcome is unknown, and where a compensated undo exists for the actions that can be compensated.

**Scope and deliverables.** Effect classes for board changes (move within the user's own board, comment, set due date, create a card, archive or unarchive) with the grant each requires. An intent record with an idempotency key, the pre-state observed (list, due date, assignee), the requested post-state and the receipt. A reconciler that runs after an unknown outcome, reads the current board state and classifies the intent as applied, not applied, or ambiguous, without blindly retrying. Compensation rules for the reversible subset (move, due date, archive) and an explicit statement for the irreversible subset (a comment another person has already seen, a notification already sent). A confirmation-versus-standing-grant rule: repeating a low-consequence action on the user's own board can run under a standing grant, while creating a card in a shared list for other people is previewed.

**Out of scope.** Board administration (members, permissions, board creation). Bulk migrations across boards. Any second card client.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Consumes C10's mapping and C12's broker; produces receipts in the same vocabulary as the mail and calendar action leaves. The follow-through master consumes the reconciliation outcome so a nudged card does not get nudged again.

**Dependencies and why.** C10 for card and list identity (an action cannot target a card without the mapping). C12 for grants: without the broker this path must not exist.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A move executed once is not repeated on retry with the same intent key. A dispatch that times out reports an unknown outcome and is reconciled against the board within a bounded window, and the reconciler verdict is recorded. A comment already visible to others is never described as undone. An action without the required grant performs zero network calls and writes one audit line. A board that changed between preview and execution is detected (the pre-state no longer matches) and the action is re-presented rather than forced. A restart between dispatch and receipt resumes reconciliation from the intent record.

**Validation.** Future tests over a fake card service: idempotent re-execution, unknown-outcome reconciliation with each verdict, pre-state drift detection, grant refusal with a no-network assertion, restart resume, and a compensation test for the reversible subset. An adverse test asserts that an instruction arriving inside card text cannot create authority for an action.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** Card text is often other people's words: keep it out of logs and evidence, and never let model-generated card content be treated as an instruction. Reconciliation reads are cached and bounded so a retry storm cannot hammer the service.

**Evidence.** Verified by reading the existing private card tool source at a pinned revision (no link): write verbs exist for create, move, archive, comment, labels, due dates, assignment and checklists, with no idempotency, receipt or grant layer. Public reference: the card service's REST API documentation for these endpoints, cited at implementation time. A08 owns the intent, receipt and reconciliation contract this leaf's reconciliation writes into.

nodes.title: [C12] Grants, allowlists and the deterministic effect broker
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** The product's usefulness depends on acting for the user, and its trustworthiness on never acting beyond what the user granted. Without one decision point, each adapter invents its own rule, model text becomes an argument for permission, and a refusal has no evidence. The recorded design direction is a host-owned broker with per user, account, tool, action and resource grants, durable intents and receipts, credential references and an egress policy; reasoning text and untrusted tool output never create authority.

**Outcome.** One local decision function answers whether this may be done, for this account, on this resource, now; it returns a decision with a reason and records the attempt. Reads, preparations and reminders run under standing grants without a confirmation prompt. Consequential effects require a capability the user granted for that effect, and a refusal is total: no network call, no partial write, one audit line.

**Scope and deliverables.** A grant record: subject (user, account, tool, action, resource pattern, effect class), state (active, expired, revoked), origin (user or organization), created and last-used times. A decision API returning allow, deny-with-reason, or require-approval, with the matched grant named. An approval freshness rule: an approval is bound to one intent reference and expires rather than lingering. A revocation path that takes effect at dispatch, with the honest limit that an already-dispatched effect may be unknown until reconciled. Durable intents written before dispatch and updated after, so a crash leaves evidence. An allowlist of enabled tools and sources per user, fail-safe-off, resolved once and frozen for a session, with the change and revocation surface left to the native experience master. No blanket per-action confirmation for already-granted capabilities, and no quiet authorization of sends or deletions.

**Out of scope.** Runtime mechanics of the queue and process lifecycle (runtime master). The UI used to grant and revoke (native experience master). Organization policy content, an overlay input rather than a product default.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** C14 supplies the capability manifests this broker evaluates. Every adapter leaf calls the broker and never decides for itself. A per-deployment explicit allowlist with fail-safe-off behaviour and a per-session frozen flag snapshot are the two prior patterns identified in this planning set to reuse rather than invent.

**Dependencies and why.** C14, because a grant is expressed against a declared capability with an effect class; without the registry the broker has nothing to match on.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A calendar read under a standing grant proceeds with no prompt. A send attempt with no grant is refused with zero network calls and one audit line. An approval does not authorize a different intent, and it expires. Revoking a grant stops the next dispatch and reports the state of an already-dispatched action as unknown, not as cancelled. A model message claiming prior authorization changes nothing. Two accounts: a grant for one account does not authorize the other. A crash between intent write and dispatch leaves a reconcilable record. An unlisted tool is not callable and absent from the model-facing tool list.

**Validation.** Future tests over a fake clock and fake adapters: decision matrix per effect class, refusal with a no-network assertion, approval binding and expiry, revocation at dispatch, crash-resume reconciliation, unlisted-tool absence, and a prompt-injection case asserting a non-existent grant.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** This module is the authority boundary: it never calls a model, never reads a credential value, and its decisions must be reproducible from records. Decision latency must stay negligible beside a network call, and the audit trail must be append-only for permitted actions.

**Evidence.** The program's accepted design directions (internal, not published) name the broker, effect classes and grant dimensions. Reuse patterns verified in this planning set: a per-deployment explicit allowlist where an unlisted tool is never registered, and a per-session resolved feature snapshot frozen for the session's life. The existing private adapter suite has no grant layer, which is the gap this task closes. A05 owns the durable task state this broker checks at dispatch, so revocation and cancel semantics are agreed at that boundary rather than duplicated.

nodes.title: [C13] Mongoose per-user permission adapter
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** Company knowledge is governed by the company, not by the local assistant. If the product queries a company knowledge service with a broad credential and caches results locally, it can show a user a fact they are not permitted to see, and it can hold company content in a store the company does not control. Treating a company service as just another source would quietly convert a permission system into a cache.

**Outcome.** Company knowledge is reachable per user, under the requesting user's own identity and the service's own permissions, with results labelled by origin and never mistaken for the user's private material.

**Scope and deliverables.** An adapter that authenticates as the user (not as a shared bot) and returns results with origin labels, coverage and a permission-derived may-cache decision. A rule that company content is not written into the product's private store unless the service's terms and the user's permissions allow it, and that a cached result is invalidated when the permission source says access changed. A user-visible distinction between private and company knowledge in every composed answer. A failure mode where the service is unavailable or the user is unauthorized: report it as a coverage gap and never answer from stale company content silently. An organization overlay input to C12: organization restrictions narrow the effective grant set and can never widen it.

**Out of scope.** The company service's own internals, tenant model and administration. Building any company index locally. Any use of company data for personality or memory learning.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Consumes C12 for the decision and C15 for the egress decision (company content leaving the machine to a hosted model is a company-policy question, not only a user one). The memory master consumes the origin label to keep private and company material separate in recall. Reuse the existing transport and authentication shape of the company service as documented rather than inventing a parallel client; this planning set did not verify the company service source, so that shape is a contract to confirm at implementation time.

**Dependencies and why.** C12 decides whether the call is permitted; C15 decides whether the result may leave the machine. Without either, this adapter would be a permission bypass.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A user with access receives results labelled company-scoped. A user without access receives an authorization failure from the service, reported as a gap, with nothing cached. Cached company results are dropped when access is revoked upstream. A composed answer never merges company and private sources without labelling each. An organization restriction blocks a capability the user's own grant would allow. A service outage degrades to an explicit gap.

**Validation.** Future tests over a fake company service: authorized and unauthorized users, revocation propagation, origin labelling in composed answers, organization overlay narrowing, and a storage assertion that no company content is persisted while caching is disallowed. Legal or contractual questions are decisions, not tests, and are recorded as such.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** Company content is the most sensitive class in the product: no egress without a policy decision, no local persistence without permission, and no mixing with private content. Queries must be bounded and rate-limited, and an unreachable service must never be retried in a tight loop.

**Evidence.** The company knowledge service's permission model was asserted by a sibling research lane in this planning set from service documentation and was explicitly not re-read against service source in this lane, so every claim about tenant, role or tool semantics is UNVERIFIED here and must be confirmed before implementation. Public reference to confirm at implementation time: the service's own API and permission documentation.

Evidence: internal planning baseline (non-public, no link); company service permission semantics are unverified here and must be confirmed before implementation.

nodes.title: [C14] Tool capability registry and adapter manifests
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** Tools currently arrive with no declaration of what they do to the world. A caller cannot tell a read from a send, a local computation from an external effect, or a cheap call from one that reaches third parties. Without that declaration, an allowlist has nothing to allow, a broker nothing to match, an egress policy nothing to classify, and a model sees capabilities it should not.

**Outcome.** Every capability the product can invoke is declared once, in a machine-readable manifest, with the facts needed to govern it: effect class, required grant, credential reference, egress destination class, data classes received and produced, reversibility, idempotency, cost class and a human description. The registry is the single source for the model-facing tool list and for the broker's checks.

**Scope and deliverables.** A manifest schema and its validation rules, with a strict parser that fails loudly on unknown keys or missing required fields. Adapter manifests for the first-party adapter families (mail, calendar, documents, chat, board, knowledge, model providers) covering read, prepare and effect capabilities separately. A registry API: enumerate by enabled state for a user, look up one capability, and expose governance facts for a name. A derived tool list for the model, built only from enabled and permitted capabilities, so a disabled capability is absent rather than erroring. Versioning rules so a manifest change is a reviewable contract change with fixtures. A conformance test that every shipped capability has a manifest and that no manifest describes an absent capability.

**Out of scope.** The decision logic itself (C12), the egress policy content (C15), and the model-facing presentation of the tool list (native experience and runtime masters). Transport is not modelled: an adapter reached over a local protocol and one reached by subprocess declare the same governance facts.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** This is a shared contract authored by this master and proposed to the runtime master for sequencing. Every other master consumes it: the authority master to decide, the commitments master to reason about effects, the native master to present surfaces. Reuse the planning set's finding that a tool absent from an explicit allowlist should never be registered at all, and that tool definitions themselves are an injection surface at runtime, so the manifest is also a review boundary.

**Dependencies and why.** None. It is the first contract: C12 cannot be implemented without an effect class to match, and a fail-safe-off allowlist cannot exist without a capability list.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A capability with a missing effect class fails validation at build time rather than defaulting to read. Enumerating for a user with one tool disabled omits that tool entirely. A manifest claiming a capability that no adapter implements fails the conformance test. Unknown manifest keys are rejected, so a typo cannot silently change governance facts. A manifest revision is visible in the registry version so a stored grant can name the version it was granted against. An adapter that is installed but not enrolled in the user's allowlist contributes no capability.

**Validation.** Future schema tests over valid and invalid manifests, a conformance test over the shipped adapter set, and a registry test asserting that a disabled capability is absent from the derived tool list. Fixtures are synthetic.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** The manifest must not embed credentials, endpoints or personal identifiers, only their references and classes. Registry lookup is local and constant-time relative to a network call. Because the derived list feeds the model, manifest review is a security review: an ungoverned capability must not appear by accident.

**Evidence.** Verified by reading the existing private adapter suite at a pinned revision (no link): the tools expose read, draft and effect verbs with no machine-readable effect declaration, and the documentation distinguishes them only in prose. Public reference: the model-context protocol specification for tool definitions as a runtime injection surface, and the planning set's recorded finding on explicit allowlists with fail-safe-off defaults. A02 owns the versioned cross-track contract mechanism and fixtures, and this registry is one of those contracts.

Under PLAN-R3, Lux Knowledge, Lux CLI, Lux Coworker and Lux Harness are reached through declared tool and adapter seams. No service becomes a mandatory embedded monolith and no two services share a database directly.

nodes.title: [C15] Provider egress and credential policy with route assessment
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** The assistant reads mail, chat, calendar and documents, then needs a model. Local storage does not make that free: content sent to a hosted model leaves the machine, and the provider's retention behaviour is a contract question, not a code question. Policy may forbid some routes.

**Outcome.** One declared route table: for each (source, data class, destination, purpose) there is a decision, and every outbound call is checked against it. Credentials are references in a broker, never values in model context, and never passed into a subprocess environment beyond an allowlist. When a route is not permitted, the product says so and degrades (summarise locally, or ask) rather than sending anyway.

**Scope and deliverables.** A data-class vocabulary (public, personal, third-party personal, company-restricted, credential) and a route table mapping destination and purpose to permitted classes, defaulting to deny for unclassified routes. Each route entry carries the source-side obligation: the provider's limits on transfer and reading, plus any organisation restriction. Mail and document classes default to deny where a destination's retention class permits human review. A model-call wrapper that classifies the payload before dispatch and refuses or redacts per the table, applied to every model turn through the shared contract, whether the turn is a plain answer, a tool turn or a provider fallback, so no call path bypasses the check by choosing another provider or another entry point. A credential-handling rule: values resolved only at the call boundary, never logged, exported or placed in model context, and passed to subprocesses only through an allowlisted environment or a keychain reference. A provider assessment record as an evidence task: which provider routes are used, what each provider's data-handling terms say, which route the operator approved, and what happens if terms change (re-evaluate, route disabled until then). The record states the operator's approved data-handling route; it asserts no blanket legal exemption and no guaranteed provider-contract coverage, and it keeps one open question visible: whether forwarding restricted-scope content to a hosted model is itself access through a third-party server, which is a policy reading for the owner, not a code property. A local-only mode where no content leaves the machine, with the lost capability stated. An honest limit: a permitted route cannot be proven semantically safe.

**Out of scope.** Model selection, prompt design and budget policy (runtime master). Any general legal exemption claim; the assessment produces decisions and gaps.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Every adapter and model call goes through this wrapper. A local core does not settle a restricted-data assessment, because forwarding that content to a hosted provider is itself a route with its own obligations.

**Dependencies and why.** C01, because a route decision is per account: without account identity the policy cannot state whose content is leaving.

**Acceptance scenarios.** Third-party mail content, or an unclassified destination, is refused before any request, with a recorded reason. A destination whose retention class permits human review is refused for mail and document content by default, and the refusal names the missing operator approval. The gate covers tool results, transcripts and tool definitions, not prompts alone, and its decision (allow, or deny with reason) is recorded in the receipt. A payload no component labelled fails closed. An approved route for one destination does not approve another. A credential value never appears in logs, model context or an evidence export. An organization restriction blocks a route the user would otherwise allow. 

**Validation.** Future tests over a fake model client: classification, default-deny for an unclassified destination, refusal of a human-review destination for mail content, a no-call assertion on refusal, credential scanning of logs and payloads, and local-only degradation. The provider assessment is a dated decision, not a test.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** This is the privacy boundary, where "local" is stated honestly. It must not promise zero leakage or injection immunity, and it must record every route decision an outbound call relied on. 

**Evidence.** Public references fetched 2026-10-09: the restricted-scope verification page (developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/restricted-scope-verification) states that apps accessing restricted data from or through a third-party server must undergo an annual security assessment, and that storing or transmitting restricted-scope data on servers brings additional requirements; the OAuth 2.0 overview states the seven-day refresh token expiry for the testing audience; the source provider's own API services user data policy, which limits use to user-facing features and forbids transfers and human reading except named cases. The provider's actual terms are NOT verified here: the assessment's deliverable, and the default stays deny until the operator records an approved route. A02 owns the versioned cross-track contract mechanism this egress contract is registered through. The contract is consumed by every model turn path, including the provider registry and the tool-turn orchestrator, rather than this leaf depending on a provider, because a provider dependency here would make provider selection and egress policy circular.

Evidence: public Google OAuth policy documentation (https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/policies, https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/native-app) and internal planning research (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [C16] Injection and account isolation adverse test suite
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** The product reads text written by other people: mail bodies, chat messages, documents, card descriptions and tool output, any of which can contain an instruction. It also handles several accounts on one machine, so a resolution mistake can answer from the wrong account. The product also handles several accounts on one machine, so a resolution mistake can answer from the wrong account. Both are trust boundaries to test adversarially.

**Outcome.** A synthetic suite that runs without credentials or personal data and proves, per case, that untrusted content cannot widen authority and account scoping holds. Failures are explicit: a case that cannot be evaluated is reported as not evaluated, never as passed.

**Scope and deliverables.** Fixture families of synthetic content: an instruction embedded in a mail body, in a chat message, in a document, in a card description, in a tool result field, in a tool definition or description, in a file name, and in a model-visible metadata field. Each case asserts: no new grant, no network call to a new destination, no newly callable tool, and fetched content presented as data. An import-time config isolation case: credential and config locations resolve from the bound account at call time, so a module-level resolution cannot re-point a running process at another account's config root, including after a restart. A no-secret diagnostic corpus: synthetic samples carrying credential-shaped strings and a private path, over which the diagnostic writer must produce no credential value and no personal content, asserted structurally (the writer accepts only typed allowlisted fields, so a credential has no path into the output) plus the bounded corpus, never a never-claim. Account-isolation cases: two accounts on one source, same display label, one account with a revoked credential, an account-scoped query that must not return the other account's rows, a cached projection written under one account and read under another, and a draft prepared under the wrong-account attempt. A runner reporting each case with an explicit not-evaluated state, cheap enough to run locally with no network and no credentials.

**Out of scope.** Model-quality evaluation of instruction resistance in general (memory and persona tracks), operating-system penetration testing, and third-party service testing.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Consumes C12's decision API, C15's route table and C14's manifests as objects under test, and C03's ingestion path as the vehicle for injected content. The planning set's recorded adverse list (account mix-up, revoked grant, injection inside tool results, provider-change egress, forgotten item reingestion, missing optional integrations) is the source for the cases this epic owns; the rest belongs to the other masters. Fixtures remain synthetic.

**Dependencies and why.** C12 and C15 supply the objects being adversarially tested; C03 supplies a real ingestion path so injection is exercised through the product rather than in a unit stub. Without C03 the injection cases would only test a mock.

**Acceptance scenarios.** Injected text in a mail body produces a tool call attempt that is refused and recorded with zero network calls. A tool result or tool description containing an instruction to disable a grant changes nothing. A wrong-account attempt cannot reach a send path for a mailbox that is not the bound account, and a revoked grant fails at dispatch with one audit line. Two accounts sharing a display label resolve to different ids and never cross-read. A revoked account's cached projection becomes unreadable. A cross-account read returns an explicit empty-with-reason. A case whose fixture cannot be built is reported not evaluated, and the suite fails loudly if the not-evaluated count rises without review.

**Validation.** Fixture families and the diagnostic corpus start immediately from recorded samples and need no adapter, so this leaf can begin before the leaves it exercises; the end-to-end injection case completes only when the ingestion path lands, and the corpus completes when the diagnostic writer lands, so those dependencies gate completion rather than start. This task is the validation: each case is a test with a named trust property, runnable locally with no credentials. A meta-test asserts the fixture inventory so a fixture cannot be silently removed.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** Fixtures are synthetic: no real names, addresses, message text or tenant identifiers. The suite calls no provider. It keeps authority claims honest, so a skipped case is a visible defect, not a quiet gap.

**Evidence.** The planning set's recorded adverse list (internal, not published) names account mix-up, injection inside tool results and revoked grants. Verified by reading the existing private adapter source at a pinned revision (no link): no injection or account-isolation suite exists, and the clients have no account dimension, so account mix-up is unrepresentable. Public reference: the model-context protocol specification's treatment of tool definitions and results as untrusted input. A16 owns the diagnostic writer this corpus targets, so the corpus is its acceptance evidence, not a second diagnostics implementation.

Milestone note: the essential source-injection, account-isolation and egress-denial cases gate the first useful loop in M1, and the M1 baseline depends on the A16 diagnostics baseline, which is also M1. The extended adversarial corpus follows from M2 on.

nodes.title: [C17] Disconnect, revoke and cache propagation
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** Users disconnect accounts, revoke access at the provider, uninstall, and expect "forget this" to mean something. What usually happens instead is that a revoked credential is discovered on the next call, cached content keeps being served, and material derived from the revoked account stays in recall. Deletion of derived data is also misreported: removing a local memory does not delete the provider's original, and saying otherwise is a false claim.

**Outcome.** Disconnecting is a first-class operation with an honest, visible propagation result: which credentials were removed, which caches were purged, which derived items are pending propagation, and which external originals the product does not own. Every adapter reports the same shape.

**Scope and deliverables.** A disconnect flow per account that removes credential records, marks the account's state, and enumerates the local artifacts derived from it (cached projections, cursors, ingestion outcomes, prepared drafts, receipts). A purge with per-artifact outcomes and a pending state for anything that cannot be removed immediately, so a partial purge is reported rather than assumed complete. A revocation-detection path: a provider-side revocation surfaces as a needs-reauthorization state for that account only, other accounts unaffected. A cache-invalidation rule so a purge cannot be undone by a queued job re-ingesting the source (a forgotten item must not return). A statement of the ownership limit: the product reports that it removed its own copies and does not claim to have deleted external originals. A user-visible summary suitable for the review surfaces the native master owns.

**Out of scope.** Deleting the user's provider data, which needs provider-specific deletion capabilities that may not exist. Account administration on the provider side. The retention policy of the memory store itself.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Consumes C01 for the credential references to remove and C12 for grants on the account being disconnected (grants for a removed account must not remain effective). The memory master consumes the pending-propagation status so recall can exclude revoked material. Reuse the planning set's decided rule that deterministic suppression overlays are consulted before planning and that background extraction cannot silently reopen resolved or forgotten items.

**Dependencies and why.** C01 for the credential references to remove; C12 so that removing an account also neutralises its grants and queued intents. Without C12 the purge could race a queued action.

**Acceptance scenarios.** Disconnecting one account leaves the other fully working. A revoked provider credential is detected on the next use and reported per account, with no silent retry loop. After a purge, a query that previously returned content from that account returns nothing and says why. A queued ingestion job for the removed account is cancelled or invalidated, and its completion cannot restore content. A partial purge lists exactly what remains and why. The summary never claims to have deleted a provider original. Restart preserves the revoked state and does not re-enable the account.

**Validation.** Future tests: disconnect with two accounts, revocation detection, purge with an injected failure to force a partial result, a queued-job race that must not resurrect content, a restart-stability case, and a wording assertion that the summary does not claim external deletion.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** This is the product's honest-deletion boundary and must distinguish what it owns from what it does not. Purge must be bounded and resumable; a large cache purge must not block the user's session, and its progress must be reportable.

**Evidence.** The planning set's accepted design record names the honest-propagation rule and the suppression overlay requirement (internal, not published). Verified by reading the existing private adapter suite at a pinned revision (no link): credentials are per-tool files with no revocation state and no purge path, so both the detection and the propagation shapes are new work here. Public reference: the provider authorization documentation on revoked and expired refresh tokens. A04 owns the stores being purged and A05 owns the queued work that must not resurrect content after a disconnect.

Milestone note: initial disconnect, revocation and coverage gaps, including local grant revocation, must exist in M1 with the first loop. Broader cache propagation and cross-service reconciliation testing can extend later.

nodes.title: [C18] Optional Coworker consultation adapter with explicit context routing
nodes.body:
**Trigger and problem.** An optional consultation service can give the assistant a second opinion, a critique or a research pass. Using it casually is a privacy and cost hazard: the context sent must be deliberate, the destination is a third party, and a consultation must never widen the product's authority or substitute for a decision the user should make.

**Outcome.** A per-user opt-in adapter where each call states which content classes it sends, to which destination, for which purpose, and returns an answer labelled as advice with its provenance, never as a verified fact and never as authority.

**Scope and deliverables.** An adapter that (a) is disabled unless the user enables it, (b) composes its context from explicitly named material rather than "everything relevant", (c) passes through C15's route decision before dispatch, (d) returns the answer with a provider-identifying label, a routing summary and a cost class, and (e) cannot call any product capability as a side effect. A consultation record: what was asked, which content classes were sent, which destination, what was returned, and what the user did with it, retained under an explicit policy. A refusal path: when the route policy forbids the needed content classes, the adapter says so and offers a reduced, locally computed alternative. A non-goal enforced in code: a consultation result never changes a grant, never enables a provider route and never becomes a stored preference. When the service is not installed, the feature is absent and every other capability still works.

**Out of scope.** Choosing or replacing the preferred model provider for ordinary turns (runtime master). Ensemble routing policy, budgets and provider fallbacks (runtime master). Any claim that a consultation is authoritative.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Consumes C12 for the standing grant that allows consultations and C15 for the route decision on the payload. The memory master consumes the consultation label so an advisory answer is not stored as a verified fact. Where the product already talks to an interoperability server, reuse that transport rather than adding a second protocol; an absent optional server must degrade to "not available" rather than a startup failure.

**Dependencies and why.** C12 for the grant: a consultation sends user content out, so it cannot exist without an authorization decision. C15 for the egress classification of the payload, which is the whole risk of the feature.

**Acceptance scenarios.** With the feature disabled, no consultation call is possible and no optional service is contacted. With it enabled, a consultation sends only the explicitly named material, and the record shows exactly what was sent. A payload containing a content class the route forbids is refused with a reduced alternative offered. A returned answer cannot enable a route, change a grant or become a stored preference, and a test asserts this because the failure would be silent. The optional service being absent leaves all other capabilities working. A consultation that times out returns an honest failure with no partial local write.

**Validation.** Future tests over a fake consultation service: disabled-state absence, payload composition with an explicit content-class assertion, route refusal, authority-invariance after an answer that claims new permission, missing-service degradation, and time-out honesty. The invocation count per session is asserted so a retry loop cannot multiply cost.

**Privacy, authority and performance.** This path sends user content to a third party, so it is opt-in, per-call labelled and policy-checked. Cost and rate limits are attributed per user, and background extraction must never trigger a consultation without a standing grant and a stated purpose.
