**Evidence.** The planning set's accepted design record states that authorized remote inference is not automatically a privacy breach while grant checks do not prove semantic safety, which this leaf implements (internal, not published). Public reference for the transport shape: the model-context protocol specification, since an interoperability server is an adapter rather than a core dependency. No provider contract is asserted here; the provider assessment belongs to C15. A14 owns the interoperability transport and server lifecycle this adapter reuses instead of adding a second protocol.

nodes.title: [C19] Channel-neutral inbox and outbox with delivery receipts
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Mail, Mattermost and a messaging channel each have an
adapter, but there is no common way to receive a message and to send one with a receipt.
Outcome: one channel-neutral envelope with an inbox and an outbox, used by every adapter.

**Scope and deliverables.** A channel envelope carrying channel kind, source account, external
conversation identifier, direction, timestamp and delivery state; an inbox that records inbound
messages before any interpretation; an outbox with an at-least-once send and a deduplication
key; a delivery receipt model with sent, delivered, failed and unknown states; and an adapter
contract that a new channel implements.

**Out of scope.** Treating a channel message as identity proof, creating a grant from a message,
and a channel that writes domain state directly instead of through the outbox.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the envelope and the outbox. C01 owns the
account identity map, C03 and C08 own their source adapters, A15 owns durable delivery and crash
recovery, C21 owns the authority epoch. Adapters reuse the envelope rather than each defining a
message shape.

**Dependencies.** C01 for account binding, C03 for mail ingestion and C08 for the Mattermost
archive path.

**Acceptance and adverse.** An inbound message is recorded once and an outbound message reaches
a terminal delivery state. Adverse scenarios: the send succeeds but the receipt is lost and the
message is retried with the same deduplication key and is not delivered twice; an adapter returns
an ambiguous failure and the outbox records unknown rather than sent; a message arrives for a
channel that is not configured and is quarantined rather than interpreted.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario replays recorded adapter fixtures and
measures the duplicate-send and unknown-state counts. Public references:
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5322 for mail and https://api.mattermost.com/ for the channel
API. Privacy baseline: fixtures are synthetic and the internal channel transcripts are
non-public and are not linked here.

nodes.title: [C20] Channel identity separated from source-account identity
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** A message arrives from an address or handle that looks
familiar, and the product must not silently promote that into authority. Outcome: two separate
records, one for the source account the user bound and one for the channel identity that carried
a message, with an explicit and auditable link between them.

**Scope and deliverables.** A channel identity record (channel kind, handle, display name,
first seen, verification state), a binding record that links a channel identity to a source
account only through an explicit user action, a rule that an unbound or mismatched identity can
still be read but cannot act, and a report that lists every binding with when and how it was
made.

**Out of scope.** Treating a verified sender address, a workspace membership or a phone number
as identity proof, implicit bindings learned from conversation, and any administrative action
granted by sending a message.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the channel identity record and the
binding rule. C01 owns the source account map, C12 owns grants, C19 owns the envelope, and B01
owns source identity for evidence. Bindings create evidence records through B01 rather than a
parallel table.

**Dependencies.** C01 for the account map and C19 for the channel envelope.

**Acceptance and adverse.** An unbound handle can be read and cannot act, and an explicitly
bound handle resolves to the account. Adverse scenarios: a display name collides with a bound
identity and the message is attributed by handle, not by name; a sender spoofs an address and
still cannot act; revoking a binding leaves previously recorded evidence attributed to the
handle that carried it.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario replays spoofed and colliding fixtures and
measures the count of actions permitted to unbound identities, which must be zero. Public
reference: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8601 for the timestamp form used by the records.
Privacy baseline: handles and addresses in fixtures are synthetic example.invalid values.

nodes.title: [C21] Single active authority epoch and host transfer
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** The same assistant may run on a laptop and later on a
virtual machine, and nothing may let both be authoritative at once. Outcome: one authority epoch
record, with a defined transfer procedure that revokes the previous epoch before the next one
becomes active.

**Scope and deliverables.** An authority epoch record with holder, start time, end time and
reason; a transfer procedure with prepare, quiesce, revoke, activate and verify steps; a lease or
epoch token that every write path must present; a rule that a stale epoch token is refused rather
than merged; and an audit entry for every transfer with its evidence.

**Out of scope.** Multi-writer synchronisation, last-writer-wins merging, any automatic transfer
without an explicit intent, and any transfer that carries local operating-system authority with
it.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the epoch record and the transfer
procedure. C12 owns grants and the effect broker, A08 owns intents and receipts, A04 owns the
store, C19 owns the channel envelope, and A24 owns the hosting boundary. The write path asks the
epoch record rather than each module keeping its own writer flag.

**Dependencies.** C12 for grants, A08 for intent receipts and C19 for the channel envelope.

**Acceptance and adverse.** A transfer leaves exactly one active epoch and the previous holder's
writes are refused. Adverse scenarios: the old holder keeps running after transfer and its writes
are rejected with a stale-epoch error; a transfer is interrupted after revocation and the
assistant runs read-only until an operator completes it; a clock skew between hosts does not
create two active epochs.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario runs two service instances against one epoch
record and measures the count of writes accepted from the non-holder, which must be zero. Public
reference: https://raft.github.io/ for the lease and term vocabulary this borrows from. Privacy
baseline: no real host name or credential appears in the transfer record schema.

Unavailability never triggers a transfer by itself. When the previous holder is partitioned or powered off and cannot acknowledge revocation, the epoch is not reassigned automatically: an operator must first demonstrate that the old holder is fenced, and a returning holder with its own restored store has its writes and queued intents refused and its state never merged. The acceptance case therefore runs a separate restored store through a partition and resume cycle, in addition to two instances sharing one epoch record.

nodes.title: [C22] Device grants and scoped expiring intents pulled outbound
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** A device needs to perform a local action, and the
service must be able to authorize it without the device holding standing authority. Outcome: the
device pulls scoped, expiring intents outbound and independently enforces its own local grants.

**Scope and deliverables.** An intent record with target device, action class, scope, expiry,
nonce and issuing epoch; a pull endpoint the device polls outbound so no inbound connection to
the device is required; a device-side grant check that runs before the effect regardless of what
the service asked for; a single-use rule with replay detection; and a refusal path that reports
the reason to the service.

**Out of scope.** Pushing commands into a device over an inbound port, standing device
authority, an intent that carries local operating-system authority from the service, and any
intent without an expiry.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the intent record and the pull contract.
C12 owns grants and the effect broker, C14 owns the capability registry, F16 owns pairing,
revocation and transport, F17 owns mobile control, A08 owns action receipts. The device
reuses A08's receipt model to report outcomes.

**Dependencies.** C12 for grants, F16 for pairing and transport and C21 for the authority epoch.

**Acceptance and adverse.** An intent pulled once is performed once and reported once. Adverse
scenarios: a replayed intent is refused by the nonce check; an expired intent is refused; a
device that has revoked its own local grant refuses the service's intent and reports a refusal;
the service asks for an action class the device never granted and the device refuses.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario replays intents against a device simulator
and measures the count of effects performed without a fresh unexpired intent, which must be
zero. Public reference: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6750 for the bearer-token shape this
borrows. Privacy baseline: the device simulator uses synthetic identifiers.

The page holds no authority over a device. A device effect still requires a scoped intent that the device pulls and enforces locally, and the shared web interface cannot mint one.

nodes.title: [C23] Revocation epochs and offline delivery queue
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** A laptop closes, a phone goes offline and a
credential is revoked, and deliveries and intents must not silently rot or replay later.
Outcome: revocation carrying an epoch, plus a bounded offline delivery queue that replays once.

**Scope and deliverables.** A revocation record naming the device or credential, the epoch in
which it took effect and the reason; propagation to the outbox and the intent store; an offline
delivery queue with per-item expiry, a retry ceiling and a terminal expired state; a reconnect
procedure that replays once and never duplicates an effect; and a report of items expired while
offline.

**Out of scope.** Unbounded retry, delivery of private content into a shared or unauthenticated
channel, and any replay that re-establishes a revoked device.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the revocation epoch binding and the
offline queue. C17 owns disconnect and cache propagation, C22 owns intents and device grants,
C21 owns the authority epoch, A15 owns the durable outbox and crash recovery, C19 owns the
channel outbox. The queue is a view over A15's outbox with an expiry policy rather than a second
queue.

**Dependencies.** C17 for revocation propagation, C22 for intents and A15 for the durable
outbox.

**Acceptance and adverse.** Items queued while offline are delivered once after reconnect or
expire with a report. Adverse scenarios: a device is revoked while items are queued and the
items expire rather than deliver; a partial send is retried and the deduplication key prevents
a duplicate; the queue grows past its ceiling and the oldest low-priority items expire first.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario disconnects, queues, revokes and reconnects,
and measures duplicate deliveries, expired items and the recovery time. Public reference:
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7231 for retry and caching semantics. Privacy baseline: the
queue fixtures are synthetic and the internal revocation log is non-public and is not linked
here.

nodes.title: [D01] Commitment lifecycle schema and state machine contract
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: today a promise is captured as free text, so the same obligation can exist simultaneously as a note, a claim and a task summary with no shared identity, no due state and no way to distinguish something the system inferred from something the user decided. Any feature built on that shape invents its own variant, and the user cannot ask a factual question about what is still outstanding. The outcome here is one versioned record and one explicit state machine that every later leaf writes to, with fixtures and a validator, so that a downstream change cannot quietly redefine what done means.

Scope and deliverables:
- The record: identity, kind, owner and counterparties as portable person references, canonical statement, source anchors (source kind, document reference, revision, verbatim quote, relocation rule), due instant with a precision class, condition text, provenance class (inferred, confirmed, corrected, rejected), audience label, state, completion evidence reference, notification sub-record and timestamps.
- The state set and every legal transition with its guard, including the rule that a reconciliation pass may update anchors but never moves a terminal row back to an active state.
- The deterministic fingerprint used for re-extraction identity, versioned so a later change is detectable.
- JSON Schema plus synthetic fixtures: a plain promise, a suggestion, a hypothetical, a request to the user, a correction, a completed item and a stale item. All fixture text is invented and contains no real person or private content.
- A validator that refuses a completion with no stable evidence reference and refuses an anchor with no quote.

Out of scope: extraction quality (D02), dedup and merge policy (D03), the storage engine, migrations and backup (A04), person resolution (C01), transcript retrieval (B03) and every surface.

Interface and ownership: core/commitments/ owns the schema, the fixtures and the validator. Cross-track contract versioning and the fixture mechanism follow A02. Person references and source references stay opaque, so this schema never embeds a display name, an account email or a local filesystem path.

Dependencies: A02 is required because the schema is a cross-track contract and must be published through the shared versioning and fixture mechanism; without it other masters cannot pin a version to build against.

Acceptance scenarios: a promise round-trips through serialize, validate and deserialize with identical semantics; a completion without evidence is rejected with a visible error; a re-extraction carrying the same fingerprint creates no second row; a correction record survives a schema version bump; and in an adverse case where the source document disappeared, the row remains valid with its anchor marked unreachable rather than being dropped.

Validation: a future test scenario consists of schema validation over the fixture pack, a store round-trip test and a negative test for the two validator refusals. No executable command is claimed to exist at authoring time.

Privacy and authority: the record holds private quotes, so it stays local, never appears in plaintext diagnostics and never enters public fixtures except as invented text. The schema records provenance but grants no authority to act.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on commitment lifecycle (non-public, no link); the schema and suppression rules are design until implemented.

nodes.title: [D02] Promise extraction with attribution, negative rules and evidence spans
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: transcripts, mail and chat mix first-person promises with suggestions, hypotheticals, requests and third-person intentions. Older research on meeting action items and email speech acts contributes two durable design points and no performance bound: an action item is better decomposed into description, owner, timeframe and agreement than treated as one flat act, and non-commitments must be suppressed explicitly and inspectably. Those historical score lines measured the tooling of their time, so this leaf defines its own current synthetic acceptance evaluation instead of inheriting a number. The outcome is a two-stage design that favours precision at the decision point: a deterministic candidate router with high recall, then a structured model pass that must return spans, with a negative-rule table that makes suppression explicit and inspectable.

Scope and deliverables:
- The candidate router: cue classes for first-person future phrasing, self-directed obligations and explicit promises, with the rule that the router only nominates and never decides.
- The structured extraction contract: field names, types and validation for description, owner, timeframe, condition, agreement evidence and quote, versioned so a later comparison is like for like.
- Attribution: self, a named third party, or an unresolved mention that is recorded as unresolved; a display name is never treated as identity.
- The negative-rule table: suggestion, hypothetical, directive to another person, request to the user, opinion, past intention, retraction inside the same segment, and informational note. Each fired rule is stored with the span.
- Time handling: a relative date resolves against the source timestamp, never the current clock, and a missing timeframe is recorded as unknown rather than invented.
- Budget: a per-pass call budget, with deferred work recorded as deferred instead of dropped.

Out of scope: dedup and supersession (D03), plan rendering (D06), retrieval of transcript originals (B03), provider and model selection (A06), and any decision about whether a permitted effect may be performed (master C).

Interface and ownership: core/commitments/extraction. Model calls go through the provider seam owned by A06 so no model identifier is hardcoded. Quote anchoring uses the relocation rule owned by B01 so an anchor survives a document revision. Existing private extraction pipelines are an optional reuse path for a connected install and never a required dependency: a standalone install, and every new voice, mail or chat source, must reach the same record shape through this generic path, and the fixtures for that path are synthetic.

Dependencies: D01 for the record the output must satisfy, and A06 for the provider seam, because hardcoding a provider here would contradict the replaceable-provider requirement.

Acceptance scenarios: the decoy suite produces zero auto-accepted commitments while the promise fixture is captured with owner, quote and due precision; a transcript dated two weeks ago yields a due date in the past rather than one shifted into the future; a conditional promise is stored with its condition and is not scheduled; a re-extraction of an unchanged document makes no model call; a provider timeout leaves a deferred marker and no half-written row; and a retraction inside one segment does not produce a commitment.

Validation: the current acceptance evaluation is a versioned synthetic corpus of invented transcripts, threads and chat conversations carrying the expected owner, timeframe, condition and quote for each item. Each run pins the prompt and provider version and reports per-class precision and recall, owner-attribution error and user-correction rate; the gate requires zero auto-accepted decoy candidates and no regression against the previous run for the same corpus version. Any prompt, model or rule change re-runs it. No executable command is claimed to exist at authoring time.

Privacy and authority: quotes are private content and the provider call is subject to the egress policy owned by C15; fixtures contain invented text only. Extraction produces candidates, never authorization. Evidence: the decomposition and the explicit-suppression approach are public research findings, cited as design references only; no historical score is used as a bound and no measured result is claimed by this leaf.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on attribution and evidence classes (non-public, no link); extraction behaviour is design, not measured.

nodes.title: [D03] Dedup, reconciliation and closed-state suppression
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: three different duplicate problems are usually conflated. Re-extraction of the same document regenerates the same claim; one promise stated three times in a meeting becomes three rows; the same obligation arrives through a transcript, a mail thread and a chat message. The most damaging failure is the reverse one: a reconciliation pass that re-opens something the user completed, dismissed or corrected, which teaches the user that closing an item is pointless. The outcome is one live row per real obligation, with several anchors where several sources witnessed it, and a guarantee that terminal states and user corrections survive any later ingest.

Scope and deliverables:
- Re-extraction identity: the versioned fingerprint, evaluated per document revision, with the rule that one fingerprint yields one row and updates first-seen and last-seen markers.
- Same-channel merge: same owner, same counterparties and same action within a bounded window, producing one row with several anchors.
- Cross-channel clustering: compatible kind, compatible due state, similarity above a configured floor, inside a window; with an explicit forbidden list, namely never across audience, never across owner, never across counterparties, never merging a supersession link, and never merging completion evidence into the claim itself.
- Supersession as a link rather than a merge, so the history remains readable and the successor inherits anchors, notification identity and snooze state. Inheritance is what stops the user being nudged twice under two identifiers for one obligation.
- Closed-state suppression on every ingest path, including a late-arriving source that predates the closure.
- Anchor validity: a row whose anchors all became unreachable is marked as unverified rather than deleted, and a deletion of a source does not silently remove an obligation.

Out of scope: the record itself (D01), extraction (D02), any cross-plane merge between private and company data (owned by C13 and the correction semantics in B08), and model training.

Interface and ownership: core/commitments. Consumes source identity from B01 and reuses the correction and suppression semantics owned by B08 instead of creating a second correction store. Merge and suppression decisions are logged with a reason so the user can ask why an item was hidden or combined.

Dependencies: D01 and D02, because identity, state and the merge inputs all presuppose the record and the extractor output.

Acceptance scenarios: several extractions of one document leave one row; the same promise seen in a transcript, a thread and a message yields one row with three anchors; a completed row stays completed after a re-harvest and after an extraction version bump; a corrected attribute is not resurrected by a later pass; a merge attempt across audiences is refused with a visible reason; after a source is deleted the row survives with an unreachable anchor; and a commitment that arrives from a source dated before its closure is suppressed rather than re-opened.

Validation: a future property test over generated duplicate sets plus a fixed regression corpus for terminal-state preservation and for each forbidden merge. No command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: cross-plane merging is a privacy boundary, so the rule set is deterministic, logged and reviewable, and no fingerprint is computed over company data by a private-context process.

Suppression boundary: a new promise or a recurring task from a later source keeps its own identity and evidence. Suppression applies to the closed item, not to a global phrase ban, so a genuinely new commitment on the same topic is created rather than silently dropped; the adverse case covers exactly this.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on deduplication and suppression (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [D04] Unanswered inbox and chat prioritization
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: nothing becomes a commitment until something decides it deserves attention, and mail provides no reliable awaiting-reply flag. A naive unread rule returns hundreds of items, while a keyword rule misses the one thread where a person is blocked. The outcome is a per-source rule set that produces a small, explainable list of reply-owed and reply-awaited items, each anchored to a message or post, each with an age, and each carrying the reason it was selected. The first loop is mail-only: Gmail prioritization is staged because it is what makes the daily plan useful, and chat prioritization is a capability that switches on when a chat connector is installed.

Scope and deliverables:
- Reply-owed rules: the last message is not from the user; the user is a direct recipient rather than copied; it contains a question, a direct request or a stated deadline; and the thread is not muted, archived or marked done.
- Reply-awaited rules: the user spoke last to a known person, producing a waiting item with an age rather than a nudge to the other party.
- Chat rules, staged behind the chat capability: a direct message where the last post is not the user is an item; a mention of the user is an item; a reply inside a thread the user started is an item; unrelated channel volume is never an item. While no chat connector is installed these rules are inert and the source renders as not configured.
- Age and priority: a business-day clock and an age ladder that decides digest versus notification.
- Negative list applied before selection: newsletters, service notifications, marketing, copied-only threads, a closing thank-you, and a message already answered from another account.
- Mapping into the commitment kinds from D01 with the message identifier as the anchor and a coverage-aware empty result.

Out of scope: drafting or sending replies (C04, C09), the interruption policy (D10), promise extraction from bodies (D02), chat archive ownership (C08) and any interface rendering.

Interface and ownership: core/commitments/sources. Consumes normalized envelopes and per-account cursors from the mail connector for the staged first loop, and from the chat connector once installed. The connector decides what it can read; this leaf decides what deserves attention, and it must report a degraded, disconnected or not-configured source as a coverage gap rather than an empty result. The rules are written against the generic envelope so a later source gets the same treatment without depending on any private pipeline, and all fixtures are synthetic.

Dependencies: C03 for incremental mail ingestion, because without a cursor the mail rules can only run on a full listing, which the roadmap forbids; D01 for the record the items become. The chat connector is a capability dependency, not a blocking edge: the first loop ships with no chat install, so those rules are accepted when the adapter lands and stay inert until then.

Acceptance scenarios: a fixture mailbox containing a question from a person, a newsletter, a copied-only message and a thread where the user replied last yields exactly one reply-owed item with the naming rule recorded; once chat is installed, a chat fixture with a direct message, one mention and unrelated channel chatter yields two items; an automated sender is suppressed with a reason; a disconnected source yields no items plus one coverage line; an install with no chat connector renders that source as not configured and makes no no-action claim for it; and a message the user answers from a second account is not reported as owed.

Validation: a future fixture test per source asserting precision on the selection and the coverage line, plus a rate check that selection work is proportional to changed items rather than mailbox size. No command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: reading mail and chat requires an explicit per-account grant, and an item stores a reference plus a short quote rather than the body. The rules are deterministic so the user can audit why something was raised.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on prioritization (non-public, no link); no real inbox content is asserted anywhere in this plan.

nodes.title: [D05] Meeting preparation with continuity from prior commitments
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: preparation today means rereading the last transcript, which does not scale and does not answer the question a user actually has before a meeting, namely what I promised these people, what they promised me, and what is still open between us. The outcome is a preparation bundle per meeting identity, assembled inside a token budget, refreshed when the meeting changes, and honest when the material it would need is missing.

Scope and deliverables:
- Bundle content: open commitments in both directions with each attendee, the commitments produced by the previous meeting in that series with their current state, unanswered threads with those attendees, questions left unresolved at the last meeting, and any stated intent that is approaching its date.
- Ranking and a token cap, with explicit disclosure of any section dropped because of the budget, so a partial bundle never looks complete.
- Readiness timing: the bundle becomes available a configurable lead time before the start and is refreshed when the event changes materially.
- Item lifecycle: created, refreshed, dismissed; a dismissed bundle is not re-created by a refresh that changes nothing material, and a materially changed meeting produces a new one.
- Provenance per section, so each line in the bundle can be traced to a message, a transcript span or a commitment record.

Out of scope: transcript retrieval internals (B03), calendar synchronisation (C05), the interruption policy that decides when the bundle is mentioned (D10), the notification surface (F09), and any mutation of calendar events (C06).

Interface and ownership: core/planning/prep. It consumes the retrieval contract with its token cap from the knowledge and transcript leaves, and event identity from the calendar connector. It owns what the bundle contains and when it is ready; it does not own how a missing transcript is represented, which is B03's coverage contract.

Dependencies: C05 for event identity and recurrence, because a bundle keyed on a start time duplicates itself on the first reschedule; B03 for transcript originals and their coverage, because a bundle that silently omits the previous meeting is worse than one that says the transcript is missing; D01 for the commitment record it summarises.

Acceptance scenarios: two events sharing a recurrence identity but differing in start time produce one bundle that moves rather than two; a bundle whose previous transcript is unavailable says so rather than implying there was nothing to report; a bundle for a synthetic five-attendee meeting stays within the token cap and names the dropped section; a dismissed bundle is not recreated by a refresh that changes nothing material; and a cancelled event removes its bundle with the cancellation recorded.

Adverse and restart cases: a restart during assembly either completes the bundle or leaves no partial artefact; a failing source yields a partial bundle with a named gap; and a permission change that revokes transcript access degrades the bundle to the sections that remain available with the loss stated.

Validation: a future fixture test over synthetic meetings asserting bundle content, the budget behaviour, the coverage disclosure and the reschedule identity rule. No executable command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: bundle content is private, assembly runs locally, and retrieval of originals is subject to the egress policy. The bundle grants no authority to send anything.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on meeting preparation (non-public, no link); calendar and transcript interfaces are design to verify against real providers.

nodes.title: [D06] Realistic daily plan and capacity
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: a plan that lists everything open is not a plan, and a plan that reshuffles every hour cannot be followed. The outcome is a rendered day that fits the user's actual shape: the meetings already on the calendar, the focus blocks they declared, their quiet hours, a small set of commitments that can realistically be advanced today, and an explicit account of everything that was not included and why.

Scope and deliverables:
- Planning inputs: the day shape from the calendar, commitment priority, age, whether a counterparty is waiting, whether preparation is ready, and condition state.
- Selection and ordering: a deterministic rule with a capacity cap, so the same inputs always produce the same plan and the user can learn what the plan means.
- Full accounting: every open item appears in exactly one bucket, planned, deferred with a reason, or waiting on someone else. Nothing disappears silently, which is the property that makes the plan trustworthy.
- A coverage line per configured source inside the plan itself, so the plan states what it could not see.
- Plan stability: two renders within one hour over unchanged inputs are identical, and a mid-day change re-plans without discarding an item the user already acted on.
- A structured output contract rather than a prose message, because presentation belongs to the native layer.

Out of scope: mutating the calendar (C06), drafting or sending anything (C04, C09), notification content and urgency (D08, D10), and any optimisation beyond a bounded deterministic selection. This leaf deliberately contains no scheduling engine, because the roadmap assigns simple durable queues and due timers rather than a general workflow engine.

Interface and ownership: core/planning/. Consumes the day shape from the calendar connector and the item set from the commitment record, unanswered-source selection and preparation bundles. It owns selection and accounting; it does not own the priority signals themselves.

Dependencies: C05, because without recurrence-correct events the day shape is wrong and the plan is confidently wrong; D01, because the plan is a projection of the record and cannot invent its own item model.

Acceptance scenarios: a synthetic day with three meetings and twenty open items produces a plan with a small committed set while all twenty are accounted for and a coverage line is present; a calendar insertion mid-day re-plans and keeps an item the user already closed out of the plan; a degraded source produces a coverage warning and not a confident empty plan; two renders in one hour are identical; a conditional commitment appears as waiting rather than as due.

Adverse and restart cases: a restart between selection and render produces either the previous plan or the new one, never a partial list with missing buckets; a calendar outage yields a plan with the meeting section marked unavailable rather than an empty day; and a clock change or timezone shift recomputes the day boundary without duplicating items.

Validation: a future golden-file test over one synthetic day, a stability test across two renders, and an accounting assertion that no open item is unrepresented. No command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: the plan is private and rendering must not write quotes to diagnostics; the plan is a proposal and confers no authority to act on the day.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on planning and capacity (non-public, no link); the plan model is a design proposal.

nodes.title: [D07] Incremental trigger and due processing loop
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: the product must notice changes and fire on time without rescanning an account or paying for a model call every heartbeat. The outcome is an event-driven loop that consumes source deltas and due timers, does nothing measurable while idle, and degrades honestly when a source is unavailable.

Scope and deliverables:
- Trigger classes: a source delta, a due boundary, a meeting lifecycle transition, a supervised harness run transition and a user action. Each trigger carries references, never payload bodies.
- A durable timer set for due and snooze boundaries, evaluated from stored state, never from model output.
- Stale-schedule revalidation: every pending boundary is rechecked against current state before it fires, so a timer that came due while the process was stopped, or whose commitment was completed, superseded or corrected meanwhile, is dropped or rescheduled instead of fired late. This is also the first-slice guarantee that a resume cannot produce a burst: a resume fires at most one caught-up reminder, never one per missed boundary.
- Reconciliation tiers with bounds: a per-event tier routing only affected threads, meetings or commitments; a periodic sweep draining connector cursors with bounded queries; and targeted re-verification of open items against their anchors.
- Per-account cursors with the invalid-cursor path, using the documented full-sync fallback for that source only and recording a coverage gap with its window.
- An idle assertion: an idle period performs zero model calls and zero account-wide listings, an explicit checkable property rather than an aspiration.
- A per-window budget with visible deferral, so work clipped by the budget is reported as deferred instead of vanishing.
- Idempotency: reprocessing the same delta after a crash produces no duplicate state change or notification.

Out of scope: connector transport, cursor storage mechanics and the watch renewal or full-sync plumbing owned by the connector leaves; durable job progress and cancellation (A05); notification delivery and the reminder baseline it applies (D08); the interruption policy (D10); and the multi-day offline catch-up with its coverage gaps and cross-device suppression (D18, which extends this leaf's no-burst guarantee rather than duplicating it). This leaf decides when the system looks and how much it looks at, not how it talks to a provider.

Interface and ownership: core/proactivity/triggers. It consumes the normalized envelope and cursor contract from the connector master and owns the routing, tiering and budgeting on top of it.

Dependencies: C03 and C05 for incremental mail and calendar deltas, because without cursors every check becomes a full listing, which is the failure this leaf exists to prevent; D01 for the record whose due boundaries are evaluated.

Acceptance scenarios: an idle period produces zero model calls and zero account-wide listing calls; a delta for one thread causes work proportional to that thread and no other; a due boundary fires once inside its window and does not re-fire after a restart; a timer whose commitment closed while the process was stopped is dropped rather than fired late, and a short sleep yields at most one caught-up reminder rather than one per missed boundary; an invalid cursor triggers the documented bounded full resync for that source only and records a coverage gap; a missing connector produces a coverage line and does not block the rest of the loop; and a budget-clipped window reports deferred work rather than a false empty result.

Adverse and restart cases: a kill between a delta being consumed and its effect being committed leaves no lost or duplicated work; a clock jump backwards does not re-fire past boundaries; and a source returning an error repeatedly is backed off rather than retried in a tight loop.

Validation: a future test with a fake clock, a fake connector and a model-call counter, asserting the idle property, the proportionality rule, the stale-timer drop and the resume-without-burst rule on a simulated short sleep. No command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: triggers carry references and reason codes only. The loop reads what the granted scope allows and performs no effect on its own.

Baseline note: the due loop is source-agnostic and manual reminders work with no Google account. Completion prerequisites are D01, A04, A05 and the D10 quiet policy contract; C03 and C05 are optional intake providers, and source-triggered integration is validated separately by A17. Basic sleep catch-up belongs to this M1 baseline; advanced burst behaviour stays in D18.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on due processing (non-public, no link); due-loop behaviour is design, validated by the A17 scenario when implemented.

nodes.title: [D08] Reminder intent and outbox semantics
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: a reminder held only in memory vanishes on restart, and one that fires twice destroys trust. The outcome is a reminder as a durable intent with a receipt, so the system knows what it decided to say, whether it said it, and what is still owed after a crash.

Scope and deliverables:
- The intent record: subject commitment, reason, scheduled instant, correlation identifier, evidence link, notification identity and the justifying policy.
- A deterministic reason set (due today, overdue by days, a counterparty waiting, a preparation window opening, a reschedule detected, a supervised run finishing). A model may propose urgency but a fixed rule decides, so the explanation is stable and testable.
- Deduplication and coalescing on the logical notification identity across restarts and devices, so one obligation is announced once and several items due in one window become one message.
- The M1 baseline attention discipline, since reminders exist before the fuller policy: a default night window holds informational reminders, one opt-out suppresses all proactive reminders without hiding results on request, and every suppression records its reason.
- Delivery versus display: an acknowledgement is not proof of being seen.
- The unknown-outcome state: when a delivery cannot be confirmed, the intent is marked unknown and reconciled rather than resent blindly, reusing the runtime receipt discipline instead of reimplementing it.
- Cancellation that distinguishes a stopped voice turn, cancelled queued work, a dispatched effect, an unknown outcome and completed work.
- Receipt retention for audit, holding references and reason codes rather than bodies.

Out of scope: native presentation (F09, F02), the fuller interruption policy (D10), the multi-day catch-up (D18) and the outbox and crash-recovery mechanics owned by the runtime master, which this leaf builds on rather than replaces. Sending to another person, and reusing or copying an upstream notification helper, are out of scope. The minimal native notification surface belongs to the same first slice, so this baseline has a delivery path; if absent, reminders render in conversation rather than being dropped.

Interface and ownership: core/proactivity/outbox. It defines reminder intents over the runtime outbox contract and owns the reason set and the notification identity. Didi owns its notification core, including the dedup identity, the quiet-hours gate and the suppression log, so no private notification utility is a dependency and no code is copied. Where another notifier is active, coordination is explicit: one owner per notification key, with an upstream notifier standing down for keys Didi owns, so one event is never announced twice.

Dependencies: A05 because a reminder is exactly the durable progress and cancellation case the runtime master owns, and duplicating it would create two truths about what is in flight; A08 for the shared unknown-outcome discipline; D01 because an intent references a commitment whose evidence it must show.

Acceptance scenarios: a reminder survives a process kill and fires exactly once after restart; a second trigger inside the same window is refused with a logged reason; a delivery whose acknowledgement never arrives is marked unknown and reconciled without a blind resend; a cancellation of queued work is distinguishable from a cancellation of a dispatched effect; and the receipt shows the rule that justified the reminder plus the evidence quote; a reminder inside the night window is held with a logged reason and remains visible on request; and after a restart the resumed conversation shows the same outstanding items with no duplicate or lost reminder.

Adverse and restart cases: a crash between enqueue and dispatch leaves an intent dispatched once or reconciled as unknown; a clock change does not duplicate an intent; and a device reporting seen suppresses the second delivery.

Validation: a future test with a simulated crash between enqueue and dispatch, a fake clock for the window refusal and night window, an acknowledgement-lost path, and a restart preserving the outstanding set. No command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: receipts reference private content rather than copying it, and an intent never carries authority to send on the user's behalf.

Baseline note: reminder intents and policy decisions consume the A15 outbox and never create a second retry queue. The D10 quiet policy baseline and basic sleep catch-up are part of this M1 leaf; advanced behaviour stays in D18.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on reminder semantics (non-public, no link); delivery limits are design, and A18 pins the budgets by measurement.

nodes.title: [D09] Snooze, dismiss and defer conversation
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: every proactive system eventually raises something the user does not want right now, and the difference between a useful assistant and a nuisance is what happens next. The outcome is a small, explicit set of conversation acts, snooze, dismiss and defer, that change future behaviour deterministically, are reversible for a bounded period, and never destroy the underlying obligation.

Scope and deliverables:
- The three acts and their exact semantics: snooze until a stated or inferred time, defer to the next natural window, and dismiss as not now. Every act records the reason the user gave, if any, so the log explains the system's later behaviour.
- Per-item backoff: a first defer moves the item to the next window, a second doubles the interval, and a third demotes it to the digest so it stops interrupting. Backoff is per item and never global, because a global mute lets one noisy source silence a quiet one.
- Per-item mute, with the same per-item rule, for an item the user never wants raised again although the obligation may remain.
- A bounded undo window for the last act, and the rule that an undo restores the previous ladder position and history rather than restarting the ladder or immediately re-notifying.
- The effect on state: a dismiss defers the commitment, it does not complete it. Completing something requires evidence, which is owned elsewhere, so this leaf cannot be used as a quiet way to close work.
- Nothing is deleted by any of these acts.

Out of scope: the policy that decides when interruption is allowed (D10), the notification transport and the conversation surface (F09, F02), the record and its states (D01), and any learning that tunes the ladder from outcomes (D16 owns calibration). This leaf implements a fixed, inspectable ladder; it does not adapt.

Interface and ownership: core/proactivity. It reuses the correction and suppression semantics owned by the knowledge master rather than creating a second preference store, so user intent about an item has one home. It exposes the acts to whichever surface the native master builds, and it must work identically whether the act arrives by voice, by keyboard or by clicking a notification.

Dependencies: D01 for the item identity and states the acts modify; D08 because a deferral must interact with an already queued intent, and the two must not disagree about what will happen next.

Acceptance scenarios: a first dismiss defers to the next window and logs the reason; a second dismiss increases the interval; a third demotes the item to the digest and it stops interrupting; an undo inside the window restores the previous position without an immediate notification; muting one item does not affect another item from the same source; a dismissed commitment is still visible as open in the plan; and a deferral that collides with a queued reminder produces one outcome rather than two.

Adverse and restart cases: a restart preserves the ladder position and the undo window; a deferral into quiet hours lands in the next permitted window rather than waking the user; and a deferral beyond the item's due date does not silently make the item overdue without a plan entry.

Validation: a future test walking the ladder with a fake clock, an undo test, and a collision test between a deferral and an existing intent. No command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: preference data stays local and participates in the export and forget paths owned by the knowledge master. These acts express user intent about attention; they never authorize or perform an action on another person's behalf.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on snooze and defer (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [D10] Urgency, quiet hours and focus-aware interruption policy
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: proactive systems fail in two directions. They interrupt when the user is concentrating or asleep, or they stay silent through the one item that genuinely needed attention today. The outcome is one explicit policy that maps a commitment state to an attention level, explains itself every time, and stays inside a daily budget the user set.

Scope and deliverables:
- The urgency rule set, deterministic and enumerable: due today, overdue by a number of days, a counterparty is waiting, a preparation window has opened, a reschedule was detected, a supervised run finished. A model may propose a level but a fixed rule decides, so the same state always yields the same answer.
- The first-slice baseline owned by the reminder leaf stays in force: the default night window, the single opt-out and the suppression log are guarantees this policy may extend but never remove.
- The ladder: a digest line, a silent badge, one notification, and a spoken offer that can be taken up at the hotkey. Each item may climb at most one step per natural window, and the ladder state is stored so a restart does not reset it.
- A daily interruption budget with a configured ceiling, and a held-back count reported in the digest so the user knows something was withheld rather than lost.
- Quiet hours with per-user windows, and automatic widening when the user's own calendar marks focus time or out-of-office time. The widening is shown in the plan rather than applied invisibly, and the product honours the platform focus state without claiming any entitlement to bypass it.
- The Didi-owned notification core: the dedup identity, the quiet-hours gate, the per-key throttle and the suppression log all live in this product, so no private utility is a dependency and no code is copied. Every suppression writes a reason, and a gate that hides its own suppressions is treated as a defect.
- Coordination against double announcements: one owner per notification key, and a recorded stand-down for keys another notifier owns.
- Display is not proof of being seen. Seeing is recorded from an explicit acknowledgement only, never inferred from a delivery receipt.

Out of scope: delivery transport and the notification-to-conversation surface (F09), the snooze and dismiss acts themselves (D09), reminder intent durability (D08), and mobile delivery (F17). This leaf decides whether an interruption is allowed, not how it is drawn.

Interface and ownership: core/proactivity/policy plus the notification core. It consumes reminder intents and exposes a decision plus an explanation to whichever surface exists.

Dependencies: D08 for the logical notification identity the policy throttles against, and F09 because the policy must know whether a notification can open a conversation before it chooses the voice step.

Acceptance scenarios: during quiet hours an informational item is held and the suppression reason is logged while a genuinely urgent item still reaches the user; a calendar focus block widens quiet hours and the widening is visible; when the budget is exhausted the remaining items are counted in the digest rather than dropped; a dismissed item demotes instead of escalating; and one event produced by both this core and another notifier on the machine results in a single announcement; and a user who has opted out gets no proactive reminder at all while requested results stay available.

Adverse and restart cases: a restart during quiet hours does not release a held item early; a clock change does not duplicate the budget window; and a source that floods events cannot consume another source's budget because throttling is per key.

Validation: a future test suite with a fake clock covering each rule, the budget ceiling, the focus widening, the double-announcement stand-down and the suppression log. No executable command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: quiet hours, focus state and the budget are local preferences. The explanation payload carries the evidence quote and the rule name, never a full message body, and the policy never grants authority to act on the user's behalf.

Baseline note: this is a pure product contract with its baseline in M1, consumed by D07 and D08. Fuller policy sophistication follows later, and no notification implementation is a prerequisite for it.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on interruption policy (non-public, no link); platform notification behaviour is documented but not exercised here.

nodes.title: [D11] Asynchronous investigation with conversational progress
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: a useful check across mail, calendar, transcripts and boards takes longer than a voice turn, and a system that goes quiet reads as broken while one that streams every step is unusable. The outcome is a small, honest progress contract: the assistant says what it is about to inspect, works in the background, returns once with a result, and reports failure or partial coverage as plainly as success.

Scope and deliverables:
- The investigation job: intent, the scope being inspected, a budget, a correlation identifier, and the commitment or question that justified it, so a later question about the outcome is answerable by identifier.
- The immediate acknowledgement, produced from a template rather than a model call, naming the sources it will read and what it is looking for.
- At most one progress note when the job is still running after a threshold, and never a stream of intermediate messages.
- The result note: counts, the top few items, the coverage line, and the identifier so the user can ask for more without repeating the request.
- Honest failure and partial outcomes: a job that could not read a source says which source and from when, and a job that was interrupted by a restart is reported as interrupted rather than silently forgotten. Nothing is reported as complete when part of the scope was skipped.
- An answer to the direct question of what is running right now, from the list of live jobs, including how long each has been working.
- No model call while merely waiting, so a long investigation does not burn a heartbeat.

Out of scope: job durability, cancellation state and crash recovery internals (A05), voice transport and session recovery (F04, F06, F07), notification delivery (D08, D10), and the content of what is checked, which belongs to the source prioritisation, preparation and planning leaves. This leaf makes long work legible; it does not decide what to investigate.

Interface and ownership: core/proactivity/jobs. It uses the runtime job and progress contract rather than a private queue, and exposes a structured status object that any surface can render, so the same investigation reads correctly in a voice answer, a job card or a digest.

Dependencies: A05 because durable progress and cancellation already exist there and duplicating them would create two answers about what is in flight; F02 because an asynchronous card is the natural home for a result that outlives one spoken turn.

Acceptance scenarios: a deliberately slow job emits exactly one progress note and one result; a job whose second source is unavailable returns a partial result naming the gap instead of an empty success; a restart mid-job produces an interrupted status that the user can resume; asking what is running lists the live jobs with their elapsed time; and a cancelled investigation reports what it did finish.

Adverse and restart cases: two investigations racing on the same scope do not double-report; a job that outlives its budget stops and says what remains; and a job whose result arrives after the user has moved on is filed rather than interrupting.

Validation: a future test using a fake slow job, an injected source failure and a restart, asserting one progress note, one result, and correct interrupted status. No executable command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: the job record holds references and counts, not bodies or transcripts. An investigation reads only what the granted scope allows and performs no effect beyond reading.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on asynchronous progress (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [D12] Calendar change detection and replanning
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: a reschedule is the most common realistic disturbance in a working day, and it is where naive implementations visibly break by creating a second preparation bundle, a second reminder and a stale plan entry. The outcome is that a change to an event moves everything that hangs off it, exactly once, with the change recorded in plain language.

Scope and deliverables:
- Change classes to handle: a time move, a duration change, a cancellation, an attendee added or removed, a brand new invitation, an instance of a recurring series moved or edited, and a timezone or daylight-saving shift.
- Identity rules: items hang off the event identity and, for a recurring series, off the instance identity derived from the recurring-event reference and the original start instant, never off the displayed start time. This is the single rule that prevents duplication, and it must be stated explicitly in the code comment and in the fixtures.
- Propagation: moving preparation bundles, reminder intents and plan entries that reference the event, plus open commitments whose counterparty set intersects the attendee list, which are re-timed rather than copied.
- Deduplication: one live bundle and one live reminder per event identity after any number of change events, including out-of-order delivery where an older change arrives after a newer one.
- A change log entry per handled change stating what moved, why it was detected, and what the user-facing effect was.
- Honest handling when the calendar source is unavailable: existing items keep their last known time and the plan shows the calendar section as unverified rather than silently correct.

Out of scope: calendar synchronisation, recurrence expansion and timezone mechanics (C05), creating, moving or cancelling events (C06), the contents of a preparation bundle (D05), and the interruption decision when a change is detected (D10). This leaf never writes to a calendar.

Interface and ownership: core/planning/changes. It consumes the changed-event stream and the identity fields the calendar connector owns, and it owns propagation into preparation, reminders and the plan. Preparation owns what a bundle contains; this leaf owns where and when it lives.

Dependencies: C05 because correct instance identity and recurrence are prerequisites and cannot be reconstructed from a start time; D05 because the bundle is the main artefact that must move rather than duplicate.

Acceptance scenarios: moving an event by an hour moves exactly one preparation bundle and one reminder set and leaves no orphan; moving a single instance of a recurring series keeps that instance's identity and does not touch its siblings; a cancellation removes the bundle and the reminders and records the cancellation; an out-of-order delta does not resurrect a superseded time; a timezone shift re-plans once and does not create a second series of reminders; and a new invitation creates one bundle when its start is inside the preparation horizon.

Adverse and restart cases: a burst of edits resolves to the final state with one live bundle; a restart between detecting and propagating a change leaves either the old or the new time, never both; and a revoked calendar grant degrades to the last known schedule with the section marked unverified.

Validation: a future fixture test over synthetic events covering each change class, the out-of-order case, the recurrence case and the daylight-saving boundary. No executable command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: event and attendee data is private, and the change log stores identifiers and reasons rather than event bodies. This leaf performs no calendar mutation.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on replanning (non-public, no link); calendar change semantics are design to verify against C05.

nodes.title: [D13] Dormant project and open-loop follow-up
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: work that stops moving disappears quietly. A project discussed for months, an open loop with a colleague, a thread that never resolved, all fall out of view because nothing in the day ever contradicted their absence. The outcome is a single, low-volume surface that notices a stalled thread or project once, without turning into a nag.

Scope and deliverables:
- A project reference that can point at an external board, a repository, a conversation cluster or a set of labelled threads, without this leaf owning identity resolution.
- The activity definition: a new message in a linked thread, a commit, a card move, a new transcript mention, or a new commitment in the group. Only these count; a passive read never resets dormancy.
- The dormancy rule: no qualifying activity for a configured number of days while the group still has an open commitment or a stated intent. A group with nothing open is never raised, because a finished thing is not a dormant thing.
- The surface: a weekly review entry, never an interruption, containing the last activity date, the last stated intent quote, and the last open item. One entry per dormancy period, and a second quiet period produces a second entry only after activity resumed in between.
- Resumption: any qualifying activity clears the entry, and the item does not re-appear in that period.
- The difference between dormant and abandoned, where abandoned is a user decision recorded explicitly and never an inference drawn from silence.

Out of scope: project identity and board mapping (C10), task transport and reconciliation (C11, D15), one-on-one continuity (D14, which covers relationships rather than projects), and the plan composition rules (D06 owns the day; this leaf only supplies a weekly-review section).

Interface and ownership: core/planning/dormancy. It consumes activity signals from the source prioritisation and planning leaves and from optional external reconciliation, and it owns the dormancy rule, the entry content and the anti-nag guarantee.

Dependencies: D04 because an open loop with a person is one of the two things worth noticing and its detection rules live there; D06 because the weekly review is a view over the planning surface, and the entry must not contradict what the plan says about the same item.

Acceptance scenarios: a group with an open item and fifteen days of silence produces exactly one weekly entry; a single message then clears it; a second silent period after that activity produces a second entry and not a third for the same period; a group with no open item is never raised even after months; marking a project abandoned stops it permanently until the user reverses that; and a project whose only activity is the user reading it stays dormant.

Adverse and restart cases: a source outage does not count as activity and does not silently clear an entry; a restart does not reset the dormancy clock; and timezone or clock changes do not shift the quiet period by more than a day.

Validation: a future fake-clock test covering the dormancy window, the resumption rule, the no-open-item rule and the weekly cadence, alongside an assertion that no notification is emitted by this leaf. No executable command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: entries quote at most one short intent phrase and otherwise reference items. The surface is private and its content is included in the export and forget paths of the memory master.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on open-loop follow-up (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [D14] One-on-one preparation and recurring follow-through
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: recurring one-on-ones lose continuity. Topics raised repeatedly are never settled, promises made in both directions are forgotten by the next round, and neither side can tell whether last month's concern was addressed. The outcome is a relationship record that persists across rounds and makes the second and third conversation better than the first, while staying strictly private.

Scope and deliverables:
- Detection of a one-on-one as a small recurring meeting with a stable counterparty, expressed as an identity rather than a calendar title, so a renamed series keeps its history.
- The relationship record: topics raised with the round they were raised in, whether a topic was covered, the age of an uncovered topic, commitments in both directions with their state, and questions left open at the end of a round.
- The covered rule: a topic is marked covered only on positive evidence from the next transcript, such as a discussion span addressing it, never on the absence of a repeat mention.
- The stale-topic rule: a topic raised a configured number of rounds without being covered surfaces exactly once per round as a plain statement, and the record shows how many rounds it has waited.
- Pre-meeting composition: the record contributes a section to the preparation bundle together with the open commitments and unanswered threads with that person.
- Post-meeting extraction: promises made by either side are extracted through the normal pipeline and become commitments with the counterparty set to the other attendee, with the record referencing them.

Out of scope: transcript retrieval and coverage (B03), the mechanics of assembling and budgeting a preparation bundle (D05), any company-plane publication of the record, and audio or note-taking features. Sensitivity labelling of the resulting content belongs to the memory master.

Interface and ownership: core/planning/one-on-one. It owns the record, the covered and stale rules and the section it contributes; it does not own bundle assembly and it holds no copy of transcript text, only references and short quotes.

Dependencies: D02 because both directions of the commitment flow come from extraction; D05 because the value of the record is only realised through the preparation bundle.

Acceptance scenarios: a topic covered in round two stops being raised in round three; a topic rolled three times surfaces exactly once with its age; a promise made by the counterparty appears as a commitment with the counterparty set correctly and the user as owner of nothing; a moved or renamed 1:1 keeps one record and its history; and a cancellation does not produce an empty round.

Adverse and restart cases: a missing transcript for one round leaves that round's topics at their previous status rather than marking them covered or lost; a restart preserves the record; a counterparty change on the series is treated as a new relationship and the old record is retained and linked rather than merged.

Validation: a future three-round synthetic fixture asserting the covered rule, the stale rule, both commitment directions and the rename case. No executable command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: this record is the most sensitive artefact in the epic. It stays private, is excluded from any company-plane publication by default, retains references rather than transcript text, and participates in the user's export and forget paths. It grants no authority over the counterparty or the calendar.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on recurring follow-through (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [D15] Optional external task reconciliation with honest completion semantics
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: a user may keep the same task on an external board, and duplicating it inside Didi creates two truths. Treating a card moved to a done column as proof of real-world delivery is wrong by default: boards get tidied, cards move for unrelated reasons, and a column name is a convention rather than a fact. The outcome is an optional link that keeps one identity across both systems, proposes completion instead of asserting it, and offers an explicit mode for a user who decides their board is the truth.

Scope and deliverables:
- Read mapping: boards, lists, cards, due fields, completion flags, membership and last activity, expressed as a small adapter shape so a second task system can be added without touching this logic.
- Link identity: one link per commitment and card, storing direction and identifiers, idempotent in both directions so a retry never creates a second card or a second commitment.
- Two completion semantics chosen explicitly by the user, never inferred: propose mode, the default, where a board change raises one non-interrupting confirmation and the commitment closes only on the user's answer; and board-is-truth mode, scoped to a signal the user designates, where a matching change closes the commitment with the card as evidence and the chosen semantic recorded on the closure so it can be explained and reversed.
- The pre-existing rule: a card already complete when the commitment was captured can never close it, because its history predates the promise.
- The weak-signal rule: a comment, a checklist tick or a moved subtask never counts as delivery in either mode, because none is the signal the user selected.
- Polling suited to a local install: an external webhook needs a publicly reachable callback, so the link observes the board change stream and per-card last activity, with backoff on retries and rate limits.
- Disconnection behaviour: if the board grant is revoked, the commitment stays open and the link is marked stale with its last observed state, rather than vanishing or closing implicitly.

Out of scope: board authentication, transport and idempotent reconciliation primitives (C10, C11), the general completion model used by other evidence kinds, any other task system, and any requirement that a user adopt a board at all. An install with no board configured behaves exactly as before, with the link section showing as not configured.

Interface and ownership: core/commitments/external. It owns the link record, both completion modes, the pre-existing and weak-signal rules and the polling policy; the connector master owns talking to the service.

Dependencies: C10 and C11 because the read mapping and idempotent write path belong there; D01 because the link and its closure semantics are fields on the record.

Acceptance scenarios: repeated retries after a network failure produce one card and one link; in propose mode a card moved to a done list raises exactly one confirmation and does not close the commitment; in board-is-truth mode the same change closes it with the card recorded as evidence and the selected semantic written on the closure; a card that was already complete when the promise was captured closes nothing; a comment is ignored in both modes; revoking the board leaves it open with a stale link.

Adverse and restart cases: a restart between the board change and the closure leaves either a closure with evidence or an open item with a pending confirmation, never a closure without evidence; a clock skew does not make a pre-existing card look newer than the promise; and repeated board errors back off and report degraded coverage.

Validation: a future test with synthetic board payloads for each mode and both adverse cases, plus one manual scratch-board check of the polling semantics. No executable command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: board content is third-party data and only the linked item is read. Writing to a board is an effect, allowed only under the user's granted scope, recorded with a receipt, and never inferred from the commitment record alone.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on external task reconciliation (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [D16] Outcome learning and nudge calibration with hard bounds
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: a fixed interruption policy will be wrong for some users, but an adaptive one can drift into two bad states, banner blindness from over-notification or missing something urgent through over-silence. The outcome is a bounded calibration that adjusts only within user-set limits, records every change it makes, and can always be reverted.

Scope and deliverables:
- Outcome counters recorded per decision: raised, seen, acted on, dismissed, snoozed, completed after a reminder, and corrected. Counters must distinguish seen from acted on, because a notification that is displayed and ignored is the primary evidence of noise.
- The correction-rate metric over auto-accepted commitments, reported with its denominator and time window, as the headline trust signal for the whole lane.
- The calibration levers and their hard bounds: per-key throttle interval, digest threshold, and escalation eligibility. The daily interruption budget, quiet hours and focus widening are never relaxed automatically under any calibration, because those are user limits rather than heuristic values.
- A review surface that lists each policy change with the trigger that caused it, the before and after value, and the affected key, so a change is never invisible.
- Reversal: any calibration step can be reverted, and the reversal is recorded as a user decision rather than a new automatic adjustment.
- The evidence rule: calibration uses only the user's own actions in this install. It never learns from other users, never from company data, and never from model inference about whether a nudge was welcome.
- Versioning: each decision records the policy version that produced it, so a later outcome can be attributed to the policy in force at the time.

Out of scope: the default policy values and the rules themselves (D10 owns the fixed defaults; D09 owns per-item backoff), model fine-tuning, any cross-user aggregation, and any change to the interruption budget ceiling. This leaf tunes within the envelope; it never widens the envelope.

Interface and ownership: core/proactivity/calibration plus the review surface data. It consumes decision records from the reminder outbox and the policy, and writes only policy parameters and their history.

Dependencies: D09 because the per-item backoff outcomes are a primary input, and D10 because the envelope it must respect is defined there.

Acceptance scenarios: calibration never raises the interruption budget above the configured ceiling even when every nudge is acted on; a week with no user action leaves the policy unchanged; counters correctly separate displayed from acted; the review surface lists each change with its trigger and a revert action; a reverted step does not immediately re-apply itself; and a new policy version is visible in the next decision record.

Adverse and restart cases: a counter store that fails to write does not cause a calibration step, since the absence of evidence must not read as a signal; a restart mid-week does not double-count or reset the window; and a flood from one key cannot shift a global parameter because the levers are per key.

Validation: a future simulation over synthetic outcome streams asserting the bound invariants, the no-evidence rule and the revert path, plus a check that the reporting metric refuses to display without a denominator. No executable command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: the counters are behavioural data, so they stay local, are visible to the user in the review surface, and participate in the export and forget paths. Calibration changes how the product speaks, never what it is permitted to do.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on calibration (non-public, no link); counters are behavioural data and stay local.

nodes.title: [D17] Proactivity and false-promise evaluation gate over a current synthetic corpus
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: proactive behaviour fails quietly in both directions, by accepting a commitment the user never made or by missing one they did, and a spoken assistant gives the user no way to review a week of decisions at once. The outcome is one versioned evaluation that measures the pipeline as it is today, gates a release on the failures that matter most, and refuses to report a number without the corpus version that produced it.

Scope and deliverables:
- The corpus: entirely synthetic and invented, covering transcripts, mail threads, chat conversations, calendar days and board states. It carries, per item, the expected classification, owner, timeframe, condition and quote, plus the decoy classes namely suggestion, hypothetical, directive to another person, request to the user, informational note, past intention and retraction.
- The class and metric list: per-class precision and recall; owner-attribution error; due-date resolution error including the past-date case for older sources; the user-correction rate over auto-accepted items; false-interruption rate; missed-overdue rate; duplicate notification count per logical identity; and catch-up burst count after a simulated offline period.
- The release gate: zero auto-accepted items from the decoy classes, no regression against the previous recorded run for the same corpus version, the interruption budget respected under the simulated week, and a coverage line present in every rendered plan.
- Re-run policy: any change to a prompt, model, provider, negative-rule table or interruption policy re-runs the gate and records the delta, so a swap is measured rather than assumed.
- Comparability: results are stored with the corpus version, the pipeline version and the provider identity, and the harness reports a comparison or an explicit incomparable marker.
- Scope discipline about evidence: this evaluation is current and synthetic. No historical published score from earlier work is treated as a bound on what a modern pipeline may achieve, and no evaluation result from this corpus is presented as a real-user measurement.

Out of scope: real user content, private transcripts or mail of any person, the implementation of the measured features, and any claim about production behaviour. This leaf owns measurement and the gate; the leaves it measures own their own fixtures and must be runnable without it.

Interface and ownership: evals/follow-through/. It aggregates fixture packs contributed by the extraction, dedup and planning leaves, and it owns the metric definitions, the gate and the reporting format. It must be runnable from a clean checkout with synthetic data only.

Dependencies: D02 and D03 because the corpus needs extraction output and terminal-state semantics to be meaningful; the gate has nothing to measure before those produce rows.
