Acceptance scenarios: the gate fails when a decoy class starts producing auto-accepted commitments; the corpus is versioned so two runs are comparable and an incomparable pair is labelled; a provider swap re-runs the gate and records a per-metric delta; the correction-rate report refuses to display without its denominator and window; a simulated offline week asserts the burst count and the duplicate-notification count; and a run over the corpus from a clean checkout requires no account, no network and no private data.

Adverse and restart cases: a partially completed run reports the tests it did execute and marks the remainder as not run rather than reporting a green result; a corpus file that fails to parse fails the gate; and a flaky metric is re-run rather than averaged into a false pass.

Validation: the evaluation harness run itself is the check, over the versioned synthetic corpus, with the recorded comparison against the previous run. No executable command is claimed to exist at authoring time and no test is claimed to be implemented.

Privacy and authority: the corpus is synthetic and publishable, so the gate can run in the open repository. No private content, prompt text or personal detail may enter the corpus, and the harness holds no credentials.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on proactivity evaluation (non-public, no link); the corpus and rubric are proposals.

nodes.title: [D18] Sleep, offline and catch-up without notification bursts
nodes.body:
Problem and outcome: a laptop sleeps, a network drops, a flight lasts six hours, and the naive response is a burst of one alert per missed item at the worst possible moment, which is how users learn to silence an assistant permanently. The outcome is a resume path that catches up honestly, consolidates, and reports what it could not see, without ever shouting a backlog.

Scope and deliverables:
- The resume contract with the platform layer: what the service learns on wake, and the rule that a resume is treated as a normal trigger with a bounded budget rather than a special full scan.
- Ordering and budget: most recent first, with a wall-clock ceiling and an item ceiling, so a long absence degrades gracefully into a partial catch-up that states what remains.
- Burst collapse: when more than a configured number of items are found, the output is one consolidated message with counts and the top few items, and individual nudges are deferred into the normal windows. The collapse threshold and the consolidation format are owned here.
- Coverage honesty: an invalid cursor records its gap window and the catch-up names the uncovered period rather than reporting an empty success.
- Cross-device suppression: an item already acknowledged on another device before sleep is not announced again at wake.
- The no-resurrection rule: catch-up never re-opens or re-announces something the user already closed, dismissed or corrected, even if the missed period contains the source item that produced it.
- Degradation: a source unreachable at wake is marked as such in the coverage line, and the rest of the catch-up proceeds.
- Baseline inheritance: the first slice already guarantees that a resume cannot burst, because due boundaries are revalidated before firing and several items coalesce into one message. This leaf extends that guarantee to a multi-day absence, invalid cursors and cross-device suppression, and does not reimplement it.

Out of scope: power, login and background management (F13), voice session reconnect (F07), per-source cursor mechanics (the connector leaves), and the interruption policy itself (D10 owns whether an item may interrupt at all). This leaf owns the resume path and the consolidation behaviour.

Interface and ownership: core/proactivity/resume. It consumes the trigger loop, the reminder intents and the coverage rows, and it exposes a single catch-up summary plus an updated coverage state.

Dependencies: A03 for a lifecycle that defines what a resume is and can report the interrupted service state; D07 for the cursor and tiering machinery the catch-up drains; D10 because the consolidated message must respect quiet hours and the interruption budget rather than bypassing them.

Acceptance scenarios: a simulated seven-day offline period produces at most one notification and one coverage summary; an item acknowledged on another device before sleep is not re-announced; an invalid cursor records its window and the summary names the uncovered period; a wake during quiet hours yields the digest section and no sound; and a catch-up interrupted by a second sleep resumes from its cursor instead of starting over; a resume after a short sleep stays at one reminder, matching the first-slice guarantee rather than exceeding it.

Adverse and restart cases: a resume where the network is still unavailable leaves the cursor untouched and reports the attempt as unsuccessful rather than as an empty result; a clock jump after wake does not duplicate a boundary already processed; and a very large backlog that exceeds the budget stops, reports the remainder, and continues in the next window.

Validation: a future simulated-sleep test with a fake clock and a fake connector, asserting the burst count, the duplicate count, the coverage gap record and the no-resurrection rule. No executable command is claimed to exist.

Privacy and authority: catch-up reads only what the granted scope allows, keeps counts and references in its summary, and performs no effect. The consolidation message is a convenience, not permission to act.

Scope note: this leaf owns advanced catch-up behaviour; the basic sleep catch-up baseline belongs to D07 and D08 in M1.

Evidence: internal planning decisions on sleep and offline behaviour (non-public, no link); basic catch-up belongs to D07 and D08 in M1.

nodes.title: [F01] Native hotkey and menu bar shell
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Today there is no Mac entry point for Didi. A colleague needs to summon and dismiss the assistant with one familiar gesture and see at a glance whether it is idle, listening, working or muted. Outcome: a menu bar presence plus a user-configurable global hotkey that opens a lightweight conversation surface without disrupting the frontmost application.

**Scope / deliverables.** A menu bar status item exposing state (idle, listening, working, muted, needs attention) and a small menu (open, mute, settings, quit). Global hotkey registration with conflict detection and a clear rebind path. A panel or overlay window that appears near the active display, takes a single keyboard focus target, and returns focus to the previous application on dismiss. Toggle behavior and an escape-to-dismiss path. A launch-at-login toggle. A thin native Mac companion that communicates with the authoritative Node service over the versioned command, query and progress contract rather than embedding core logic.

**Out of scope.** Audio capture and playback (F03, F04), notification routing (F09), packaging, signing and updates (F15), and persona content (owned by the memory and persona track).

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the macOS application directory. The window and menu consume view models provided by other tracks through the shared local contract proposed in the contracts leaf; this shell holds no account, memory or commitment data of its own. Reuse an existing menu bar and hotkey library only if its maintenance burden and license are acceptable, per the foundation decision.

**Dependencies.** None. This is the first-slice entry point and must not wait on other tracks.

**Acceptance scenarios.** Pressing the hotkey opens the surface within the agreed responsiveness budget and dismissing it restores prior focus. A conflicting hotkey shows a specific message and offers rebinding rather than silently failing. A second press while open toggles closed. The window restores onto the display where the pointer and menu bar are active after a monitor is added or removed. The surface opens and closes with no network available. Quitting from the menu leaves no lingering process.

**Validation (future).** A native UI test that synthesizes the hotkey, asserts the surface appears and focus returns, and an adverse case with a pre-bound combination. A restart case asserting the chosen hotkey persists across a relaunch.

**Privacy and performance.** This layer reads no account or content data, writes no memory, and holds no secrets. Keep the shell resident footprint modest; the foundation leaf owns the measured energy budget.

**Evidence.** Public Apple platform documentation for global hotkeys, menu bar items and window focus; internal private baseline research (non-public, no link). No existing test command is claimed.

Under PLAN-R3 the companion hosts the shared web interface in its own web view (F23) and does not duplicate business screens in SwiftUI. It keeps the hotkey, the menu bar, window lifecycle, on-device speech, notifications, the credential store and the outbound service client.

nodes.title: [F02] Text conversation and async job cards
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Before voice is trusted, a colleague still needs a usable assistant. Outcome: a text conversation that streams responses, shows tool and job activity as cards, and lets the user keep working while a longer job runs, without the conversation blocking or losing its place.

**Scope / deliverables.** A conversation view with message history, streaming text rendering, and a composer that supports multi-line input and send. Visual job and tool cards that show kind, state (queued, running, waiting for approval, done, failed, cancelled), short progress, and the source or receipt for finished work. A way to expand a card to details and to cancel or approve inline. Reconnect-safe rendering so history is restored from the local store, not re-fetched from a model. Clear empty, error and offline states. Message-level copy and a stop-generation control. A MINIMAL inline memory affordance so the first slice can correct mistakes without a full review surface: the user can correct or drop a remembered fact from the conversation (for example "forget that"), and the change is applied through the owning memory service. This is the M1 minimum; the full memory, authority and action review surfaces land later in F11.

**Out of scope.** Voice capture and playback (F03, F04), the full review surfaces (F11), connector-specific card content (accounts and connectors track), and commitment scheduling (follow-through track).

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the view. Job and tool state arrives from the runtime track as view models over the shared local contract; this issue defines the card shape but not the job engine. The card vocabulary should be generic (kind, state, progress, receipt) so new sources do not require new UI code. Persistence of conversation text belongs to the memory track; this view renders what the store returns, and the inline correction calls the owning service rather than mutating memory locally.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F01 for the companion shell and on A19 for the command, query and progress contract. It coordinates with the runtime durable task progress leaf for the job states it renders and with the memory track for the inline correction, and it is the dependency of F09's minimal notification baseline. No shared migration is touched here.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A typed question streams an answer and finishes cleanly. A long job shows a running card, updates progress, and lets the user send another message meanwhile. Approving a waiting job from its card dispatches it once. Cancelling a running job moves it to cancelled and no late result is appended as success. Correcting a remembered fact in the conversation changes later recall, and no review surface is required for that first-slice correction. Killing and reopening the app restores the conversation and card states from the local store. With the model provider unreachable, the view shows an explicit error rather than a fake empty success.

**Validation (future).** A component test that feeds synthetic job-state fixtures through the card reducer covering running, approval, done, failed, cancelled and unknown-outcome states, plus a restart case rehydrating from stored fixtures and a correction case asserting the owning service was called.

**Privacy and performance.** Rendering must not log message bodies to crash reports. Cards must display receipts from the owning system, not reconstructed from memory.

**Evidence.** Internal private baseline research (non-public, no link); public desktop chat UI conventions. No existing command is claimed.

The conversation surface is the shared web interface (F19), hosted by the companion through F23. SwiftUI keeps only chrome, not a second implementation of the conversation.

nodes.title: [F03] Microphone, audio devices and permissions
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Voice is the primary surface, but a desktop app must request microphone access honestly and behave when devices change or permission is denied. Outcome: reliable capture with clear permission and device-selection behavior that never records without an explicit, visible state.

**Scope / deliverables.** Microphone permission request flow with an honest pre-prompt and a route to system settings when denied. Input device enumeration, selection and a live level indicator. Handling of default-device switches and device unplug during a session. A visible always-on recording indicator tied to capture state. Output device selection and a test tone. A mute control that is unambiguous. Audio format negotiation to the duplex adapter. Graceful degradation to text when no microphone is available or permission is denied.

**Out of scope.** The duplex protocol and barge-in (F04, F06), and packaging. Memory of audio belongs to the memory track.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the audio adapter. Capture feeds the voice adapter over a proposed contract; the adapter exposes capture state to the shell for the recording indicator. Prefer the platform audio framework and reuse only well-maintained audio helper components. Device selection is stored as local configuration, not in the shared store.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F01. Coordinates with the runtime lifecycle leaf for process-level audio session ownership.

**Acceptance scenarios.** On first use, the permission prompt appears with a clear reason; denying it leaves the app fully usable in text mode and offers a route to enable it later. Changing the default input device mid-session reroutes capture without crashing. Unplugging the selected device falls back to the system default and notifies the user. The recording indicator is visible whenever capture is active and never appears while muted. A restart preserves the chosen devices.

**Validation (future).** An integration test with a synthetic audio source and a fake permission service covering granted, denied and later-enabled states, plus a device-change case. No real audio is uploaded in tests.

**Privacy and performance.** Capture is local; audio is retained only per the memory track's policy. The indicator and mute state must reflect real capture, not a UI guess. Keep capture latency within the target set for the voice adapter.

**Evidence.** Public Apple audio and privacy permission documentation; internal private baseline research (non-public, no link).

Under the shared-interface decision, starting and stopping speech stays a native control. Recognised text travels through the service API and the page learns about it through its normal refresh and event stream. There is no inbound JavaScript authority bridge and the page receives no audio authority.

nodes.title: [F04] Gemini Live duplex adapter
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** The live voice experience needs a real-time duplex transport. Outcome: a Mac duplex voice adapter that opens a streaming session, sends microphone audio, receives spoken audio and text, executes tools through the local tool-turn path, and exposes a replaceable provider boundary. Gemini is the preferred first provider but must not be hardcoded.

**Verified provider behaviour (source claim, provider docs fetched 2026-10-09).** The current Live API documents two live models: a low-latency voice model that accepts no thinking level, and an extended-thinking model that takes low, medium or high with the minimal level unsupported. This reverses an earlier internal assumption, so the adapter must derive model capability from configuration and a probe, never from a baked-in default. Audio-only sessions are limited without compression (about fifteen minutes) and the underlying connection is about ten minutes; the server sends a go-away message before the end. Context-window compression with a sliding window extends a session, and session resumption is available. Input and output transcription can both be enabled in setup. An interruption is reported by the server, cancels the ongoing generation, discards pending function calls and reports their ids. Manual voice activity should use an end-of-speech silence threshold of at least 500 ms.

**Scope / deliverables.** A provider interface covering setup, audio frames, text, tool calls and responses, interruption signals and session restore. A Gemini Live implementation with endpoints, model id and voice config supplied as configuration. A capability probe. Bounded reconnection. A session-state machine (connecting, live, working, reconnecting, ended).

**Proof versus design.** This issue is design plus a provider-doc claim. The proof is the platform spike: a recorded two-sided audio round trip, both transcriptions arriving, a barge-in that stops playback, and timings. Treat latency targets as proposals the spike falsifies.

**Out of scope.** Barge-in detection and echo handling (F06), fallback provider behaviour (F05), session recovery UX (F07), and account coverage, which is unverified.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the adapter. It consumes the runtime replaceable-provider leaf for selection and budgets, and the tool-turn path for execution. Reuse baseline voice-session patterns conceptually, rewritten to public generic contracts with no copied prompt text.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F03 and on the runtime replaceable-provider leaf.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A session opens and a spoken turn returns spoken and text output with both transcriptions. A tool round-trips. A drop triggers a bounded reconnect and reports recovered state. A session that reaches the provider lifetime limit is extended by compression or resumed, and if neither is possible it ends with an explicit message. A configuration with an unknown model id fails fast. A provider that cannot do duplex voice offers the fallback path.

**Operating-system floor.** The observed spike host is macOS 26.6.2 arm64, but the minimum deployment target is a design decision to set and validate, not the current machine. On-device streaming speech recognition is only available on recent macOS, so any feature that depends on it raises the floor and must be stated.

**Function-calling note.** A non-blocking function declaration lets a call run while the conversation continues, and the response can carry a scheduling hint. This is a provider turn behaviour, not a durable task engine; durable jobs and reconciliation are owned by the runtime track, and the adapter must not claim durability from a provider flag.

**Privacy and performance.** Audio leaves the machine only under an approved session; egress policy is owned by the trust track. Speech-to-first-audio latency is a target to measure, not a claimed fact.

**Evidence.** Public provider live-api documentation; internal private baseline research (non-public, no link). Endpoint and account coverage unverified.

Validation note: a future comparison against the duplex path on a fixed synthetic turn set, checking the documented capability fallback; no command exists yet and no latency claim is made.

The duplex adapter remains native. The page never opens the audio device, never receives audio authority and never drives the session directly; it renders state that the service and the native control report.

nodes.title: [F05] Alternate speech and text fallback provider capabilities
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Cloud duplex voice may be unavailable, undesired for a sensitive turn, or unsupported by an alternate provider. Outcome: a fallback path that keeps Didi usable when the primary live voice provider cannot be used, using speech-to-text plus text-to-speech, or plain text, selected per capability and per user preference.

**Scope / deliverables.** A capability model describing what a configured provider can do (duplex voice, streaming text, tool use, speech in and out separately, languages). A fallback chain the user can see and reorder. An on-device speech-to-text path where the platform offers one, and a local text-to-speech path for spoken replies. A text-only mode. Clear indication in the surface of which mode is active and why. A preference for local speech on turns the user marks private, without forcing all traffic local. Per-mode latency and quality expectations stated as targets to measure.

**Out of scope.** The primary duplex adapter (F04), account coverage decisions, and the egress policy itself (trust track). This issue consumes policy, it does not define it.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the adapter directory. Fallback selection reads provider capabilities from the runtime provider leaf and egress policy from the trust track. On-device speech components should be reviewed for license and maintenance; a permissively licensed in-repo speech component identified in the alternatives research is a candidate to evaluate, not a decision.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F04 for the primary adapter and interface, and on the runtime replaceable-provider leaf for capability metadata.

**Acceptance scenarios.** With the primary duplex provider disabled, a voice turn still completes through speech-to-text plus text-to-speech. A user-triggered text-only mode suppresses audio in and out. If no speech component is available, the surface degrades to text and says so. A provider that claims a capability it does not deliver is caught by a probe and removed from the chain.

**Validation (future).** A capability-matrix test using synthetic provider descriptors and a fallback-selection test covering the full chain, plus an adverse case with an empty chain that must produce an explicit error.

**Privacy and performance.** A local speech option must be genuinely local; the surface must not imply privacy it cannot guarantee. Do not promise a latency that has not been measured.

**Evidence.** Public platform speech and accessibility documentation; internal private baseline research and alternatives research (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [F06] Barge-in, echo and cancel
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Natural conversation requires that the user can speak over the assistant and be understood, without the assistant hearing its own voice. Outcome: barge-in that stops playback promptly when the user speaks, echo handling so the microphone does not treat Didi's own audio as input, and an explicit cancel that stops the current turn cleanly.

**Scope / deliverables.** Voice activity detection that is sensitive to the user's speech but not to playback. Playback ducking or stop on detected barge-in. Echo cancellation, or a headphone-first guidance when cancellation is not reliable, with an honest residual hint. A cancel gesture that stops spoken output and the current turn, distinct from stopping a queued job. Turn-boundary rules so a cancelled turn cannot later append a success. A visible, testable difference between voice stop, queued-work stop and dispatched-action stop.

**Out of scope.** The duplex transport (F04), the job engine (runtime track) and the cancellation semantics of dispatched effects (runtime action receipts).

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the audio and interruption layer. It consumes the interruption signal from the duplex adapter and reports cancel intent to the runtime turn path. Cancellation categories map to the runtime vocabulary (voice stop, queued work, dispatched effect, unknown outcome, completed), which this issue renders but does not redefine.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F04. Coordinates with the runtime action-receipts leaf so a cancelled turn never reports a completed side effect.

**Acceptance scenarios.** Speaking over an answer stops playback within the target onset budget and the new turn begins clean. The assistant does not transcribe its own output as user speech under normal speaker use. Cancelling a spoken answer does not cancel a queued job. Cancelling a queued job does not cancel a dispatched action. A cancel during an in-flight tool call leaves an explicit unknown-outcome state rather than a false success. A restart after cancel leaves no orphaned audio playback.

**Validation (future).** A synthetic audio test injecting a barge-in over playback and asserting stop and turn reset, an echo case with a loopback fixture, and a cancellation-state test across the five categories.

**Privacy and performance.** Barge-in detection must run locally and must not upload audio beyond an active session. The onset budget is a target to measure, not a claimed number.

**Evidence.** Public platform audio documentation; internal private baseline research (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [F07] Session reconnect, expiry and recovery
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Live sessions drop or expire: provider outages, network changes, laptop sleep, connection lifetime limits and token expiry. Outcome: a session that resumes or rebuilds predictably, tells the user the truth about what survived, and never duplicates or resurrects finished work.

**Provider lifetime facts (source claim, docs fetched 2026-10-09).** An audio-only live session is limited without compression and the underlying connection has its own shorter lifetime; the server sends a go-away message before the end, and context-window compression with a sliding window extends a session. Session resumption is available. The adapter therefore treats the provider lifetime as a first-class reason to rotate or resume, separate from a network drop, and must handle go-away explicitly rather than waiting for a hard close.

**Scope / deliverables.** A session state model with distinct resume, rebuild and new-session outcomes driven by the close reason. A bounded retry policy with backoff and a user-visible reconnecting state. A continuation acknowledgment so the user hears the session is live rather than staring at a spinner. Continuity handling that restates a short recent context after a cold rebuild instead of relying on provider-side history. Token and session-expiry handling that re-authenticates locally and reports clearly when it cannot. A rule that a clean transport close is not user intent to end, and that a deliberate end differs from a pause. Recovery that restores in-progress job cards.

**Proof versus design.** The state machine and close-code matrix are design and are testable as a pure function. The behaviour of resumption and go-away against the real provider is a proof item owned by the platform spike. Do not assert measured recovery times.

**Out of scope.** The duplex protocol (F04), commitment scheduling, and memory summarization (memory track). The content of the continuity restatement is provided by the memory track; this issue renders and triggers it.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the client session controller. It consumes the runtime local-service lifecycle leaf for availability and the memory track for a continuity artifact. Resume versus rebuild should be a pure function of close code and session state, mirroring the internal baseline approach without copying private code.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F04. Coordinates with the runtime lifecycle leaf and the memory continuity leaf; no shared migration is touched.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A dropped provider socket triggers a bounded reconnect and the session reports recovered. A go-away message leads to a planned rotation or resume before the hard close. A deliberate quit does not auto-reconnect. On resume, the user hears a short acknowledgment and prior context is present. On a cold rebuild, a short recap appears and no duplicate answer is produced. An expired session re-authenticates or reports that the user must sign in. After a restart during a reconnect window, the state is consistent and no job card is duplicated.

**Operating-system floor.** Recovery must work on the minimum supported macOS, not only the current spike host; sleep and wake behaviour in particular must be validated on the target floor.

**Validation (future).** A pure-function test over a close-code, go-away and state matrix, plus integration tests with a fake transport covering drop, lifetime limit, sleep, expiry and deliberate end.

**Privacy and performance.** Recovery must not replay sensitive audio or content beyond the agreed continuity artifact. Retry backoff must avoid tight loops that drain battery.

**Evidence.** Internal private baseline research on reconnect contracts and public provider session-management documentation (non-public links omitted).

nodes.title: [F08] Voice, personality, localization and accessibility
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Didi must sound like a warm, direct, witty companion, not a generic assistant, and must be usable by people who rely on accessibility features or speak a language other than the author's. Outcome: a voice and delivery layer that applies the public persona specification consistently, adapts languages and accents reasonably, and meets accessibility expectations.

**Scope / deliverables.** Voice selection from the provider's available voices with a small named set and previews. Delivery configuration (pace, warmth) exposed as user preferences, not hidden biography. Language and locale handling for input, output and mixed-language turns, with a clear rule for which language is spoken. Accessibility: full keyboard operation of the conversation surface, screen reader labels and live regions for streaming and job states, reduced-motion behavior, and captions for spoken output. A public persona specification consumed as configuration so no model-specific biography is baked in. Copy and error text that stays in character without hiding failures.

**Out of scope.** Persona memory and personalization (memory and persona track), the persona content itself, and the duplex transport (F04).

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the presentation and locale layer. The persona specification is provided by the memory and persona track as a public, model-independent artifact; this layer renders it as voice and text settings. Do not copy any private prompt. Do not embed a per-model or per-person biography.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F04 and on the public persona specification leaf. Coordinates with the provider capability metadata for language and voice availability.

**Acceptance scenarios.** The chosen voice and delivery persist across restarts. A screen reader announces streaming text and job-state changes. Every control is reachable by keyboard. In a non-default locale, the assistant answers in the expected language and reads numbers and dates sensibly. Switching the model provider keeps voice and persona settings and re-maps to an available voice, reporting when an exact match is unavailable. A serious user intent suppresses wit for that turn without breaking character.

**Validation (future).** Accessibility checks (keyboard traversal, screen reader live regions) and a localization test with synthetic strings, plus a persona-application test asserting configuration is applied and no per-model biography is present.

**Privacy and performance.** Voice and locale preferences are local configuration. Do not ship a profile of any individual; all personalization comes from the user's own configuration and memory.

**Evidence.** Public accessibility and localization guidance; internal private baseline research (non-public, no link).

Under PLAN-R3 the visual orb and the voice character follow the authorized first-party Naya surface patterns rather than a newly invented interface, and accessibility and localization requirements apply to that shared surface.

nodes.title: [F09] Native notification-to-conversation
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Proactive follow-through is only useful if it reaches the user and can be acted on, and the first real-user slice already schedules a reminder and opens the conversation from it. Outcome: a native macOS notification that, when opened, brings up the conversation already grounded in the commitment or job that triggered it. Stage 1 is the minimal delivery and deep link for the first slice; Stage 2 adds coalescing, interruption levels and action richness.

**Stage 1 (minimal, phase M1, with F02).** Deliver a reminder notification through the notification center and deep-link its tap into the conversation at the right context, so the first slice can go reminder to conversation. Tapping a job-result notification opens the corresponding job card. Short, character-consistent copy. This stage ships the smallest path making the slice real; it does not yet need coalescing, action buttons or interruption-level tuning.

**Stage 2 (richness, phase M2).** Add coalescing so a backlog after sleep or offline time does not fire as a burst, snooze and dismiss actions that are recorded, job-result routing at scale, and a privacy setting controlling how much detail appears on the lock screen.

**Verified notification limits (source claim, platform docs).** The system offers several interruption levels. The active level presents immediately and can light the screen and sound. The passive level adds to the list without sound or screen wake. The time-sensitive level can break through notification summary and focus controls, but the user can revoke that ability, so the product must never promise it. A critical level that bypasses mute requires a special entitlement requested from Apple and is not a prerequisite for this product. Notification display is not proof that the user saw it.

**Interruption policy.** Use the passive or active level by default, and the time-sensitive level only when the user has left time-sensitive interruptions enabled, treating it as user-revocable. Do not build any requirement on the critical entitlement; a time-sensitive notification is the highest rung the product may rely on, and even that depends on the user's settings. Never claim the product always interrupts, overrides focus or guarantees delivery, and note that a scheduled notification is presented on wake, not during sleep.

**Out of scope.** Deciding what is urgent or when to notify (follow-through track), and the commitment content itself. This issue is the native delivery and routing surface.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the notification adapter. It consumes notification intents and urgency policy from the follow-through track and maps them to system notifications and deep links. Timing, urgency and quiet policy are owned elsewhere; this layer enforces platform constraints and reports what the system actually allowed.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F02 for the conversation surface and card rendering, and its Stage 1 baseline is the F09 work that the M1 slice needs. Coordinates with the follow-through reminder-outbox leaf for intents.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A due reminder produces one notification that, when opened, shows the conversation at the relevant commitment (Stage 1). Snooze and dismiss are available and recorded (Stage 2). After sleep or offline time, a backlog coalesces into few notifications (Stage 2). With focus or quiet mode on, delivery follows system behaviour and the app records that a seen state was not guaranteed. A job-result notification opens the matching card. Stale notifications for a resolved item are not shown. A user who has disabled time-sensitive interruptions still receives the default-level notification.

**Validation (future).** A test with a fake notification service asserting Stage 1 intent-to-notification and deep-link routing and Stage 2 level selection and coalescing, plus an adverse case where notification permission is denied and the app degrades to an in-app inbox.

**Privacy and performance.** Notification content must be terse and avoid sensitive detail on the lock screen. Coalescing must not poll the network on a blind timer.

**Evidence.** Public Apple notification and focus documentation; internal private baseline research and the platform notification matrix spike (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [F10] Clean-user onboarding, accounts and grants
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** The first real-user slice starts from a clean Mac account. Outcome: a guided first run that installs a local identity, connects the user's own accounts, and records explicit, revocable grants before any tool acts, with no dependency on a private checkout, an internal harness, or a paid developer account.

**Scope / deliverables.** A first-run flow: welcome, local identity creation, account connection (starting with one account), scope explanation, and a grant review. A local identity that is the basis for memory scoping, separate from any cloud account. Per-account, per-tool and per-resource grant requests that name the effect and the resource in plain language and are revocable. A visible list of what was granted and when. Honest failure states for denied or partial OAuth consent. A skip path so the assistant is usable with no accounts. No secret values shown or logged, and any stored credential handled through the platform keychain by handle.

**Out of scope.** The connector internals and the grant broker logic (accounts and trust track), and memory review (F11). This issue owns the onboarding and grant UX and the local identity presentation.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the onboarding surface. It consumes the identity map, the grant broker and the credential handle discipline from the trust track. The identity and grant model is defined there; this layer presents it and never invents authority. Reasoning text or tool output must never be able to create a grant from this UI.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F15 Stage A only, a locally built or ad-hoc pilot install, and on the trust track's grants and allowlists leaf. It explicitly does not depend on signing, notarization or a paid Apple developer-program enrollment, so the first slice is not gated on spending. It also uses the identity map leaf for a single account and degrades gracefully if only one account is connected, so that is not a blocking link.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A clean account completes onboarding on a pilot build and reaches the conversation with no account connected. Connecting one account requests exactly the scopes shown, and a denial leaves the app usable with a clear message. A grant names its effect and resource and can be revoked, after which the related tool fails closed. Restarting mid-onboarding resumes without duplicate account entries. No secret is displayed in the UI or written to logs. Onboarding completes without a paid developer account or a notarized build.

**Validation (future).** An onboarding flow test with a fake OAuth provider and grant service covering granted, denied, partial and revoked states, plus a restart-resume case, run against a Stage A build.

**Privacy and authority.** Grants are explicit and user-visible; a denied or revoked grant fails closed. Local data and control do not imply no approved cloud inference, but every egress is governed by the trust track's policy, which this surface only reflects.

**Evidence.** Public OAuth for installed apps and platform keychain documentation; internal private baseline research (non-public, no link).

Baseline note: onboarding requires the generic C01 identity, C12 grants and the Stage A install path in F15, and verifies the C02 Google path for the first-slice integration. A no-account path stays available: manual reminders work without Google, and non-Google sources never require a Google login.

nodes.title: [F11] Memory, authority and action review surfaces
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** A private assistant earns trust by showing what it remembers and what it can do. Outcome: user-facing review surfaces for stored personal memory, current grants and pending or completed actions, with correction and revocation available where the user expects them. These full surfaces land in M3, and that is acceptable only because the first slice already carries the minimum controls it needs.

**First-slice precondition (M1).** The M3 placement of this leaf assumes the M1 slice already provides the needed controls elsewhere: F10 provides explicit, revocable grants and a local identity, and F02 provides a minimal in-conversation correction or forget so the user can fix a remembered fact without a review surface. This issue must not be the first place a user can revoke or correct anything; if either M1 control is missing, this leaf pulls its minimum forward rather than leaving the slice without a remedy.

**Scope / deliverables.** A memory review view listing what Didi remembers about the user, grouped by kind, each item linked to its source, with edit, correct and forget actions. An authority view listing active grants by account, tool and resource, with revoke. An action view listing dispatched effects with their receipts, including unknown-outcome states that can be reconciled. Clear provenance labels distinguishing what the user said, what a source asserted, and what the assistant inferred. Empty and error states that do not imply data was lost. A short explanation of the local-versus-cloud data path for each entry.

**Out of scope.** Memory storage, consolidation and forget propagation (memory track), and grant enforcement (trust track). This issue renders and requests; it does not implement storage or enforcement.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the review views. It consumes memory inspector services and the grant broker from their owning tracks over the shared local contract. It must not keep a second copy of memory or authority state; it reads and requests changes. Every displayed item carries a source reference from the owning system.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F10 for onboarding and identity and on the memory inspector services leaf. Coordinates with the action-receipts leaf for dispatched-effect states.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A stored fact is corrected and a later recall returns the corrected value, with the previous value no longer asserted. Forgetting an item removes it and its derived uses, and the surface reports propagation. Revoking a grant disables the related action and the action view shows the change. An unknown-outcome action can be marked resolved with evidence. Opening a memory item shows its source. An empty review view reads as "nothing stored yet," never as an error.

**Validation (future).** A view test with synthetic memory and receipt fixtures covering present, corrected, forgotten and unknown-outcome states, plus a revocation propagation case.

**Privacy and authority.** The review surface must not expose one person's memory to another and must never mint authority. Reasoning text or untrusted tool output cannot create or widen a grant from here.

**Evidence.** Internal private baseline research on memory review and provenance (non-public, no link); public privacy transparency conventions.

nodes.title: [F12] Native computer-use controls, TCC and screen capture
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Didi can help with real work only if it can act on the Mac with the user's permission. Outcome: native computer-use controls behind explicit operating-system permissions, with a clear broad mode, honest residual risk, and receipts for every action.

**Scope / deliverables.** A permission walkthrough for accessibility, screen recording and automation prompts, with plain-language reasons and graceful behavior when any is denied. Bounded controls for the common cases (read active window content where allowed, capture a region the user selects, type into a focused field, click a named control) and an explicit broad computer-control mode that is separate, clearly labeled, and off until enabled. A visible indicator whenever control or capture is active. Per-action receipts. A kill switch and an obvious way to hand control back. Honest wording that same-user cooperation is not a security boundary.

**Out of scope.** The scoped command and filesystem tools and their broad-mode policy (runtime track), and the grant broker (trust track). This issue owns the native permission prompts, capture controls and the surface for the broad mode.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the computer-use UI and the platform permission bridge. It consumes the scoped-tool and broad-mode decisions from the runtime track and authority from the trust track. Screen capture and input synthesis use platform APIs; the action vocabulary maps to the runtime action-intent and receipt model so every action is auditable.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F10 for onboarding and grants and on the runtime scoped-tools leaf for the bounded tool surface and its explicit broad mode.

**Acceptance scenarios.** Enabling bounded control requests each OS permission with a clear reason; denying one leaves the bounded features that remain usable and disables the rest. Broad mode cannot be enabled without an explicit confirmation that states the residual risk. An active capture shows an indicator that cannot be hidden. Killing control stops capture and input immediately. Every executed action produces a receipt. A permission revoked in system settings disables the feature and the app reports it.

**Validation (future).** A permission-state test with a fake platform bridge covering granted, denied, revoked and broad-mode-off states, plus an adverse case asserting no action runs without a receipt.

**Privacy and performance.** Capture and input are local and only under an enabled mode. No blanket confirmation is required once granted, but sends and deletions are never quietly authorized.

**Evidence.** Public Apple accessibility, screen capture and automation permission documentation; internal private baseline research (non-public, no link).

The web page owns no operating-system permission. Screen capture, accessibility and automation grants belong to the native process, and same-user process separation is not a security sandbox.

nodes.title: [F13] Login, background, sleep and power
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** A desktop assistant must survive the real power lifecycle, and the first real-user slice must be honest about it immediately: while the Mac is asleep nothing runs and nothing is sent. Outcome: predictable background behavior where jobs, timers and voice sessions pause and resume without losing state. Stage 1 is the minimum sleep and offline honesty the first slice needs; Stage 2 adds battery, thermal and coalescing richness.

**Stage 1 (minimum, phase M1).** Explicit behavior on sleep, wake, lock and unlock for the local service, the voice session and due timers. A resume path that reports what happened while asleep: overdue work is reported, not silently fired. While the Mac is asleep it executes nothing and sends nothing, and the surface must not imply that a queued action ran. The runtime track's local-service lifecycle baseline owns the service-level plumbing and is the cross-reference for it; this issue owns the native platform bridge and the minimum honesty the slice needs. A launch-at-login and background-running preference. Honest handling of network loss with queued intent rather than silent failure.

**Stage 2 (richness, phase M2).** Battery and thermal awareness that pauses non-urgent work and says so. Coalescing of overdue work after sleep so reminders do not stampede. A rule that the app does not keep the machine awake except during an explicit active task, and shows when it is doing so. A wake-lock indicator.

**Out of scope.** The service lifecycle itself (runtime track, the cross-referenced baseline) and notification urgency policy (follow-through track). This issue owns the native lifecycle hooks and the surface that reflects pauses.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the platform lifecycle bridge. It consumes the local service lifecycle contract from the runtime track and the durable job queue and due timers, so pausing is a coordination, not a reimplementation. Do not build a second scheduler; report lifecycle events to the core and render the resulting state.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F01 and on the runtime local-service lifecycle leaf (which explicitly owns the Stage 1 baseline). It coordinates with the durable task queue and the follow-through timer processing; no shared migration is touched.

**Acceptance scenarios.** After sleep, overdue reminders are reported rather than fired all at once, and in Stage 2 they coalesce. A voice session interrupted by sleep reports a recoverable state on wake. A running job pauses during sleep and resumes without duplication. While asleep, the app executes nothing and sends nothing, and no surface claims an action ran. On low battery, non-urgent work pauses and the state is visible (Stage 2). With no network, an attempted action queues and reports rather than failing silently, and no blind heartbeat call is made. Locking the screen does not lose a mid-typing draft.

**Validation (future).** A lifecycle test with a fake power monitor simulating sleep, wake, lock, low battery and network loss, asserting honest reporting in Stage 1 and coalescing and no duplicate job execution in Stage 2.

**Privacy and performance.** Background behavior must respect the measured energy budget and never keep the machine awake without a visible active-task indicator. Do not poll on a blind timer.

**Evidence.** Public Apple power and app lifecycle documentation; internal private baseline research (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [F14] Opt-in wake phrase feasibility
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Hands-free activation is desirable but expensive and privacy-sensitive. Outcome: a feasibility spike and, only if it passes, an explicitly opt-in local wake phrase that activates listening without always transmitting audio.

**Scope / deliverables.** A written feasibility assessment covering on-device detection options, energy and memory cost, false-accept and false-reject behavior, microphone permission implications, and the honest privacy trade of an always-listening local detector. If viable, a local detector that runs only when the user has explicitly enabled it, with a visible always-on indicator, an immediate disable, and activation that opens the normal hotkey surface rather than a hidden channel. A stated rule that detection is local and no audio leaves the machine until the normal session begins.

**Out of scope.** The duplex transport (F04) and any claim of always-listening without an indicator. Do not promise bypassing focus or other OS protections.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the spike and, if approved, the detector integration. It uses the platform audio framework and, where a local model is needed, an on-device component reviewed for license and maintenance. It reuses the F03 capture path and F04 session start; it does not add a second audio pipeline.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F04 and F13. It is last in the native track because it is optional and its cost is unknown.

**Acceptance scenarios.** With the feature off, no audio is captured. When enabled, the indicator is always visible and disabling it stops detection immediately. A wake phrase opens the normal surface and a session; a near-miss does not. Energy cost during idle detection is measured against the budget and reported, and the feature is withdrawn if it exceeds it.

**Validation (future).** A detector test with synthetic audio fixtures for true hits and near-misses, plus an idle-energy measurement scenario. No persistent audio recording in tests.

**Privacy and performance.** The spike must state residual risk honestly and default to off. An unmeasured energy cost is a reason not to ship, not a detail to defer.

**Evidence.** Public platform audio and privacy documentation; internal private baseline research (non-public, no link). Cost is explicitly unmeasured.

nodes.title: [F15] Packaging, signing, notarization, update and uninstall
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** A colleague must be able to reach the first daily loop without waiting on paid distribution, and later be able to share a properly signed build. Outcome: one packaging issue with two clearly separated stages. Stage A is a locally built or ad-hoc pilot install for the first real-user slice. Stage B is signed and notarized shareable distribution, planned for the later integration phase and gated on a real developer identity and spending decision.

**Stage A (pilot install, phase M1).** Build an application bundle with a stable bundle identifier that runs on a developer or tester machine and supports onboarding, the hotkey shell, text conversation and the voice spike. Locally built or ad-hoc signing is acceptable at this stage, and notarization and Developer ID signing are explicitly not required. This build is a pilot for the team and testers only and is not shareable public distribution: an unsigned or ad-hoc build triggers operating-system warnings or refusal on other people's machines, and the issue must not present it as a smooth public install. Uninstall must work on the pilot. A documented minimum deployment target is set here as a design decision and validated on that target, not assumed from the current development machine; if a capability needs a higher floor, the raised floor is recorded.

**Stage B (shareable distribution, later, gated).** This stage needs a real Apple developer identity and a paid developer-program membership, which is the spending decision owned by the owner; the enrollment fee is taken from Apple's own enrollment page when the owner decides, not from any third-party figure. Stage B covers Developer ID signing, notarization, an opt-in update check that respects network and battery state and never blocks startup, upgrade and rollback for the local store, and an uninstall path that removes the application and, with consent, local data. Until the owner decides, Stage B is a documented spike with a fallback, never a blocked prerequisite.

**Proof versus design.** Stage A requires only a runnable pilot build. Stage B's identity and permission proof is a platform spike item: install a signed build, grant microphone, accessibility and screen recording, rebuild and re-sign with the same Developer ID, and confirm the grants persist with no re-prompt and that app-side checks agree with the system panes.

**Out of scope.** The local store schema and its migrations (runtime track) and store distribution. This issue owns packaging, signing and updates only.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns packaging and distribution. It consumes the runtime service start contract and the store migration entry point. Reuse standard platform notarization and update tooling rather than inventing a custom updater, subject to license review.

**Dependencies.** Stage A has no blocking dependency and is the first-slice prerequisite; F10 depends on Stage A only. Stage B has no hard dependency but requires the owner's enrollment decision. Packaging does not depend on mobile, and the daily loop must not be blocked behind F17.

**Acceptance scenarios.** Stage A: a clean test account installs the pilot build, launches it and reaches the first-run flow, with the documented minimum target respected, and uninstall removes it. Stage B: Gatekeeper accepts the notarized build; an update preserves local data and is reversible; uninstall removes the app and offers to remove local data; a build with a missing signature fails clearly in a developer context rather than shipping silently.

**Validation (future).** A packaging check producing a Stage A pilot artifact and, at Stage B, validating signature and notarization and running an upgrade-and-rollback test on a synthetic store. No paid continuous integration is added during planning.

**Privacy and performance.** No secrets, private keys or private prompts embedded in the bundle. Update checks are cheap and opt-in.

**Evidence.** Public Apple signing, notarization and enrollment documentation; internal private baseline research and the platform spike (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [F16] Companion device pairing, revocation and transport
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** A colleague may want a second device (a phone) to receive notifications or send commands to the Mac assistant. Outcome: a pairing flow where the active authority epoch stays single, every command from a companion device is queued, expired and validated, and revocation is immediate and complete.

**Scope / deliverables.** A device pairing flow using a short-lived code or an approved platform mechanism, with device naming and a visible paired-device list. A transport that carries notifications and queued commands only, never a second writable source of truth on the companion. Each queued command carries an idempotency key and an expiry; a command past expiry is refused and reported, never executed on wake. Command validation on the Mac before execution, with a clear rejection path. Per-device revocation that drops the device credential, drops its live sessions and invalidates its outstanding queued commands, and does not depend on the lost device cooperating. Pairing uses a per-device revocable credential; the secure-storage proof is chosen in implementation from supported platform mechanisms. Normal operation requires no mandated hardware-bound key and no monotonic assertion counter; where a platform offers attestation it may be used as additional evidence, but it is not a universal requirement. A synced or multi-device credential is treated as step-up verification only, never as the sole authenticator for a device.

**Out of scope.** The mobile client's own experience (mobile lane) and the Mac's store and policy (runtime and trust tracks). This issue owns pairing, revocation and the transport contract on the Mac side.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the Mac-side pairing and transport. It consumes the identity and grant model from the trust track and the command queue from the runtime track. The mobile lane owns the client; this issue defines the Mac-side contract. Do not build a second orchestrator or a second store. A versioned, authorized cache on the phone is allowed and is not a second authority; it never becomes a writable source of truth.

**Authority.** A companion command may act only on resources the local user's authority covers, and a recovery-only override is never standing authority. Where the harness supervision authority leaf already states this, this is a one-sentence cross-reference rather than a restatement.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F15 (the Stage A pilot artifact suffices). Coordinates with the mobile lane's protocol and the trust track's identity map.

**Acceptance scenarios.** Pairing shows the device with a name and last-seen time. A command is validated on the Mac and either dispatched or rejected with a reason; a command past its expiry is refused and reported and is not executed on wake. Dispatch is at most once under normal operation; if the process dies after dispatch, the outcome is marked unknown and reconciled, never silently retried as a duplicate effect. Revoking a device drops its credential, its live sessions and its queued commands immediately, without the lost device cooperating. A multi-device synced credential alone cannot authenticate after revocation. A versioned authorized cache on the phone is readable but cannot create authority.

**Validation (future).** A pairing, expiry and revocation test with a fake second device asserting idempotency-key dedup, expiry refusal, unknown-outcome reconciliation and immediate revocation, plus an adverse case where a revoked device retries.

**Privacy and performance.** The service holds the single writer role for the active authority epoch, and a device pulls scoped, expiring intents (C22) rather than receiving pushed commands. Companion commands never create grants and never bypass the grant broker. Transport is encrypted and keys rotate on revocation.

**Evidence.** Public platform pairing and secure storage guidance; internal private baseline research and the mobile lane review (non-public, no link).

Pairing uses the page's own scoped HttpOnly cookie and a same-origin CSRF flow as the authority for the browser session, while the service bearer stays in the native credential store and never enters JavaScript.

nodes.title: [F17] Mobile notifications and control with one Mac authority
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Mobile is secondary, but a phone is often where a colleague notices a reminder. Outcome: phone notifications and lightweight control that reflect the service state and act only through the active authority epoch, without the phone becoming a second assistant or a second source of truth.

**Scope / deliverables.** Phone notifications for reminders and job results, sourced from the Mac and mirroring the native notification policy. Lightweight controls: snooze, dismiss, retry, and send a short text command that is queued for the Mac. Clear indication on the phone when the Mac is offline or asleep and the action is queued rather than performed. A single-authority statement enforced in the contract: the phone holds no durable private memory, no grants and no worker state, and a versioned authorized cache plus an ordinary conversation UI cache is allowed but is not a source of truth.

**Semantics.** A queued or overdue command has an expiry; a stale command must be re-issued by the user, not replayed, and is refused and reported. Retry is a new request subject to current validation and policy, not a replay of a captured command. An approval names one pending action by a digest of its canonical plan, is single use and short lived, and is re-verified on the Mac with a refusal on any mismatch. Push delivery is best effort: a dropped or throttled notification must never become a delivered or seen state, and alerting push is the only viable channel.

**Sleep honesty.** While the Mac is asleep it executes nothing and sends nothing, so a proactive overnight notification requires an awake host; the authority epoch belongs to the service and is transferred explicitly when the host moves. The phone must not imply that a queued action ran.

**Out of scope.** The Mac-side pairing and transport (F16) and the mobile client build (mobile lane). This issue specifies the Mac-side mobile product contract and its policy alignment.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the Mac-side mobile contract, coordinated with the mobile lane. It consumes notification intents from the follow-through track and the identity and grant model from the trust track. Reuse the F09 notification policy so phone and Mac agree on urgency and quiet behavior.

**Authority.** A companion command may act only on resources the local user's authority covers, and a recovery-only override is not standing authority; cross-reference the harness supervision authority leaf rather than restating it.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F16 for pairing and transport. Deliberately later and secondary; it must not block the Mac beta.

**Acceptance scenarios.** A due reminder notifies on the phone and, when acted on, the change is reflected on the Mac. A command sent while the Mac is asleep queues and, on wake, is dispatched only if it is still within expiry; a stale one is refused and reported. A retry creates a new request and does not duplicate an effect. An approval for one action is refused if replayed or if the plan digest has changed. A throttled push produces no delivered or seen state. Revoking the phone stops notifications and commands. A duplicate delivery attempts no second external effect; where an outcome is unknown it is surfaced, not assumed done.

**Validation (future).** A contract test with a fake phone asserting expiry refusal, retry-as-new-request, approval digest binding, push no-false-delivered and offline queueing, plus a revocation case.

**Privacy and authority.** The phone displays only what the service sends and holds no durable private state or authority. Notification detail follows the user's privacy setting.

**Evidence.** Public mobile notification guidance; internal private baseline research and the mobile lane review (non-public, no link).

nodes.title: [F18] Windows port seam and conformance guide
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** A future Windows client should not require a rewrite of the product. Outcome: a documented port seam and a conformance guide that let a Windows implementation reuse the local core and contracts while replacing only the native platform layer.

**Scope / deliverables.** A written boundary between platform-neutral code (local core, contracts, memory, policy) and platform-specific code (hotkey, notifications, audio devices, permissions, packaging). A conformance checklist of behaviors a Windows implementation must satisfy (hotkey and menu presence, text conversation, voice adapter, barge-in, session recovery, notifications, onboarding, grants, review surfaces, packaging). A list of the platform APIs that must be substituted, including the companion client and the message and notification route, so the port map covers the product as described. Where the core already runs portably, a minimal proof that it starts on a non-Apple host. Explicit non-goals: no Windows runtime dependency in the Mac product and no second core.

**Boundary rule.** A platform call made behind an explicit adapter interface is allowed; a platform-neutral module that imports a platform API directly is a violation. The boundary check scans neutral directories and fails on a direct platform import while permitting the adapter interface.

**Out of scope.** Building a shipping Windows client. This is a seam and a conformance guide, not a port. If the companion client is deliberately excluded from this seam, the guide states that explicitly rather than leaving it out silently.

**Interfaces, ownership and reuse.** Master E owns the seam document and the conformance guide, coordinating with the foundation leaf that decides the host and runtime. The platform-neutral core is owned by the runtime track; this guide must not duplicate it. Reuse the same local contracts; do not fork them for Windows.

**Dependencies.** Depends on F15 Stage A for a defined package shape and on the foundation host and runtime decision for the neutral boundary.

**Acceptance scenarios.** The conformance guide lists each required behavior with a testable statement, and a reader can map every Mac platform call to a Windows substitute, including the companion client and the message and notification route. The boundary check flags a platform import in neutral code and permits the same call behind an adapter. A non-Apple start attempt of the core either succeeds or fails with an explicit, documented reason.

**Validation (future).** A boundary check that scans neutral directories for platform imports and fails on a violation, plus a minimal core-start smoke on a non-Apple host where available.

**Privacy and authority.** The port preserves the same privacy and authority model; the guide states that permissions and credential storage are platform-specific but the policy is shared. No secrets or private paths in the guide.

**Evidence.** Public Windows platform documentation and the platform portability review; internal private baseline research and the mobile lane review (non-public, no link). Windows is a future seam, not a shipping target.

nodes.title: [F19] Responsive PWA shell over the service contract
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** The user wants to reach the assistant from a phone
browser while the laptop stays the immediate priority. Outcome: an installable progressive web
application shell that renders conversation and job state from the service contract at laptop,
tablet and phone widths.

**Scope and deliverables.** An application shell with a manifest and installability metadata,
a conversation view, a job and progress view fed by the progress stream, responsive layout
rules for three breakpoint classes, a connection state indicator that distinguishes loopback
from a remote service, and an offline notice that states what is unavailable offline.

**Out of scope.** Domain logic in the browser, a second backend, offline writing of private
records, and any browser storage of session content or credentials.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the shell and the layout rules. F02 owns
the conversation surface and its interaction pattern, A19 owns the command, query and progress
contract, F20 owns the cache policy, A23 owns endpoint configuration. The shell reuses the A02
envelopes and A19's endpoints rather than defining its own.

**Dependencies.** F02 for the conversation surface and A19 for the service contract.

**Acceptance and adverse.** A phone browser opens the installed shell, lists jobs and shows live
progress. Adverse scenarios: the service goes away and the shell shows a clear disconnected state
rather than a blank page; a slow progress stream does not block the conversation view; the shell
loads at a narrow width without horizontal scrolling.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario drives the shell against a loopback service
at three viewport widths and records the measured layout pass and error counts, the install
prompt outcome and the reconnect time after the service restarts. The report names the breakpoint
class, the viewport size and the observed result for each case rather than a single pass claim.
Public references: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Progressive_web_apps and
https://web.dev/responsive-web-design-basics/. Privacy baseline: the shell ships with synthetic
fixtures and holds no private record in browser storage.

PLAN-R3 scopes the tonight proof: a laptop browser at a phone-width viewport renders the shared shell and the companion hosts the same shell in its own web view. A physical phone is a later milestone owned by F21 and is not claimed tonight, because reaching a phone requires a bound local network interface and pairing, neither of which is in tonight's slice. The device path itself is proved later over an explicitly bound and paired local network path; the laptop loopback address is never a phone's path.

nodes.title: [F20] Browser shell-only cache and private-data offline policy
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** A browser client on a shared or stolen device must not
keep a readable copy of private assistant data. Outcome: a serviceworker that caches the shell
only, plus a written offline policy for private data.

**Scope and deliverables.** A serviceworker that caches the shell, the manifest and static
assets, and never caches a command, a query result or a progress payload; a cache partitioning
rule that is cleared on sign-out; an offline policy stating that private records are read-only
and unavailable when the service is unreachable; a documented list of what may be stored in
browser storage; and a cache-eviction test.

**Out of scope.** Offline reading of commitments, sessions or recall results, background
synchronisation of private data, and any index that persists query results in browser storage.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the cache policy and the offline rule.
F19 owns the shell, C15 owns the data classes and the egress decision, A19 owns the endpoints,
F21 owns the Android path. The policy is expressed once and reused by every browser client.

**Dependencies.** F19 for the shell and C15 for the data classes.

**Acceptance and adverse.** After a session, browser storage contains no private record. Adverse
scenarios: a query response is captured by the serviceworker and the test that inspects cached
responses fails loudly; the shell is cached and still loads offline while private views show the
unavailable state; signing out clears the partitioned cache.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario inspects cache storage after a scripted
session and measures the count of cached private payloads, which must be zero, and separately
records the cached shell size so the shell-only rule is demonstrated rather than asserted. The
scenario also signs out and re-inspects, and reports the measured residual entry count. Public
references: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Service_Worker_API and
https://web.dev/service-workers-cache-storage/. Privacy baseline: the inspection fixture uses
synthetic content and no record from a real conversation.

nodes.title: [F21] Android installable access path on the same contract
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Android is a client the user named, and the cheapest
credible path is the same service contract installed from a browser. Outcome: a documented,
tested Android access path that adds no second backend.

**Scope and deliverables.** Installability on Android with the manifest and icons, a
verification that the same command, query and progress endpoints work over the network from the
phone, a pairing step reusing F16 and F17 that grants the phone only what it needs, a documented
limitation list for platform restrictions such as background execution, and an evaluation note
recording whether a native wrapper is ever needed and on what evidence.

**Out of scope.** A native Android rewrite, push infrastructure beyond the platform grant, and
any path that gives the phone authority over the laptop's operating system.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the Android access path and its
limitations. F19 owns the shell, F16 owns pairing and transport, F17 owns notification and
control, A23 owns endpoint configuration. The access path reuses the shell rather than forking a
mobile client.

**Dependencies.** F19 for the shell and F17 for the mobile control surface.

**Acceptance and adverse.** A phone installs the shell, pairs, and completes a query. Adverse
scenarios: the phone is out of range and shows the unavailable state instead of failing silently;
a background restriction stops progress updates and the indicator says so; revoking the phone
pairing removes its access.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario installs the shell on an Android browser,
pairs it, completes a query, rotates the pairing and records the measured success of the query,
of the revocation and of the post-revocation refusal. It reports the platform version and the
observed background-execution restriction so the limitation list is evidence rather than
speculation. Public references:
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Progressive_web_apps/Guides/Making_PWAs_installable
and https://developer.android.com/guide/webapps/. Privacy baseline: pairing fixtures use
synthetic identities.

nodes.title: [F22] Client contract conformance across breakpoints
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** Several clients now speak the same contract, and drift
between them is the realistic failure. Outcome: one conformance suite any client can run against
the declared endpoints.

**Scope and deliverables.** A conformance suite covering envelope version negotiation, command
acceptance, query shape, progress stream ordering, error classes and reconnect; runs at laptop,
tablet and phone breakpoints; a report of the measured pass count per client; a rule that a
contract change updates the suite before updating a client; and a documented expectation for how
a client pins the contract version it was tested against, so a later drift is visible in the
report instead of in a user report.

**Out of scope.** Per-client private endpoints, divergent error handling per client, and any
conformance claim without a recorded run.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the conformance suite. A19 owns the
contract, A23 owns endpoint configuration and discovery, F02 and F19 own their surfaces. The
suite is shared rather than forked per client.

**Dependencies.** F19 and F21 for the client surfaces and A23 for endpoint configuration.

**Acceptance and adverse.** Every declared client passes the suite against a loopback service.
Adverse scenarios: a client is pinned to an unsupported contract version and the suite reports
the negotiation failure; a reordered progress stream is detected; a client that swallows an
error class fails the suite rather than passing silently.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario runs the suite against each client and
records the measured pass and fail counts per breakpoint, together with the contract version each
client negotiated. A run that reports only a boolean result is not sufficient: the report names
each case, its expected class and its observed class. Public reference:
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110 for the status classes exercised. Privacy baseline: the
suite fixtures are synthetic and no private record is used.

nodes.title: [F23] Shared web UI host in WKWebView with a native-only control surface
nodes.body:
**Trigger and outcome.** The council decision and the user's reuse requirement ask for one web interface, not two: the same responsive orb and conversation surface the browser loads is displayed inside the Mac companion. Outcome: the companion hosts that page in its own web view and exposes no privileged bridge into the native process.

**Scope and deliverables.** A web view configured with a nonpersistent data store, an exact configured scheme, host and port, main-frame navigation only, and no unexpected redirects, popups, downloads, subframes or arbitrary remote content. A native bootstrap that establishes the page's own scoped HttpOnly session and a same-origin CSRF flow, while the service bearer stays in the native credential store and never enters JavaScript. Native chrome for the unavailable, setup and retry states, which preserves a draft and reports the configuration fault. No inbound JavaScript-to-native handlers and no generic native RPC, and speech starts and stops from a native control only.

**Out of scope.** A second implementation of the conversation in SwiftUI, an injected bearer or token in page scope, a native message handler that grants an effect, and any claim that same-user process separation is a security sandbox.

**Interfaces and ownership and reuse.** This task owns the web view host contract and the native unavailable state. F01 owns the companion shell, F19 owns the shared page, F03 owns the native speech control, F16 owns pairing, A19 owns the service contract, C15 owns what may leave the process. The orb and interaction surface reuse the authorized first-party Naya patterns through F19 rather than being rebuilt here.

**Dependencies.** F01 for the companion, F19 for the shared page and A19 for the service contract.

**Acceptance and adverse.** The page loads only from the configured origin, a navigation to any other origin is refused rather than followed, and the companion reports an unavailable service without losing a draft. Adverse scenarios: a remote page attempts a redirect to another origin and is blocked; a page script attempts to reach a native capability and finds no handler to call; the web content process is terminated and the companion restarts the view and reports a clean state; a popup or download attempt is refused.

**Validation and evidence.** A future test scenario exercises the real web view and records the measured cookie and navigation behaviour, the origin-refusal count and the recovery time after a content-process termination. Open questions about cookie persistence across termination and about losing a graphics context are treated as test cases, not as assumed facts, and only a test-owned surface may be terminated, never a broad sweep of web content processes. No live microphone capture or audible playback runs in an automated check. Public references: https://webkit.org/ and https://developer.apple.com/documentation/webkit/wkwebview. Privacy baseline: the fixture serves synthetic content from a configured origin.
